title: France probes suspected leaks of confidential information to Le Pen’s far-right party
summary: French authorities are investigating whether a former Interior Ministry official leaked confidential information to Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally
story: French authorities are investigating whether a former Interior Ministry official leaked confidential information to Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally

PARIS -- French authorities are investigating whether a former Interior Ministry official leaked confidential information about judicial investigations to Marine Le Pen' s far-right National Rally, adding to the party's legal troubles ahead of next year's presidential election.

Hugues Moutouh, a former general secretary in the ministry, is suspected of sharing information about investigations relating to the financing of the National Rally’s 2022 and 2024 election campaigns, according to Le Monde newspaper.
Moutouh now serves as prefect of the Centre-Val de Loire region, representing the central government there.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez confirmed Friday that a judicial investigation has been opened, and summoned Moutouh for a meeting.

The Paris prosecutor’s office confirmed to The Associated Press it opened a judicial investigation “into alleged breaches of professional confidentiality, breaches of investigative secrecy, and the handling of information obtained through these offences.” It said no one has been formally handed preliminary charges at this stage.
It added that investigators conducted searches at the party’s headquarters on Nov. 9.
Le Pen has not commented on the case.
“If the facts are confirmed, they are obviously very serious,” Nuñez told BFM TV.

Less than six months before next year’s election, it’s the latest controversy to hit Le Pen’s party following accusations in September that her running mate, Jordan Bardella, made antisemitic remarks as a young party member.

The 31-year-old Bardella, who Le Pen says will be her prime minister if she wins the presidency in May, vigorously denied authorship of the comments about supposed Jewish banking monopolies and other antisemitic conspiracy theories that investigative website Mediapart attributed to him.

Le Pen will run for the French presidency next year despite being sentenced in July to wear a court-ordered electronic monitor for embezzlement. The decision by the 57-year-old veteran of three presidential races set up a fourth campaign like no other: potentially seeking votes while subject to monitoring and with a judge possibly deciding how, and for how long, the punishment is applied.
Le Pen has appealed the ruling to France’s highest court and she believes she won’t be subjected to monitoring at all.

According to opinion polls, the nationalist Le Pen is the front-runner to replace Emmanuel Macron, ahead of hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Other aspirants include two former prime ministers of Macron. Candidates from the moderate left and right, the Green party and conservatives are also running, among others.

title: Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation, Polish leader says
summary: Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation as European militaries hold drills, Polish leader says
story: Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation as European militaries hold drills, Polish leader says
WARSAW, Poland -- Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation as European militaries hold drills, Polish leader says.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.

The Polish military is investigating a “suspected violation” of the country's airspace near its border with Ukraine after officials sought to retrieve an unidentified object that had apparently crash-landed in Poland on Friday morning.

The incident came against the backdrop of Russian attacks in Ukraine that killed three people, injured nine others and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said he believes the incident was another provocation by Russia and timed to European military exercises underway in Poland.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he would convene a meeting with government ministers, military commanders and the head of security services in response. Officials said it was too early to tell what the object was.

The potential crash site is near the village of Nowy Lipowiec, roughly 60 kilometers (37 miles) from the Poland-Ukraine border. Nearby schools suspended classes for the day, according to Polish news agency PAP.
Images from closed-circuit cameras and a mobile phone in the region collected by PAP showed a large, loud explosion in a bright flash that appeared to take place in a wooded area.
Military helicopters and rescue vehicles were spotted in the vicinity, and police set up temporary roadblocks as an investigation was underway.

The location is also about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from where thousands of European troops were taking part on Friday in an unprecedented military exercise in southeastern Poland to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.

title: Saudi Arabia intercepts more Yemen Houthi missiles and drones, and other Mideast news
summary: Saudi Arabia says Iran-backed Houthi rebels have fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom
story: Saudi Arabia says Iran-backed Houthi rebels have fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom
Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom, days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen.

Meanwhile, in Iraq, troops deployed to a militia stronghold south of the capital Baghdad after the government apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.
Iraqi security forces set up a command headquarters on the outskirts of the Jurf al-Sakhar area south of Baghdad, long a stronghold of an Iran-backed militia, Kataib Hezbollah, on Friday.
The area had been the source of rising tensions, with the government calling for the militia to withdraw amid allegations that it was using the area for oil smuggling.
Kataib Hezbollah had threatened to fight security forces if they attempted an incursion.

Two Iraqi officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, said the government and Kataib Hezbollah had reached an agreement under which security forces could enter but the militia would not immediately withdraw.

The deal followed negotiations facilitated by Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Quds Force, a branch of the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard that's responsible for operations outside Iran and is key to Iran’s influence and ties to allies across the Middle East.

Under the agreement, the Iraqi army, federal police and police tied to the energy sector will be deployed in the area. In a compromise, the deployment will also include fighters from the Popular Mobilization Forces, a collection of mostly Shiite armed groups close to Iran that are officially part of Iraq’s security forces.
Kataib Hezbollah would withdraw its fighters within a month.
— By Qassim Abdul-Zahra

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said the kingdom intercepted five drones and one ballistic missile that targeted it on Friday morning. Riyadh, the kingdom's capital and largest city, was among the targets.

The interceptions marked the latest Houthi attempts to strike Saudi territory and came a day after the Iran-backed rebels said they had targeted Saudi airports, air bases and Riyadh’s financial center.
Saudi Civil Defense has sent out 13 emergency alerts since Thursday, warning the public of potential incoming strikes or debris from interceptions.

The Houthis did not immediately comment or claim Friday’s attacks. But they traded threats Friday to strike key ports in each other’s territories, marking the latest escalation between the rebels and the kingdom.
Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia launched a major air campaign across Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
Abdul-Zahra reported from Baghdad, Khaled from Cairo and Metz from Jerusalem.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

title: Workers and students protest across Europe as a strike in Italy disrupts services
summary: Workers and students are protesting across Europe on Friday as a nationwide strike disrupted transport and school services in Italy and demonstrators gathered in several countries to press demands on issues ranging from wages and living costs to educat...
story: Workers and students are protesting across Europe on Friday as a nationwide strike disrupted transport and school services in Italy and demonstrators gathered in several countries to press demands on issues ranging from wages and living costs to educat...

ROME -- Workers and students protested across Europe on Friday as a nationwide strike disrupted transport and school services in Italy and demonstrators gathered in several countries to press demands on issues ranging from wages and living costs to education and military spending.

In Italy, the 24-hour strike called by the CGIL trade union brought demonstrations to more than 100 cities, from Milan and Turin in the north to Naples, Palermo and Rome. Protesters denounced stagnant wages, rising living costs and what organizers described as the government’s failure to strengthen public services and worker protections.

The labor action coincided with an International Day of Student Mobilization, with organizers planning demonstrations in more than 45 Italian cities. Student groups joined workers in calling for greater investment in education, measures to ease the cost-of-living crisis and policies aimed at reducing inequality.

The protests were part of a wider wave of labor and student activism across Europe. In Croatia, students boycotted classes and staged protests in about a dozen cities, demanding greater investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.

In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more spending on education and less on weapons. Police dispersed the event after reported disturbances, saying officers used pepper spray and made several arrests.

Meanwhile in Germany, demonstrators gathered to call for greater education funding and to oppose a possible return to compulsory military service. The rallies came weeks after protests on Oct. 31 that drew thousands into the streets, descending into violent incidents in some cities.
Despite their different focuses, the protests across European countries reflected common concerns about living standards, public investment, education and government spending priorities.

The strike in Italy covered both the public and private sectors. Public transportation services were reduced or disrupted in several cities, while schools and some health facilities were also affected. Planned strikes by air transport workers were canceled for Friday, though separate walkouts involving airport personnel remain scheduled for Sunday at Milan and Venice airports.

Authorities deployed additional police in several Italian cities where multiple demonstrations took place. Alongside the CGIL action, grassroots unions including Cobas organized separate strikes and marches, adding to the scale of the nationwide mobilization.
The protests also took on a political dimension, with opposition leaders joining demonstrations and criticizing Premier Giorgia Meloni’s government over wages and social spending.
Speaking at the conclusion of a rally in Rome, CGIL Secretary-General Maurizio Landini said more than 1 million people had participated in demonstrations across the country.
“The squares are full, and all generations are in the streets,” Landini told supporters. “It is a day that does not divide but unites.”

Organizers said the common thread linking the labor and student protests was a call for policies that put jobs, public services and living standards at the center of government priorities. Many demonstrators were carrying banners calling for peace and increased investment in welfare, schools and health care.
— AP journalists Geir Moulson in Berlin and Relja Dusek in Zagreb contributed to this report.

title: Russian attacks on Kyiv kill 3, cripple bridges and cut power
summary: Russia has launched missiles and drones across Kyiv, killing three people and injuring nine
story: Russia has launched missiles and drones across Kyiv, killing three people and injuring nine

KYIV, Ukraine -- Russia launched missiles and drones across Kyiv overnight that killed three people, injured nine others and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure, local authorities said Friday.

The attacks came hours after President Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate against Ukraine for three aerial attacks this week on the vital Kerch Bridge, which links occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland.

“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters Thursday in China, where he attended a summit with the Chinese and U.S. presidents. Putin said the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” and vowed to rebuild.

The Kyiv City Military Administration said the attack struck four districts of the capital. The attack caused widespread electricity disruptions. Energy provider DTEK said parts of the Pecherskyi, Solomianskyi, Holosiivskyi, Dniprovskyi and Darnytskyi districts were without power following the strikes.

Non-residential buildings were damaged in the Obolonskyi and Holosiivskyi districts, while transport and logistics infrastructure was hit in the Podilskyi and Darnytskyi districts, it said in a statement.
Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a ballistic missile attack damaged the Podilskyi Bridge, forcing authorities to close traffic from the right bank to the left bank of the Dnipro River.
The Darnitskyi Bridge was also damaged, he said.

A further strike hit the Southern Bridge, where traffic remains restricted. Only vehicles weighing up to 10 tons traveling from the left bank to the right bank, and public transport weighing up to 18 tons, are being permitted, he said.
Klitschko urged residents to avoid traveling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary. He asked businesses and institutions to arrange remote working wherever possible.

title: Myanmar dismisses the UN court's ruling on its responsibility for Rohingya genocide as 'unfair'
summary: Myanmar’s government has dismissed a landmark judgment by the United Nations’ top court finding the country guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority as “unfair.”
story: Myanmar’s government has dismissed a landmark judgment by the United Nations’ top court finding the country guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority as “unfair.”

BANGKOK -- Myanmar’s government on Friday dismissed a landmark judgment by the United Nations’ top court finding the country guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority as “unfair,” while opponents called upon the international community to follow through to ensure justice is done.

Khine Khine Soe, spokeswoman for President Min Aung Hlaing, noted that judges had only voted nine-to-six on Thursday to find Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya in a brutal 2017 military operation.
“Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she told reporters in the capital Naypyitaw. “So it was not a decision made unanimously. I would say that it was unfair.”

The ruling by The Hague-based International Court of Justice, or ICJ, was the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide. Myanmar’s government has denied the allegation, claiming it acted against insurgents in the 2017 military operation in northern Rakhine state.

The case focused on the military's so-called “clearance operations” in Rakhine state in 2017 when the democratically-elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi was in power. Min Aung Hlaing, who was commander in chief at the time, seized power from Suu Kyi in 2021 and has since consolidated his control of the government, being elected president earlier this year in a vote critics said was neither free nor fair.
The country is now embroiled in a bloody civil war, with pro-democracy and other militias fighting against the military.

The militant Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, or ARSA, whose attacks in 2017 against government outposts in Rakhine State were the trigger for the Myanmar military’s devastating crackdown, called the ruling an “important step towards justice" in a statement on Telegram.
The court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya in the campaign in which the military was accused of committing mass rapes and killings, and razing thousands of homes.

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

Nay San Lwin, an activist with the Arakan Rohingya National Council, who now lives outside Myanmar, said this was just the “first victory on our path to our final one: returning to our homeland and living there in peace and dignity.”
“Without action and support from the international community, the court’s order will remain only a declaration,” he told The Associated Press. “Every country must help in whatever way it can.”
ARSA stressed that refugees have to be allowed to return home safely and that those responsible must face justice.

“We call upon the United Nations and the international community to ensure that Myanmar complies with the Court’s judgment and that justice is not left on paper,” the group said in a statement signed by “Ustad Khalid Junun,” described as its chief of general staff.
The Rohingya Solidarity Organization, or RSO, a rival militant group, issued a similar statement.

ARSA and the RSO have been marginalized since 2017, by suppression from Myanmar authorities and infighting. They are now involved in three-way fighting in Rakhine, where the Arakan Army, a Buddhist-dominated group seeking autonomy for the state, is battling the Myanmar military but has also been accused of targeting the Rohingya.
The Arakan Army did not respond to a request for comment on the court decision.

In its ruling, the court ordered Myanmar to commit to allowing Rohingya “safe, voluntary and dignified return to their place of residence.” It also ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish people found to have committed genocidal acts and to pay compensation to Rohingya. The amount will be decided in later court proceedings.
Khine Khine Soe did not address those demands, but it was widely seen as unlikely that Myanmar would comply. She said Myanmar would reply once it reviewed the lengthy court documents.
"Since this is an international case, we will make our position known,” she said.

She also questioned the court's jurisdiction to impose conditions, and referenced a declaration on Thursday by U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at their historic trilateral meeting in China, in which they said “ the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.”

“The main point is that the ICC and similar international institutions should not abuse their judicial authority,” Khine Khine Soe told reporters. “Given that three (of the) world’s leading nations have issued statements on this matter ... you can think about it for yourselves.”

China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Friday that while the country stood ready to “play a constructive role in advancing the repatriation of displaced people from Rakhine state, ”China has concerns over issues such as jurisdiction overreach and broad interpretations, and we believe such practices are not conducive to resolving disputes."

Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government, the main organization coordinating opposition to military rule in Myanmar since the 2021 army takeover, welcomed the ICJ ruling, saying it respected the authority of the court and its judgment.
It also stressed that the pursuit of justice for the Rohingya must be accompanied by efforts to end the military’s ongoing violence against civilians across Myanmar.

title: Xi projects China’s global influence after hosting Trump and Putin at APEC
summary: China’s President Xi Jinping has emerged from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with a diplomatic win, reinforcing his global standing despite limited substantive progress
story: China’s President Xi Jinping has emerged from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with a diplomatic win, reinforcing his global standing despite limited substantive progress

BANGKOK -- Results matter in the international arena, but so do optics. This week’s high-level meetings in China gave President Xi Jinping a win, reinforcing his image as a central player in global diplomacy.

As host of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday and Thursday, Xi welcomed the leaders of 21 nations representing some of the world’s largest economies that account for about 60% of global economic activity. He also convened the first formal gathering of the three biggest nuclear powers: the United States, Russia and China.

“History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace, and when they engage in confrontation the world is thrown into turmoil,” Xi said on Thursday before the start of closed-door discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Our three countries should set an example by working together to address global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability and make greater contributions to human progress,” he added.

The summit in China's capital city was seen as emblematic of the nation's superpower status. The trilateral meeting on Thursday produced no major breakthroughs, but the image of the three leaders seated at an enormous round table with Xi at the center and Trump to his left and Putin to his right will become part of diplomatic history.

“For most, the image was a suggestion that the world increasingly revolves around Beijing’s power and preferences,” Rush Doshi, director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in an article for the council. “And for U.S. allies in particular, it was unsettling because it suggested that Washington will prioritize engagement with the other great powers over that with its own partners.”
“Xi’s clearest diplomatic gain in Shenzhen was bringing Trump and Putin to the same table,” said Yaqi Li, a Chinese foreign policy researcher at the ISEAS — Yusof Ishak Institute.

China positioned itself as a force for global stability and a go-to talking point in recent years. Xi started the meeting with Trump and Putin with a reminder of how the three countries fought together in World War II.
“History is the best textbook,” Xi said, presenting the talks as a way to push for peace for humanity. “We must remember history, learn from it and work together to shape the future.”
The meeting resulted in a joint declaration that was light on commitments and did not tackle major issues in a substantive way.

“They're using this opportunity … to highlight that China is a great power, and they're in a different status relative to other countries,” said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.

Xi and Trump held their third meeting this year, highlighting the personal rapport they have built that both men said was important to the bilateral relationship between their nations. China's government highlighted the “constructive strategic stability” of the relationship while Xi commended the U.S. president for his role.
“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi told Trump.

There were no announcements about existing trade issues between the countries such as U.S. complaints that China has not fulfilled its commitment to buy from U.S. farmers and export more rare earth materials. Nor were there announcements about the Board of Trade and the expected framework to allow trade in nonsensitive goods worth $30 billion on each side.

It was unclear if officials taking part in a diplomatic channel to discuss artificial intelligence issues met in Shenzhen, said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
However, “AI seems to be the one area where some progress has been made, with China affirming its concerns about safety and security and welcoming bilateral work,” Cutler said.

Whether the personal rapport between Xi and Trump can persist will be tested soon, according to Craig Singleton, senior fellow and senior director of the China Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“Xi treated Trump with respect in Shenzhen. He will test his resolve in Miami next month, when the bill for Beijing’s trade commitments comes due,” Singleton said in an email.
Castillo reported from Shenzhen, China.

title: Rohingya in Bangladesh welcome UN court's genocide verdict but say they want to go home to Myanmar
summary: Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh have welcomed the ruling by the United Nations' top court in the Netherlands that held Myanmar responsible for genocide
story: Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh have welcomed the ruling by the United Nations' top court in the Netherlands that held Myanmar responsible for genocide

COX’S BAZAR, Bangladesh -- Hundreds of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh sat in front of a big screen at their sprawling camp in Cox’s Bazar, watching the news from the Netherlands, where the U.N.'s top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

For many, the historic verdict on Thursday represented a “small victory” — offering a glimmer of hope that someday they would be able to return safely to their homes in Myanmar, across the border from Bangladesh.
Only then, some said, will they be “fully satisfied.”
It was a landmark judgement, finding Myanmar responsible for the crime against the country’s ethnic Rohingya — the first time the court ruled that a state committed genocide.

The Hague-based International Court of Justice also ordered Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow the Rohingya to return home safely, pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.

But it remains to be seen how much of the ruling can be implemented. The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.
There was no immediate reaction to the ruling from the Myanmar delegation in The Hague or from the government in Myanmar.
At the refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Rohingya refugees told The Associated Press of their concerns.

Mohammad Rofik, a Rohingya community leader at the camp, said the verdict was “a victory” for them as it recognized the genocide and the sufferings of their minority in the Buddhist-majority nation, but that it was “not an end” to their ordeal.
“Justice has started,” Rofik said, adding that the Rohingya still have “a long way to go.”
For Sayed Ullah, another Rohingya community leader, the verdict was a historic recognition that the Rohingya are a distinct ethnic group.
“Myanmar denies the existence of the Rohingya, but now the (U.N.) court made it clear," he said.

“The Rohingya have their own distinct culture, their own language, their own land and everything else that defines an ethnic group,” Ullah said. “We, the Rohingya, have all the characteristics of a distinct ethnic group.”
Other refugees reacted sharply, saying that the international community should punish Myanmar authorities.

“The court has stated and established that genocide was committed against the Rohingya people," said Mohammad Osman, a Rohingya refugee. "Based on this ruling, the entire Rohingya community is calling on ... (the world) to impose severe punishment on Myanmar.”

In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.

The Hague-based court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya. Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part.”

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Bangladesh has been urging the international community to help repatriate the refugees.
Associated Press writer Julhas Alam in Dhaka, Bangladesh, contributed to this report.

title: Sydney man charged with car bomb plot and downloading Islamic State group material
summary: Australian police have arrested a man in the greater Sydney area on charges of researching how to build a car bomb and downloading violent material inspired by the Islamic State group
story: Australian police have arrested a man in the greater Sydney area on charges of researching how to build a car bomb and downloading violent material inspired by the Islamic State group

MELBOURNE, Australia -- Australian police on Friday arrested a man in the greater Sydney area on charges of researching how to build a car bomb and downloading violent material inspired by the Islamic State group.

Police stressed they found no evidence of a link to the upcoming first anniversary of an IS-inspired attack at Sydney’s Bondi Beach. Two gunmen opened fire on a Dec. 14 Hanukkah celebration, leaving 15 people dead and 40 wounded.

Nowroz Rayed Amin, 35, from Ingleburn on Sydney’s southwestern outskirts, was charged with collecting documents likely to facilitate terrorist acts and possessing violent extremist material obtained online, Australian Federal Police Deputy Commissioner Hilda Sirec said.
“It will be alleged in court that the man was researching how to build a vehicle-borne, improvised explosive device, which we allege, for use in a potential terrorist act,” Sirec told reporters.
Amin appeared in the Campbelltown Local Court later Friday on the two charges, which carry a potential combined maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.
Amin did not enter pleas or apply for release on bail. He was remanded in custody to appear in court on Thursday next week, court documents show.

Investigators decided to make the arrest Friday because there was sufficient evidence and not because of any imminent threat to the community, according to Sirec, who said police suspected he had acted alone.

“I want to stress this point because we acknowledge we are just weeks away from the first anniversary of the Bondi Beach attack,” Sirec said. “There is no information to suggest that this alleged offending is connected to the anniversary of that attack. However, we know the fear that this will cause.”
The attack at Bondi Beach was Australia's worst mass shooting since 1996.

Police killed one gunman, Sajid Akram, at the scene. His son, Naveed Akram, was wounded and faces trial next year on 78 charges including 15 counts of murder, 43 of attempted murder and one of committing a terrorist act. Akram has yet to enter any plea.
Police executed 10 search warrants in the greater Sydney area Friday and made three arrests.
As well as Amin, police arrested a 33-year-old man for weapons offenses and a 34-year-old man for hindering police, Sirec said.

title: El Salvador President Nayib Bukele seeks third term while attacking gangs in Haiti
summary: El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has officially launched his bid for reelection in the February elections
story: El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has officially launched his bid for reelection in the February elections

SAN SALVADOR -- SAN SALVADOR (AP) — El Salvador President Nayib Bukele on Thursday night officially launched his candidacy for a third term in office after years of paving the way to stay in power indefinitely.

With virtually no political opposition, the highly popular leader is positioned to coast easily into a third term in office in the February elections. Recent polls put his approval ratings around 90%, largely due to his war on the country’s gangs. The crackdown, which began in 2022, has largely debilitated the criminal groups and sharply reduced violence but fueled accusations of mass human rights abuses.

The firebrand populist submitted his presidential candidate paperwork to the country’s Supreme Electoral Tribunal. His New Ideas party, which holds a supermajority in the country’s congress, cleared the way for him to be the party’s candidate in July and remain in power.

Crowds carrying “Bukele 2027” signs cheered his arrival in a fleet of police cars at the electoral tribunal building, where candidates for 60 congressional seats and 44 municipal council seats also submitted documentation ahead of the Thursday night deadline.
“In El Salvador there is total, complete open democracy,” an impassioned Bukele told roaring supporters. “We’re sending a message to the world that El Salvador will never return to the past.”

The reelection bid comes as Bukele has taken his crime offensive to Haiti. He deployed around 2,500 troops to fight gangs after the disappearance of four Salvadoran aviation technicians in an October gang attack.

Critics have described the offensive as a way to offset international scrutiny, rally domestic support ahead of elections and solidify Bukele’s long-term political project. But Bukele, a former communications strategist, often seems to relish political spectacles.

Democratic concerns hang over the February vote. El Salvador’s Constitution has long prohibited consecutive reelection, in part because of the Central American nation’s fragile democracy. But a ruling by the Supreme Court stacked with Bukele loyalists allowed him to seek a second term in 2024.

Bukele has spent years whittling away checks and balances and concentrating power. The country's congress, dominated by his party, pushed through a congressional reform in 2025 that eliminated presidential term limits and moved up national elections from 2029 and 2027.
His government also has gone after the opposition, watchdog groups and journalists, fueling the greatest exodus of civil society since the Salvadoran civil war decades before.
Political opposition figures and international observers have said Bukele's plan to continue in office is illegal, but don't deny the leader's popular support.

“Bukele is running for a third consecutive term after packing the court, rewriting the constitution to his liking and jailing or forcing into exile those who dare criticize him. The absolute concentration of power in his hands has been the defining feature of his administration,” said Juan Pappier, Human Rights Watch deputy director of the Americas.

The country's political opposition has been rendered virtually irrelevant, in part because of years of corruption and political failures by traditional parties, which helped catapult Bukele into office in 2019.
Many Salvadorans have said they prefer giving up democratic freedoms to suffocation by the gangs.
Janetsky reported from Mexico City.

title: Troops from 11 countries drill in Poland for potential postwar Ukraine mission
summary: Thousands of European troops are taking part in a major military exercise in southeastern Poland
story: Thousands of European troops are taking part in a major military exercise in southeastern Poland

NOWA DEBA, Poland -- Thousands of European troops are taking part in an unprecedented military exercise in southeastern Poland to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.
Led by France and the U.K., the multinational force is a non-NATO military initiative of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a wider political group of 37 nations supporting Ukraine.

The two-week exercise that began on Nov. 9 is for the first time checking this coalition's ability to deploy in Ukraine once the war ends. It is aimed both at testing deployment plans and sending a message to Russia and the Trump administration that European countries are stepping up militarily.

The exercise took place as leaders from Ukraine and nearly 40 other delegations met in Berlin to underline their support for Kyiv and explore Ukraine’s postwar security arrangements. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wants to ensure that Russia doesn’t invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders.

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine. Kushner and fellow U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff were in Berlin to reassure European leaders about U.S. President Donald Trump’s discussions on ending the nearly 5-year-old war at his historic trilateral talks with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Trump called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, according to Kushner.

Ukraine has long sought entry into NATO, particularly for its common defense guarantee under the alliance’s Article 5, in which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, and whether Russia and Ukraine would ultimately accept them.

After the meeting on Thursday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the military exercise in Poland “shows that the Coalition of the Willing is ready to contribute with the United States of America to securing a peace.”

Around 2,800 personnel from Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and the U.K. are taking part in the two-week exercise, with Poland providing the logistical backup and Turkey participating from Istanbul.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that 1,100 troops from France were deployed, and that “we have terrestrial, air but also maritime operations, a dozen countries that are active in this coalition.”

The exercise in Poland follows 12 months of planning by the Multinational Force-Ukraine, or MNF-U, said U.K. brigadier Campbell Close, who serves as deputy commander for operations of the French Army's 1st division. That division is in charge of the land part of the “Koalicja” exercise in Poland.

“This is a deployment exercise,” Close said on Monday at the Nowa Deba military training ground in southeastern Poland. “We have rehearsed the entry into theater, the arrival of thousands of troops and now move on to Nowa Deba training area where we are conducting integration training with eight allies.”
“I should stress we are a defensive force,” Close said.
He also praised Poland for a “no mean feat” in terms of handling the logistics of moving thousands of vehicles, people and their equipment in a short period of time.

If deployed once a ceasefire is in place, the force would help regenerate and strengthen Ukraine’s armed forces, provide the reassurance needed to open the country’s skies and help clear mines in the Black Sea, Lt. Gen. Tom Bateman, commander of MNF-U, said earlier in November. It would not have peacekeeping or peace-monitoring functions.
Coalition troops arrived in Poland by sea, air and land, the Polish government said in a statement, before traveling by rail and road to Nowa Deba, where they have been training together since.

They rehearsed transporting personnel and equipment across Poland, carried out joint command-and-control exercises, and flew fighter jets and an aerial refueling tanker in preparation for helping Ukraine reopen its airspace. They operated surveillance drones, drilled responses to drone attacks and trained in trench warfare in wooded areas.

The initial idea of the Coalition of the Willing group of nations was to provide Ukraine with security guarantees similar to NATO’s Article 5. In the absence of a NATO commitment to fulfill this function, France and the U.K. decided to go ahead with plans for a separate European proposal of countries willing to come to Ukraine’s aid if necessary.
Last year, Putin said that any foreign troops inside Ukraine would be considered “legitimate targets.”

The multinational force may have a purely defensive function, but it would still need to be a “combat force for their own force protection,” said Ed Arnold, a Senior Associate Fellow at the RUSI military think tank in London.
Geir Moulson in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: At an Italian hedgehog hospital, tiny patients face the strain of a warming climate
summary: Italy's only hedgehog rescue center is overwhelmed with underweight hoglets due to climate change
story: Italy's only hedgehog rescue center is overwhelmed with underweight hoglets due to climate change

NOVELLO, Italy -- When an underweight hoglet arrives at Italy’s only hedgehog rescue center, it is placed in an incubator, given fluids and oxygen if needed, and assigned a name — a small gesture of hope that it will survive.

Prolonged drought and unusually high summer temperatures linked to climate change have made the La Ninna rescue center in northern Italy's Piedmont region busier than ever. The center cared for 450 animals two years ago and more than 700 last year, with a similar number expected this year.

“We’re in the middle of autumn, and we are literally being inundated with tiny hedgehogs weighing 100 to 200 grams (3.5 to 7 ounces)," said veterinarian Massimo Vacchetta, who founded the center 14 years ago after recognizing the animals' increasing vulnerability. “They were born late in the season because of global warming and cannot survive outside.”
A hedgehog needs to weigh at least 700 grams (1.5 pounds) to hibernate successfully, Vacchetta said.

A decade ago, late-season second litters typically arrived by early September. Now, some are born as late as November, leaving the hoglets too little time to get to a healthy hibernation weight before winter.

The center, funded mostly through donations, has eight full-time staff along with a host of volunteers. It is equipped like an emergency clinic, with incubators, ultrasound equipment and oxygen tanks.
Staff members name the animals to distinguish them and as “a form of hope,” said Elisa Mangione, who wore a hedgehog-print medical top.
“It is precisely that name that gives them existence; they are here for a purpose, and with the goal of returning to their natural habitat,” Mangione said.

By mid-November, the center was caring for some 300 hedgehogs and Vacchetta was expecting another 100 to 200 before winter. About two-thirds were hoglets. The rest were adults that were either ill or severely malnourished due to a shortage of insects and other invertebrates, whose populations have been affected by drought and high temperatures.
The food shortage has forced the nocturnal animals to forage even during the day, Vacchetta said.
“All those arriving now will stay until spring because, obviously, the conditions outside don’t allow them to survive," Vacchetta said.

Most are found locally, but thanks to word of mouth and social media, reports of hedgehogs in distress arrive from all over Italy. In such cases, the center offers practical advice or suggests taking the animal to the nearest wildlife conservation centre.
To better understand what puts the animals under stress, the carcasses of those that do not survive are sent to the University of Turin for examination.

“We are seeing an increase in infectious agents, biological agents, primarily bacteria and various parasites,” said Maria Teresa Capucchio, associate professor at the University of Turin's veterinary sciences department.

Warming temperatures mean hedgehogs are still wandering the countryside as winter begins instead of hibernating, and they start emerging as early as February, before the insects they feed on are available, she said.
Illness, food shortages and increasing exposure to human activity — including agricultural chemicals, netting and traffic — are all contributing to declining hedgehog numbers, she said.
While hedgehogs are at risk of extinction in England, this is not yet the case in Italy, Capucchio said.
Vacchetta and his team are working to give as many as possible a chance of survival.

“We are on the front lines of the battle to defend animals, which are facing a major crisis due to climate change,” Vacchetta said. “People do not realize the gravity of the situation because these are silent deaths. Animals fall ill and die far from our sight.”

title: Brazil's Lula moves to protect Chief Raoni’s birthplace in the Amazon rainforest
summary: The Brazilian government has advanced legal protection for the territory of Raoni Metuktire, a prominent Indigenous leader in the Amazon
story: The Brazilian government has advanced legal protection for the territory of Raoni Metuktire, a prominent Indigenous leader in the Amazon

SAO PAULO -- The Brazilian government Thursday advanced legal protection for the territory of Raoni Metuktire, the Amazon’s most internationally recognized Indigenous leader, during a visit by Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to the Indigenous territory in the Brazilian rainforest.
The Justice Ministry’s order formally recognized the Mebengokre-Kayapo and Yudja-Juruna peoples’ permanent possession of the Kapot Nhinore Indigenous Territory, where chief Raoni was born.
Lula said the government still faces legal hurdles to complete the demarcation because about 200 rural properties overlap the territory.
“But we’re going to work very hard to resolve this once and for all,” he said at a public event in the Indigenous territory, streamed on the government’s official YouTube channel.
The size of the land — 362,000 hectares (895,000 acres) for 60 people — has been a sticking point in land recognition discussions.

“It doesn’t matter if it’s one person. We cannot decide whether to recognize Indigenous land based on how much land people will have," Lula said. "We must never forget that Raoni’s ancestors were here before there were any Brazilians. We are simply restoring the rights and dignity you should never have lost.”

The Kapot Nhinore territory lies along the Xingu River, a major Amazon tributary, on the border between Para and Mato Grosso states. Raoni has fought for decades for the territory’s permanent protection, but the Brazilian government only formally defined its boundaries in 2023, as part of an administrative process that began in 2004.

“This is a victory that should be celebrated by all Indigenous peoples in Brazil and around the world, especially because this is the ancestral territory of the most celebrated defender of forests,” said Danicley Aguiar, a spokesperson for Greenpeace Brazil.

Márcio Santilli, a founding member of the nonprofit Socioenvironmental Institute and former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, said the government’s recognition of the land is significant both as the traditional homeland where Chief Raoni was born and as a key safeguard for the rainforest along the Xingu River.
“This is one of the few stretches of the Xingu’s banks that remained outside protected areas. Land grabbers and loggers have occupied the region and cleared parts of this corridor.”

Protecting Indigenous territories is widely seen as one of the most effective ways to curb Amazon deforestation, which researchers warn could accelerate global warming. A 2022 analysis by MapBiomas, a network tracking land use, found Brazil’s Indigenous territories lost just 1% of their native vegetation over three decades, compared with 20% on private land nationwide.

Without formal protection, the Kapot Nhinore territory has faced intense pressure from soybean farmers and cattle ranchers. A Greenpeace report released Wednesday found that about 17% of its forest has been cleared since 1988.
Greenpeace has advocated that Brazil's banking authorities must change rural lending rules to reduce agribusiness pressure on occupied Indigenous territories.

Raoni, one of the world’s best-known advocates for the Amazon rainforest and Indigenous rights, spent decades traveling the globe to rally support for their protection. Since September, he has been receiving palliative care at home in central Brazil after being diagnosed with cancer at 94. He is surrounded by family, community members and specialized medical teams.

On Thursday afternoon, the Brazilian president published a photo on Instagram of the two holding hands during a private visit he paid to the Indigenous leader before the public event. “I thank God for giving me the chance to speak with him, to find him alive and tell him: We are legally recognizing your land,” Lula said.

At one of Raoni's most recent public appearances in April at the Free Land encampment in Brasilia, Brazil’s largest annual Indigenous mobilization, he reaffirmed his support for Lula, who won a fourth term in October.

Raoni helped secure protection for numerous Indigenous territories. An Oscar-nominated documentary brought him international recognition in the late 1970s, and he later toured with British musician Sting to promote Indigenous causes. His activism took him from communities in Canada to presidential offices and royal palaces in Europe. In October 2025, Britain’s King Charles III welcomed him to St. James’s Palace.
