Along with freezing and canceling billions in research under Kennedy’s leadership at the start of the Trump administration, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services laid off more than 10,000 workers and shut down entire offices and programs. Experts say those cuts may have impacted state and local health departments’ ability to adequately respond to outbreaks.

PAHO officials expect the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico which also lost their elimination status, to each submit a plan “in the coming weeks” for how they will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, said Dr. Daniel Salas, PAHO’s executive manager for immunizations.
A decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, Schwartz said.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans,” she said. “Vaccination does.”

She said federal officials have invested $100 million to help state and local health departments to reach communities with measles outbreaks. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”
Michaud said the designation change is “a marker for how we backtracked on public health, particularly related to measles prevention, and particularly related to vaccines.”
“It encapsulates this idea that the United States is more vulnerable than ever to infectious diseases," he said.

title: LeBron James sues makers of AI sports-betting app, saying they used his likeness
summary: NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing
story: NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing

NBA superstar LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app Tuesday, saying they have deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing.
In a lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court in New York, James' attorneys called it “a willful, bad-faith tactic” to use the player's fame, likeness and nickname to promote “a new and unknown product.”

The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using the Philadelphia 76ers star's name, to give up any money they've already made, and to award damages — including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages.

“Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app,” the lawsuit states. “They intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions."
Messages sent by The Associated Press through the app’s website and to email addresses for its founders seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday.

The app’s developer, PlayVision Inc., is based in California. It was launched by Chief Executive Anish Gupta and Chief Technology Officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans.

This year, the company released its “Bron” app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services like bet tracking and odds comparisons. It launched a marketing campaign this month that featured an image of a person resembling James — down to his tattoos, voice and number 23 jersey — sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.

James' lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter, as previously reported by Front Office Sports. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said.

Gupta responded to the attorneys' demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed, leading James' legal team to suggest the company was milking the controversy for attention. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals, and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app's marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players.

“The integrity of NBA competition — and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play — is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans,” the lawsuit said. “Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

title: Cambridge Dictionary chooses 'human' as word of the year in response to AI fears
summary: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen "human" as its word of the year, reflecting concerns about artificial intelligence
story: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen "human" as its word of the year, reflecting concerns about artificial intelligence
LONDON -- Fears of artificial intelligence inspired the Cambridge Dictionary to flip back to the 15th century for the word that best captures the 2026 cultural zeitgeist.
“Human,” the dictionary's word of the year, is not just a throwback but also a backlash of sorts that reflects the debate over how AI has blurred the lines between machines and people.

“AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children."

The adjective derived from the Latin “humanus” and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as “having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines.”
Dictionaries typically choose a novel word — sometimes slang that has crossed into the mainstream — or an existing word that has taken on a new meaning.
Artificial intelligence has factored heavily in Word of the Year distinctions across several dictionaries in recent years.

“AI” itself was chosen by Collins Dictionary in 2023 — a year when Cambridge picked “hallucinate,” in reference to the tendency of AI to fabricate information. Merriam-Webster last year named “slop” its word of the year for low quality content produced by AI while Collins went with “vibe coding” for the AI-assisted software development method.

“AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human," Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, who has promoted the smart use of AI, said in a comment on the Cambridge Dictionary selection. "The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”

Other word contenders for 2026 included “agent,” for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control and “analogue” for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology.
Editors note: This story was produced by a human.

title: In closings, Chinese tech giant Huawei is cast by prosecutors as a villain as its lawyer disagrees
summary: The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies is drawing closer to an end after two days of closing arguments
story: The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies is drawing closer to an end after two days of closing arguments

NEW YORK -- The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies approached its end Tuesday after a prosecutor told jurors that the Chinese telecommunications giant helped Iran spy on its citizens and steal from U.S. companies and a defense lawyer accused the U.S. of embracing a false narrative.

Defense attorney Brian Heberlig said in a closing argument in Brooklyn federal court after a two-month-long trial that federal prosecutors “decided Huawei was a criminal enterprise” and built a case from that premise.
“They began with guilt and worked backwards,” Heberlig said. “When the evidence didn't fit, they moved the goalposts.”

He spoke a day after Assistant U.S. Attorney Meredith Arfa said the company for two decades encouraged a workforce of over 200,000 workers in 170 countries to lie, cheat and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.”
She said Huawei had committed crimes targeting American companies, the U.S. financial system and the American government while providing Iran with the equipment to spy on its citizens.

Huawei is the world’s largest supplier of gear for wireless telecom networks, but it is not allowed to sell equipment to U.S. carriers over fears it poses a security risk. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.
Heberlig credited Huawei’s remarkable growth to its success in engineering, investment, innovation and competition.
He said prosecutors built their case in part by focusing on acts of wrongdoing by a few employees who were fired after their misdeeds were discovered.
Prosecutors sometimes blamed the company for gaining access to the intellectual property of competitors when the materials were already public, he said.
“You can't steal a secret that isn't secret,” Heberlig said.

Huawei makes phones and other consumer electronics, but it has been cut off from other lines of business. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors.

During President Donald Trump’s first term, his administration raised national security concerns about Huawei and began lobbying Western allies against including the company’s products in their next-generation high-speed wireless networks. The U.S. announced the criminal charges in early 2019 and has since expanded the allegations.
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in “economic bullying” and improperly used national security as a pretext for “oppressing Chinese companies.”
The jury was expected to begin deliberations sometime on Wednesday.

title: What tech CEOs are saying about the saga around Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has sparked widespread discussion, especially at a recent forum held by Semafor in Menlo Park, California
story: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has sparked widespread discussion, especially at a recent forum held by Semafor in Menlo Park, California

MENLO PARK, Calif. -- The saga surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has riveted Silicon Valley like few other stories, from reports of extramarital affairs to his resignation last week and short-lived comeback bid.

Huang and Nvidia, a computer chip company that has been driving the AI boom, were top of mind this week at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World forum, a gathering of tech executives, investors, policymakers and government officials.
Here is what prominent business leaders and officials in attendance had to say about the episode and its aftermath.

Altman, co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, said Monday at the forum that he feels “personal strong empathy” for Huang in the wake of his resignation. Altman, who himself was removed as CEO in 2023 before being quickly reinstated, said that he doesn’t think he knows enough to answer the question of whether Huang should return to Nvidia, but said “Jensen has long been a hero of mine.”

“Heroes have flaws. I am grateful for the company he’s built,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen. The company he has built took an early bet on us, we took an early bet on him. I have extreme, extreme gratitude for that.”
Altman also said Nvidia is “like a behemoth of a company” and that he believes “people still trust their guarantees very much.”
Amazon founder Bezos similarly said he doesn’t know enough of the details to say whether Huang should return to Nvidia.

“But what I can tell you for sure is that Jensen is a remarkable guy who founded and built a remarkable company with a lot of hard work and foresight, and he deserves admiration and respect no matter what and that will never go away,” Bezos said.
Asked if he had any advice for Nvidia’s board, Bezos said the company should hire internally.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider,” he said. “Nvidia is too complicated. I think outside CEOs in complex companies have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding. And so I would always think that’s a last resort.”

Bezos, who left the CEO post at Amazon in 2021 after 27 years but still serves as executive chairman, said the Amazon-Nvidia analogy would be a “very poor one.” “There has never been a more planful transition,” he said as the room of tech industry insiders erupted in laughter.
“Just to be clear, that is a very different situation,” Bezos continued. “A multiyear, planned transition.”

Jassy, Amazon's CEO, said during a session he doesn't think the incident and its fallout will have any impact on Amazon, which uses Nvidia's chips but is also building its own custom chips. He described their relationship as “coopetition,” saying that dynamic is something you have to get used to in the tech landscape.

“They’re a really important partner of ours and have been for a long time, and will be for as long as I can foresee in the future,” he said. “They’ll have to work out how they move forward as a company, but we’ll be partners with them either way, and we’re excited about what we’re building.”
Srinivas, the co-founder and CEO of Perplexity AI, lauded Huang for his contributions to the industry in an interview Monday with The Associated Press.

“I think everybody in AI who’s made a name for themselves in the last four or five years has one person to thank. It’s Jensen,” Srinivas said. “America needs more Jensens. It’s very hard — he’s singular — but at the same time, people should aspire to create a legacy of the nature that he’s done.”
Srinivas did not comment on whether he thinks the board should reinstate Huang.

Raimondo, who served as the Secretary of Commerce from 2021 through 2025, said at the forum Tuesday that the scandal highlighted American rules around exporting sensitive technology. A woman Huang reportedly had an affair with was an executive at a Singapore-based cloud computing company the U.S. suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of its export controls.

“My philosophy was be open, tell them what the rules are and expect that they follow the rules. And they weren’t always happy because they want to sell as much as possible,” Raimondo said at the Semafor forum. “What I tried to do is say ‘National security first, (you) can’t put a price on America’s national security.’ But I wanted to deny them the least amount of revenue possible, because you want American companies to be successful.”

Raimondo, who is also the CEO of RAISE US, a nonprofit focused on how AI will reshape jobs and industries, said she began work two years ago to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, which the Trump administration issued new rules for on Monday.

“Why did it take two years for that to happen? I don’t know, but I’m glad they’re moving in that direction,” she said. Raimondo added that China is constantly seeking ways to “beat America,” so she argued there should be “no tolerance” for “any kind of corruption, politics, mishandling, dealing with spies.”

title: Is it OK to have AI text your boyfriend? When using chatbots crosses a line
summary: As more people turn to chatbots to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using them for personal messages cross a line
story: As more people turn to chatbots to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using them for personal messages cross a line
A purple box set up on a folding table in San Francisco’s Alamo Square could have been mistaken for a tissue box. Instead, it held dozens of secrets.
Oliva Tai was nearby, watching as passersby puzzled over a sign that read, “Confession box: Everyone has an AI secret.”

Among confessions about farming out too much work or using artificial intelligence to suggest a first-date spot were several admissions about using it to write deeply personal messages: “I had AI write my breakup text.” “I had ChatGPT date my boyfriend. Every text.” “I used AI to write my girlfriend’s grandmother’s 80th birthday letter.”
“I used AI to win an argument. Lol, not proud, but I won.”

Tai, an artist who has repeated the project more than a dozen times in the Bay Area, New York and Denver, said calling it a “confession” suggested people were admitting that using AI made them feel at least a little guilty. But they used it anyway.

As more people turn to a chatbot to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using it for personal messages cross a line? Is it ever OK to use AI to write a holiday card or birthday message? What about a love letter or wedding vows?

As part of research for a Ph.D. in consumer behavior, Danielle Hass conducted vignette-based experiments to determine how people felt about using AI to write personal messages. She found that people who had used AI before felt just as guilty as those who hadn't.
“Everyone felt guilty,” said Hass, a professor at Kennesaw State University in Georgia. “The driver of this relationship was dishonesty, that people felt like they were manipulating.”
Even if people are honest about their AI use, others still view them negatively, said Scott Claessens, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol in the UK.
Claessens says his research suggests that people who use AI are perceived as lazier, less competent and less trustworthy.

He noted that people often already supplement social tasks, such as using pre-written birthday cards or poems in love notes. But something about the effortless way that AI works turns people off, he said.
“What we really want in our social relationships is for people to put effort in, because it shows that as a signal that you’re invested in the relationship,” he said.

Sarah Newman, who collaborated with Tai as director of art and education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, said AI adoption is happening so quickly that norms will likely emerge about when it’s appropriate and when it's not.
She suggested using conflicted feelings as a guide. If you imagine using AI to write your wedding vows, would you be comfortable telling your partner you used it? If not, then don’t.
“Personal messages don’t need to be perfect,” Newman said. “Part of what makes these messages authentic and endearing is that they are imperfect.”

Tai and Claessens said some situations could warrant using AI in personal situations, such as people in relationships who use it to communicate better with a partner who doesn’t share a native language. People with learning disabilities, such as dyslexia, could also use it for help.
Hass believes people are quickly accepting that AI can make them more efficient in some work contexts, but she said she’s glad people feel guilty using it for personal messages.
“Guilt’s purpose in this context is to show us our interpersonal wrongdoings,” Hass said. “It’s showing us, ‘hey, this is where you’re supposed to be human.’”
Albert Stumm writes about travel, food and wellness. Find his work at https://www.albertstumm.com

title: Classified communications network at the National Security Agency goes down, defense official says
summary: An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information has gone offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
story: An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information has gone offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
WASHINGTON -- An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline Tuesday after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”

The problem disrupted the operations of NSANet, a classified internal network used by employees of the agency, according to a defense official who was not authorized to discuss the matter by name and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.

“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," the NSA said in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
The intelligence agency did not provide any additional details on the cause of the outage or the scope of the disruption.
The outage was first reported by CNN.

The NSA episode is among a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions in the last week, including a system overload Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase on Monday that caused ripple effects in the financial system and an internal systems outage at United Airlines that delayed departing flights.
On Tuesday , Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages after an internal update.
Top Trump administration national security officials said there was no indication that the events are related or attributable to a cyberattack or hostile activity.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters while traveling with the president in Asia.

Rubio acknowledged that it was “unsettling to see these reports day after day of some technical failures” and that while the government is always vigilant, each of the recent events “are distinct, and they’re different in their causation — in some cases, highly technical.”

Jay Clayton, the Trump administration's director of national intelligence, attributed the problem to government institutions and private companies pushing through upgrades of their computer systems around the same time, resulting in periodic technological hiccups.

“Many people are patching their systems," Clayton said in a CNBC interview Tuesday about the spate of disruptions. "They know that their legacy systems have vulnerabilities. They're outdated, they don't work well with new systems. It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure. And as you patch and upgrade your systems — taking them down and bringing them back up — there are things like this that happen.”
Sen. Mark Warner, the Democratic vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, echoed that assessment.

“AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner said in a statement. “While we still need to get to the bottom of these incidents, the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.”

title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers
story: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers

WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.

Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.
The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia, where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade.

Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries.

“This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains.
He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology.

Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.

In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.
Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.

On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said.

In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the statement said.

Last week, the Singapore government confirmed that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations" involving servers that were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.”
The Malaysian government also said last week that it was investigating if chips brought into Malaysia have been re-exported to other countries as permitted by its own law.

“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” read the Friday statement by Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.

title: Microsoft says services fully restored after hourslong global outage
summary: Microsoft says services are fully restored after a massive, global outage that lasted for hours
story: Microsoft says services are fully restored after a massive, global outage that lasted for hours
Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours.
“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company said in an update on X.

Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.

The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hourslong episode had impacted some of their operations.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems started appearing around midday Thursday in the U.S.
The Redmond, Washington-based company apologized on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents.
It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.

The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.
“With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science.

Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”

The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.

A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.
Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.
As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks.
For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send or receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.
In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology.
The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption.

British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff’s office in Colorado’s Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.

Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.
Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.

And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.

OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

title: SpaceX’s Starship soars into orbit after booster explosion prevents an unprecedented double catch
summary: SpaceX has lost out on its attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the Texas launch pad
story: SpaceX has lost out on its attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the Texas launch pad

SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.

Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster was diverted to a point offshore. Despite the setback, the spacecraft continued on its way. It will steer toward the pad Saturday, barring further trouble. The flight could last as long as 22 hours.

It’s the first time that Starship will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. The loss of the booster meant Elon Musk's company missed out on a double catch.

The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.

Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company’s most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday’s grand finale.
SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company’s sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday's miss all the more surprising.

“Well, that certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong.

This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.

The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight’s end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket’s self-destruct system was activated.
The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.

SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is “how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000,” SpaceX’s Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.

SpaceX’s smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.

Falcon rockets “are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we’re going to catch both the first stage and second stage,” Dontchev said ahead of Friday's launch.

NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk’s Starship or Bezos’ Blue Moon.

During next summer’s Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.
“We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X after Starship reached orbit.

title: Meta fined $887M in Italy over Android gallery photos, videos on Facebook
summary: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.
story: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.

ROME -- Italy announced an €805 million ($887 million) fine against Meta on Saturday for using photos and videos from Android users’ galleries on Facebook without specific consent or adequate disclosure.

The Italian Data Protection Authority said the feature, called “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook,” violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law. The directive protects smartphones as part of a person’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” for such access, the authority said.
Investigators found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook requested gallery access through a single permission covering multiple app functions with different purposes.
The authority gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent for its use. Italy has about 20 million Android users, the agency said.
Meta made no immediate comment.
The fine was imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, which challenged Italy’s jurisdiction, according to the statement.
The authority said Meta’s “lack of cooperation” with the investigation factored into the penalty, which amounts to approximately 0.47% of the group’s global turnover.

title: White House replaces national cyber director amid widespread tech outages
summary: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross has been fired, according to a source close to the White House.
story: DOD Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will replace him, per a source.

The White House has replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, the administration's top cybersecurity adviser, amid a wave of technology outages that hit major companies and government agencies.
Cairncross, who served as President Donald Trump's principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, will be replaced by Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies.
President Trump fully supported replacing Cairncross, with one source telling ABC News that the president believed he "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job."
The official rapid response account for the White House acknowledged Davies' appointment.

"With nearly two decades of leadership experience in the technology space, Kirsten Davies will be a strong asset for the Trump administration in her new position with the Office of the National Cyber Director. It has been my pleasure to work closely with Kirsten on national security matters, and I look forward to now working with her to navigate an increasingly dynamic and fast-moving cyber landscape,” said United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton in the statement on social media.
Axios was first to report the move.

The move comes after a week of tech outages across a variety of U.S. sectors sparked public alarm, but the Trump administration has maintained the technical issues are not the result of a cyberattack or state-sponsored activity, but likely the result of upgrades and system patches.

title: New government report sparks concern over potential cyberattack on US food supply
summary: A new government report is warning that the federal government is susceptible to threats to the nation's food supply.
story: The U.S. Government Accountability Office is warning that the nation's food sector is increasingly susceptible to cybersecurity threats.

In a Thursday report, the federal watchdog group said both the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Food and Drug Administration had "reported having limited resources to address critical cybersecurity activities, such as information sharing and cybersecurity emergency preparedness activities."

The GAO specifically noted that although the agencies "have taken steps to improve cybersecurity," they "haven't conducted emergency response scenarios to prepare for potential cyberattacks on the sector since 2024."

"Both agencies reported that a lack of resources and staffing hindered their ability to meet all the requirements," the agency said in a blog post Thursday, published in tandem with the report's release. "By assessing whether there are opportunities to reprioritize or if there is a need for additional resources, the agencies would be better positioned to provide cybersecurity-related assistance and resources to the sector and help mitigate potential disruption of the food supply chain, which could lead to significant economic and environmental impacts."

The report comes a week before Thanksgiving and following a spate of prominent tech outages, including a cyber breach affecting some JPMorganChase customers' personal information, like emails and addresses.
The country's largest bank said "third parties who provide services" to the bank "were the target of a cyberattack," and some customers' info was accessed.

Other high-profile companies including Microsoft, United Airlines, Apple, and Marriott have also reported recent, separate tech outages, as well as the National Security Agency's internal system, which sends classified messages and reported technical issues this week.

In October, cyberattackers targeted grocery stores and supermarkets in France. French authorities blamed Iran for conducting the attacks, which cranked up the temperature on supermarket refrigerators, causing food to spoil and sparking fires.

The GAO has issued recommendations for changes to the Department of Health and Human Services and the USDA. They include conducting cybersecurity emergency preparedness exercises and simulations, sharing any potential threats or vulnerabilities with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and "developing planning documents for coordinated action in the event of cybersecurity disasters or emergencies."

"The food and agriculture sector is one of the nation's 16 critical infrastructure sectors and is essential to the nation's health, security, and economy," the agency wrote in its blog post Thursday. "The sector is reliant on information technology to produce, process, and deliver products, and faces increasing cybersecurity-related risks. Cyberattacks could result in unsafe food and could erode public trust and faith in the food supply."

title: Northeastern Florida faces flood threats from devastating storms
summary: Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday
story: Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday

Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida's Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday as forecasters warned flooding threats could stretch into next week when a major river is expected to crest well above record levels.

The National Weather Service posted flood warnings and watches stretching around 200 miles (320 kilometers) from just south of Melbourne to the Jacksonville area. Additional rainfall of 2 to 6 inches (5 to 15 centimeters) was expected through Saturday, while some areas could see an extra 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 centimeters).

“Severe, widespread flash flooding is expected,” the weather service said in a Friday morning forecast. “In addition, areas that normally do not experience flash flooding will flood. Furthermore, lives and property (are) in great danger.”

The St. Johns River, Florida's longest, rose above a record level Thursday near Cocoa that was set in 1953. The river is forecast to stay at least 2 feet (61 centimeters) above flood stage through early next week, the weather service said.

Also Friday, a nontropical low-pressure system was expected to form and could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding into early next week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

Parts of Florida's east coast have been deluged with rainfall totaling more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) in some spots since Tuesday, according to preliminary totals by the weather service. That's in addition to heavy rains that fell earlier this month. Several places have already seen their wettest November on record.

The storms shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of people and horses during what is supposed to be Florida's dry season that runs from October to May.
“Never seen such a thing like this in Florida,” said Jazmin Foster, whose Melbourne home was inundated with water for the second time in two weeks.

In Brevard County on Thursday, people with trailers braved knee-deep water to rescue dozens of horses and other animals at the Blue Lake Equestrian Center, an animal hospice and boarding facility in Cocoa. The animals were taken to a dry pasture elsewhere.

First responders conducted nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county, and those numbers continued to climb, Sheriff Wayne Ivey said. The city of Palm Bay conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of a mobile home community. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes.

Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help up and down the coast, the Division of Emergency Management said. Other responding agencies included about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

This week’s storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula. They're an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide.
Forecasters said El Niño conditions are expected to persist through the spring, meaning the soggy extreme weather in Florida and California will likely continue through the winter.

The California coast, from the Los Angeles to San Francisco areas, was also swamped with flooding in many areas this week, leaving neighborhoods under water and forcing some drivers to abandon stalled vehicles in floodwaters. A long stretch of the coastal Highway 1 was closed south of the Monterey Peninsula due to rock and mud slides.
Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California, and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.

title: Iran live updates: Another tanker struck in Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO says
summary: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
story: No casualties or environmental impact have been reported.

Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
Key Headlines
