Tanker struck in Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO says
Another tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, according to the UKMTO.

The tanker was struck on the port bow and a fire has been reported onboard the vessel, according to the UKMTO. No casualties or environmental impact have been reported at this time, according to the UKMTO.
"Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO, whilst authorities investigate," the UKMTO said in a statement.
Trump looks to New Year for next steps with Iran: report
President Donald Trump said he is not "rushing" to make a decision about Iran and suggested that he could wait until after the New Year, he told Axios in a phone interview.
"I am not rushing into any decision [on Iran]. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year," Trump reportedly told Axois Thursday as he traveled back from China..
Republicans block Iran war powers resolution again, in 1st since midterms
Republicans thwarted another effort by Democrats to pass a House-approved Iran War powers resolution on Thursday.
The resolution failed by a vote of 48-51. It would have needed 51 votes to pass. This was a non-binding resolution and would not have required President Donald Trump's signature to be approved.
Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski and Sen. Rand Paul were the only Republicans to vote in favor of the resolution. Sen. John Fetterman was the only Democrat to vote against it.
Thursday's vote was the first war powers vote taken in the Senate since before the midterm elections.

Many Democrats have framed their election victory as a rebuke of the Iran war, and hoped that this vote -- one of more than a dozen votes Democrats have forced on the matter -- would win over more Republicans.

Sen. Tim Kaine has led a number of Iran War powers resolutions in the Senate. In remarks on the Senate floor just before Thursday's vote, he said the war had been "deeply unpopular from its very first days."

"Its unpopularity was made absolutely manifestly clear by the election and its results from Nov. 3," Kaine said. "A historic repudiation of the party holding on to the White House with much of that energy-driven by American's deep dissatisfaction with a war waged unilaterally by a president ... causing costs to dramatically rise on every American family when the president said he would try to bring down costs."
-ABC News' Allison Pecorin
Tower in Riyadh damaged by Houthi strike, no injuries reported
A tower in Riyadh's Financial Center was damaged after it was hit by a Houthi projectile Thursday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense announced.
No injuries were reported, but damage was visible on the exterior of the building in an image posted by the Civil Defense directorate on X.
The Saudi Press Agency reported damage to several floors and neighboring buildings.

title: At China summit, Trump calls Putin 'my friend' amid Ukraine war
summary: The West has been trying to isolate the Russian leader for years.
story: The West has been trying to isolate the Russian leader for years.

LONDON -- The image of Russian President Vladimir Putin sitting with President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping was something the Kremlin leader has sought for years: to be treated as one of the top three global powers.

And in Shenzhen, he got it, at a gathering that all three leaders were eager to present as "historic." As several foreign policy experts have pointed out, it appears to have happened without Putin having to make any concessions.

The meeting lasted only around 90 minutes and produced a four-point joint declaration on "peace," even as Putin wages his full-scale war in Ukraine more intensively, a war that has already claimed hundreds of thousands of lives as it approaches its fifth anniversary.
President Trump embraced Putin at the summit as "my friend," despite years of the West trying to isolate the Russian leader.

While Putin told Trump and Xi they all have "responsibility for maintaining international peace" and strengthening international law, his military is conducting a bombing campaign against civilian infrastructure in Ukraine, aimed at leaving millions without power and water. Drones targeted central Kyiv on Thursday even as the three leaders met.

Trump also went further. Before the cameras, he attacked the International Criminal Court (ICC), which in 2023 indicted Putin for war crimes, as being "out of control." The final joint declaration from the meeting included a point that criticized the ICC, suggesting it had abused its power.
The United States once endorsed the arrest warrant for Putin. The ICC did not have an immediate response to Trump's comments.

As Jonathan Eyal, associate director at the London-based Royal United Service Institute, wrote: "Just about the only substantial outcome of the Shenzhen summit was the rejection of international law and institutions."
While Trump's attacks on the ICC may have been intended to defend Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu, whom the ICC also indicted for war crimes, they may have been more consequential for Putin.

"It's all about appearances," Boris Bondarev, a former Russian diplomat who resigned in 2022 in protest over Putin's invasion of Ukraine, told ABC News before the meeting, saying Putin has long wanted an event that confirms he is "a full member of the club" of "great powers."
Basking in front of the media afterward, taking extended questions, Putin made clear his demands for ending the war are unchanged, insisting Ukraine must surrender its eastern regions.

According to a White House official, during a telephone call into a meeting of Ukraine's "Coalition of the Willing" European allies -- at which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was present, along with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner -- Trump said he was "super upbeat about the prospects for peace" following the summit.
For his part, Zelenskyy emphasized U.S. and European cooperation in comments following the Coalition meeting as crucial to ending Russia's war with Ukraine.

"Together, we must take the necessary steps to ensure that Russia engages in serious, substantive work instead of wasting time," Zelenskyy said, in part. "And we do not want Russia to drag all of this out into the winter. Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia."

Kremlin media has framed the Shenzhen meeting as a Yalta 2.0, a reference to the 1945 Yalta Conference between Josef Stalin, Franklin Roosevelt and Winston Churchill after World War II that divided postwar Europe, placing many countries under Soviet occupation.
While the images of a congenial Putin and Trump will likely have caused worry in Europe and disgust in Ukraine, ultimately the meeting's immediate impact is unclear.

Ukraine and Europe have been developing ways to mitigate Trump's scaling back of support. That was illustrated by Ukraine's strikes this week, using Ukrainian- and European-made missiles, that partially collapsed Putin's bridge to Crimea.
But the meeting in Shenzhen may also have reinforced Putin's perception that the war is going his way.

title: Xi tells Trump US must do 'the right thing' over Taiwan to avoid 'great turbulence'
summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping used his meeting with President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday to warn against the creation of "turbulence" over the issue of Taiwan.
story: He warned in May that the U.S. and China could "come into conflict" over Taiwan.

LONDON and HONG KONG -- Chinese President Xi Jinping used his meeting with President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday to urge bilateral cooperation on issues including AI, but also warned against the creation of "turbulence" over the issue of Taiwan.

Xi and Trump met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in southwestern China, first privately and then as part of a trilateral sit down with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

According to a readout of the meeting between Xi and Trump, the state-run Xinhua News Agency said the Chinese leader suggested areas of cooperation including AI, while cautioning that divergence over the fate of Taiwan could undermine bilateral relations.
"On the Taiwan issue, the United States must keep doing the right thing to avoid the emergence of great turbulence in the China-U.S. relationship," Xi said, as quoted by Xinhua.
During their meeting in May, Xi warned Trump that China and the U.S. could "come into conflict" if the issue of Taiwan is handled "improperly."

Taiwan is an independent island nation that Beijing considers a wayward Chinese province. During the Chinese Civil War -- which took place intermittently between 1927 and 1949 -- nationalist forces retreated to the island while the Chinese Communist Party took control of the Chinese mainland.
Ever since, Chinese leaders -- with Xi among them since his rise to power -- have vowed to take control of Taiwan, whether through diplomatic or military means.

American backing for Taiwan is a longtime grievance for Beijing. Though Washington does not officially recognize Taiwan as an independent state, U.S. administrations have traditionally backed the maintenance of the status quo and provided significant military, diplomatic and economic backing for Taipei.
Xi has been pushing for the U.S. to curtail its arms sales to Taiwan, including a proposed $14 billion deal that would include American missiles, anti-drone weapons and air-defense systems.

The arms package for Taiwan was approved by the US Congress in January but has been held up by the White House, awaiting final approval from the president. Trump has previously said the deal could serve as a "negotiating chip" in talks with Beijing.

Speaking to media in Taipei, Taiwanese Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Chen Ming-chi highlighted U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments, reported by The Hill in September, that military sales to anyone require the same careful consideration.

"Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan Strait. Even though China's economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under this context, the U.S. very much understands our defense needs," he said. "We do continuously communicate with them, and we believe the U.S. understands the situation we face and our determination on defense investment completely."
China regularly conducts large-scale military drills around Taiwan, with daily air and naval patrols around the island maintaining pressure on Taipei.
From Wednesday into Thursday, Taiwan's Defense Ministry reported one sortie of Chinese military aircraft plus the presence of seven Chinese naval vessels and two other "official ships" around Taiwan.
The ministry also reported that two Russian Tu-95 bombers flew into the island's air defense identification zone on Thursday.

The joint China-U.S.-Russia statement released by the Xinhua also endorses "the principle of state consent," which holds that countries cannot be bound by international courts without their agreement, the New York Times reported. China has invoked this principle to reject a 2016 international tribunal ruling against its South China Sea claims, according to the Times.

title: DOJ dropping Alaska midterms Senate certification lawsuit, saying case is 'moot'
summary: The Justice Department is giving up on its controversial lawsuit that sought to potentially block the certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race.
story: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to win the Alaska Senate race.

The Justice Department is giving up on its controversial lawsuit that sought to potentially block the certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race, telling an appeals court Thursday evening that the issue is now "moot" in an apparent acknowledgment of Democratic Senator-elect Mary Peltola's current lead in the electoral tally.
The Associated Press projected Tuesday that Peltola will win the race for the Senate, the ninth Senate pickup for Democrats in the next Congress.

Ahead of the election, President Donald Trump had directed the Justice Department to preemptively file a lawsuit to try to block the certification of the crucial Alaska Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan lost, citing name confusion among the candidates.

Republicans have alleged that candidate Dan J. Sullivan was running a sham campaign to purposefully confuse voters and draw votes away from incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan based on their names being similar.
A federal judge in Alaska dismissed the lawsuit on Nov. 1, saying there was "no workable plan" to investigate the claims in relation to the votes submitted.

In a Thursday filing from DOJ's third-ranked official Stanley Woodward, the department requested the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals vacate the order entered by a district judge in Alaska that dismissed DOJ's lawsuit -- but still acknowledged the dispute is now not worth any further litigation.

"This Court should deny the motion to summarily affirm the district court’s judgment," Woodward said. "Instead, this Court should vacate the district court’s order dismissing this lawsuit, because the case has become moot."

Later in the filing, Woodward opines on what he describes as an unfair hand given to the Trump administration in being unable to dispute ballots that may have been accidentally cast for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan instead of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

"The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of “determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan” and vindicating the United States’ asserted injury," Woodward writes.

The filing comes after days of President Donald Trump repeatedly calling for the Alaska election results to be ruled in favor of Sen. Sullivan by combining the votes of Dan J. Sullivan as well as another Republican candidate he alleges was unlawfully recruited by Democrats as a spoiler in the race.

title: Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways
summary: Trump heads back to Washington after meeting with Xi and Putin -- the first sitdown between the three superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
story: Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.

President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.

Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."

The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.

Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.

"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.

"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.

In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.

"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.

"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.

The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.

The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.

Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.

"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.

As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.

title: What Obama said to newly elected Democrats after midterm gains
summary: Former President Barack Obama told Democratic U.S. House members-elect on Wednesday that they should value their ideological diversity even if they have disagreements.
story: The event was after Hakeem Jeffries was nominated as first Black House speaker.

Former President Barack Obama told Democratic House members-elect that they should value their ideological diversity even if they have disagreements, and that they should not forget about the constituents they serve, according to excerpts of his remarks that his office provided to ABC News.

The meeting, held at the Folger Shakespeare Library near the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday afternoon, was held just hours after New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries was nominated to become the first Black Speaker of the House.

"There is generational change coming to the Democratic Party, which is vital, in part because what that means is you are attuned to today's circumstances ... But the values that you represent stay the same, the values of that this is a country that has to include everybody and not just some," Obama said during the closed-door meeting, according to the excerpt.

He also said that "the diversity of this class is its power. And I don't just mean ethnic diversity or racial diversity or religious diversity. It's also regional diversity and ideological diversity," as he encouraged members-elect to listen to each other even when they disagree.
The incoming House members feature many new members of color as well as candidates from a wide range of economic and professional backgrounds.

"And the key, though, is to recognize that in that diversity, if you listen and you are extending grace to those inside your caucus that you don't agree with 100% of the time, you're going to agree on core values and you're going to agree on a basic direction," Obama said.
The meeting, which was announced abruptly on Wednesday, was not open to reporters.

Jeffries shared a video on Instagram where he introduced Obama at the event. After walking out to applause, Obama was greeted by chants of "four more years," to which he said, "I believe in the Constitution, people."
Obama also emphasized to members-elect, according to the excerpts, that they should not forget about the people they serve.

"There is a danger, though, that you get caught up in national politics and national debates and your national communications and showing up on cable shows and Instagramming to death and all that," he said. "... There is the danger sometimes that you forget that this really is about individual lives, regular folks, day to day, counting on you to help them in ways that you can."
But, he told attendees, they can be there for their constituents and avoid making them feel unseen.

"I think a lot of people's cynicism about politics is not just politics, but business and media, and everything, people feel as if they have no agency, that they're not seen, not listened to, and are disempowered from the major forces that control their lives," Obama said. "At the very least, if their congressman knows they're there and cares about them, that can help generate the kind of hope that we're going to need."
Obama's office did not share excerpts from a question-and-answer session the former president held with attendees.

Ohio Rep.-elect Don Leonard, who flipped a GOP-held seat in a shock result and who has said he did not vote for Jeffries in leadership elections, wrote on X on Wednesday that someone had asked Obama about Elon Musk, who spent heavily in the midterms and said Wednesday that he feels "pretty foolish about having spent so much money" without seeing much of a result.

According to Leonard, Obama had said it was time for a constitutional amendment on campaign finance. Obama has previously said he would support amending the Constitution for campaign finance reform and to regulate campaign spending.

title: Auditors concerned about billions ICE is spending to expand immigration detention
summary: Federal auditors warn that ICE is spending billions of dollars to expand immigration detention without "determining the cost effectiveness" of new initiatives.
story: Auditors say ICE is not "determining the cost effectiveness" of new initiatives.

Federal auditors warned Thursday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement is spending billions of dollars to expand immigration detention without "determining the cost effectiveness" of new initiatives or keeping its spending plan up to date.
A new report released by the Government Accountability Office examined how ICE has managed the $45 billion in detention funding provided under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

"A January 2025 Executive Order directed DHS to increase efforts to detain individuals apprehended for violations of immigration law and to allocate all available resources for ICE detention," according to the report. "ICE received significant funding in July 2025 to operate and expand detention facilities."

According to GAO, ICE acquired 11 warehouses to be converted into immigration detention centers for about $1.07 billion before scaling back the initiative and planning to sell seven of them. The facilities ranged in cost from $35 million and $145 million.

For nine of the warehouses, ICE paid at least 50% more than the state or local government assessment of taxable value, auditors found. In one example, the agency purchased a warehouse in Social Circle, Georgia, for about $128.6 million after a previous buyer purchased it in 2023 for about $29.4 million.

"Our analysis of ICE documentation and public records showed that ICE potentially overpaid for many of the warehouses it purchased," auditors wrote. "Moreover, given ICE's plans to sell seven of the warehouses -- six for which it paid at least double the assessed value -- there is risk that these sales could result in financial losses to the federal government."
In July and August 2026, ICE also bought four existing detention facilities for about $2.2 billion total.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.
Auditors also pointed to high-cost detention operations on military bases. ICE has obligated more than $1 billion to Camp East Montana on the grounds of Texas' Fort Bliss.

"ICE obligated over $1 billion to one facility, Camp East Montana, representing 36 percent of total obligations to detention facilities in the first three quarters of fiscal year 2026," auditors wrote. "We previously reported on cost efficiency concerns related to contract design and administration at Camp East Montana."

At the Guantanamo Bay Naval Base in Cuba, ICE and the Defense Department obligated roughly $111 million for two facilities despite an average daily population of fewer than 30 detainees. ICE previously said it would use Guantanamo Bay to hold "high-threat noncitizens" but has held "multiple noncitizens who had no criminal convictions or pending charges," auditors wrote.
According to the report, ICE plans to continue using Guantanamo Bay "based on direction from senior leadership and the White House."

GAO recommended that "ICE update its spending plan for detention funding in accordance with internal guidance, and develop life-cycle cost estimates, in coordination with DHS, before making new detention investments."
According to GAO, DHS concurred with the recommendations.

title: Hochul demands information from ICE about new immigration tent facility for women
summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul is demanding information from ICE and a Virginia-based construction company about a new tent immigration detention facility set to house women.
story: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul is demanding information from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and a Virginia-based construction company about a new tent immigration detention facility set to house women.
In letters released Wednesday by Hochul, two New York state agencies are pressing for information on the soft-sided facility in Batavia, New York.
The site is an addition to the Buffalo Service Processing Center, which is the largest immigration detention center in New York and currently only holds men.

According to the letters released by Hochul, the tent facility in New York is set to house up to 100 women. The detention center is being constructed by the firm Akima Infrastructure Protection amid the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown.

In the letter, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and the state's Department of Health pointed to federal laws to argue that ICE failed to coordinate or conduct proper environmental consultations and public notifications before construction began.
The New York state agencies requested a response by next week to questions about facility conditions, medical care, food and construction.
In a statement to ABC News, a spokesperson for DHS said it "should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and is actively working to expand detention space."

"ICE is targeting criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, gang members and more," the spokesperson said. "Thanks to the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, ICE has new funding to expand detention space to keep these criminals off American streets before they are removed for good from our communities."

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony on Capitol Hill Wednesday, was pressed by Democratic Rep. Timothy Kennedy about the expansion of the Batavia facility, which is located in Kennedy's district.

"Over 70% of the detainees at the Batavia Federal Detention Facility have never been convicted of a crime, yet they’re detained," Kennedy said. "This is not a facility in need of a billion-and-a-half-dollar facelift."

Mullin responded that "we could save all that money" if the administration could house immigrant detainees in the state's prison and jails -- "but because of your sanctuary policies, you're not allowed to work with us," Mullin said, referring to state policy that limits cooperation with federal authorities on immigration enforcement.

In documents previously released by New York lawmakers last month, Mullin said in a letter that the contract supports the Buffalo area through "the expansion and provision of detention services for illegal aliens."
Mullin said in his letter that the tent facility is expected to cost about $8.7 million.
The letters released by Hochul on Wednesday follow concerns raised by lawmakers and immigrant advocates about conditions at other soft-sided facilities.

The facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," a soft-sided detention center in Florida, was closed earlier this year following lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers. When the closure was announced, Florida and ICE officials said the facility was meant to be temporary.
An inspector general report in September found that some detainees at the Florida facility were confined to small metal enclosures, presenting "significant risks" to their health and safety.

The largest immigration detention center in the U.S., Camp East Montana in Texas, is also a soft-sided facility. Human rights organizations and advocacy groups have raised concerns and have filed lawsuits alleging detainees face medical neglect, a lack of adequate food and water, and prolonged confinement in windowless tents.

"Federal oversight agencies have documented unsanitary conditions, gaps in medical services, and deficiencies with clean water access at tent immigration detention facilities in Texas and Florida," wrote the commissioners of the two New York agencies.

title: Nidal Hasan is set to be executed. The military's other death row cases are in limbo
summary: There are three other former soldiers who are on the military’s death row.
story: There are three other former soldiers who are on the military’s death row.
The U.S. military hasn't executed anyone in 65 years.

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan is set to be put to death next month. The Army has no immediate plans to carry out any other executions at this time, according to two sources with direct knowledge of the matter.

The Army's three other inmates sentenced to die have spent decades on death row for crimes that include murder, rape and an attack on fellow troops in the opening weeks of the Iraq War. None of them have an execution date. Military courts can impose a death sentence, but the case must go through the Pentagon before the president gives final approval to carry it out.
It's unclear why the Trump administration singled out Hasan, the former Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.
Both the Pentagon and the White House declined to comment on whether they plan to execute any of the other death row inmates after Hasan.

Hasan is scheduled to face a firing squad Dec. 3 at the same base where he committed the attack, a method the military has not used since 1945. The Army originally planned to use lethal injection, internal documents reviewed by ABC News show.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth initially planned to livestream Hasan’s execution, which would have been the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century. Republicans and Democrats questioned the decision to broadcast the shooting death of a prisoner who uses a wheelchair and warned it could fuel anti-American propaganda and ultimately become a spectacle that has been associated with dictatorships in the past century. The plan was scrapped after President Donald Trump intervened.
The four men on the military's death row -- including Hasan -- are imprisoned at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

Ronald Gray, a former Army specialist who served as a cook with the 82nd Airborne Division at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, was convicted in a 1988 military trial on 12 charges, including two counts of premeditated murder and three counts of rape. The attacks involved five women, two of them soldiers. A civilian court separately convicted him on 22 charges and sentenced him to eight life terms.
President George W. Bush approved Gray’s execution in July 2008. It was scheduled for that December, but a federal judge halted it. Another judge lifted the stay in 2016.

Timothy Hennis, a former Army master sergeant who worked on parachutes with the 82nd Airborne Division, was convicted in civilian court in 1986 for raping and murdering a woman and killing her 5-year-old and 3-year-old daughters. His conviction was overturned on appeal, and a second trial ended in acquittal in 1989.

Years later, investigators retested evidence using new DNA tools. The acquittal barred another prosecution, but the Army could bring its own charges. The service recalled Hennis, who had retired in 2004, to active duty. A court-martial convicted him and sentenced him to death.

The fourth inmate, former Army Sgt. Hasan Akbar, attacked fellow soldiers at Camp Pennsylvania, Kuwait, in March 2003, during the opening days of the U.S. invasion of Iraq. Akbar, a combat engineer, wounded 14 soldiers and killed two officers. Akbar was convicted in a military court in 2005 on two counts of premeditated murder and three counts of attempted premeditated murder; he was sentenced to death.
In May, Hegseth awarded Purple Hearts at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, to nine veterans wounded in the attack.
It's unclear whether the other three death row inmates have maintained legal counsel.
Tim Jon Semmerling, the mitigation expert on Hasan’s defense team at his 2013 trial, said he believes the number of people Hasan killed at Fort Hood played a part in why he is being executed.
“If you believe in the death penalty, it's really difficult to argue against so many people being killed by one person,” Semmerling said.

Semmerling said he believes Hasan’s Muslim faith may also have figured into the administration's decision, as may Hasan’s stated motive for the attack, which he described as a protest against the U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Semmerling, who conducted dozens of interviews with Hasan and his family over four years, described Hasan as a devout Muslim who spends much of his time in prayer and studying the Quran and Muslim scholars.
Hegseth invoked Fort Hood in a 2015 appearance on Fox News where he argued that troops should be allowed to carry weapons on military bases, saying "Islamics are at war with us."
Hegseth told The Hill in September 2025 that he is "100% committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan" because the "victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."
As Hasan's execution approaches, Army officials say they are revising the outdated firing squad procedures, which date back to 1959.

John Galligan, a retired Army colonel who has long represented Hasan, said officials at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth promised to provide him with the execution protocols, but haven't done so yet. He wants to know how many soldiers will serve on the firing squad and whether Hasan can make a final statement.

“Those kind of details -- details about how you're going to kill someone during their execution -- are important for defense counsel to know -- particularly when, as here, the governing regulation is totally silent on the subject,” Galligan said.
The Army declined to comment when asked detailed questions about how it plans to carry out Hasan's execution.
Hasan could still file a habeas corpus petition, or a judge could delay the execution. It’s unclear whether either will happen.
The Army will have to assemble and train the soldiers who will carry out its first firing squad execution since World War II. It’s unclear what rehearsals they will undergo.

The 1959 procedures allowed prisoners to make reasonable final requests, including a meal, writing materials and access to a chaplain of their faith. On the day of the execution, the prisoner could make a final statement before being hooded and could ask the chaplain to stay until the firing squad was prepared to fire.
Hasan was partially paralyzed after police shot him during the Fort Hood attack. It’s unclear how the Army plans to account for his use of a wheelchair.

In Killeen, Texas, outside of the base where Hasan in set to be executed, officials plan to close city offices and public facilities on the day of the execution as a precautionary measure. Schools will also close, and the city has rescheduled trash collection. It’s unclear whether officials expect any significant protests.
Hasan told a military mental health panel during his trial that he wished he had been killed during his rampage and said he would still consider himself a martyr if the military put him to death.

title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
story: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
A nationwide ground stop ended around 8:15 p.m. ET, and some domestic flights have now departed from U.S. airports.
However, normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned.
Officials say the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Here’s what to know.
The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could late Friday evening Eastern time. Passengers should contact their airlines for information about their flights, the FAA said.
The ripple effect from the stoppage could be felt for days, however.
More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. on Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned Americans traveling that getting air traffic back to normal won't be quick.
International flights are being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
San Francisco airport said that flights headed across the Pacific Ocean were cleared to leave the airport from Friday evening. That included flights destined for Hawaii and Asia.
Europe’s aviation agency suspended U.S.-bound departures at the request of the FAA from 5 p.m. Eastern on Friday until midnight.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers who want to continue their journey, or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.
New technology being hooked up to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment, Trump administration officials said.
That caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, according to officials.
Duffy suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said.
The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Outlook and other services offline Thursday, a spokesperson for the company said.
Mullin said there is no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack, either.
“There was never any lives at risk,” Mullin added. “There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it."
The ground stop was enacted “out of an abundance of caution,” he said.

title: Trump administration blames ‘overloaded’ systems for ground stop after FAA lets flights resume
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems
story: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems

WASHINGTON -- Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
It was lifted in the evening after a five-hour stretch when most flights were not allowed to take off from airports in the U.S.

Thousands of flights and potentially over a million travelers were affected. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed. But Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said he could not guarantee it wouldn’t happen again.
Mullin said the FAA was installing “new equipment, new technology” and “it was overwhelming the older system.” There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, he said.

A limited number of domestic flights began departing late Friday after the ground stop was lifted, but it will likely take days for airlines to fully recover because so many planes and crews were out of position. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Asked whether he could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, Mullin said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that the problem appears to be “mechanically driven.” He said officials were still looking for the cause.

At least 827 flights had been diverted. By 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

Duffy was defensive, blaming Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He implored lawmakers to act.
“By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said.

Duffy said he expected flights around the country to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel” next weekend ahead of Thanksgiving, but he also suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said, while also noting, “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to what failed on Friday.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.

The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Many flights ended up being diverted to places including Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST.
At the time of the ground stoppage, more than 3,500 airplanes were in the sky, Duffy said.

At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals.

“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”

Ruth Coles was still stuck on her plane five hours after it landed at the Los Angeles International Airport from Newark even after the ground stop was lifted. She said they were told they were waiting for a gate to open up.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said, but that was several hours ago.

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
Duffy said NCAA teams will be prioritized ahead of football games on Saturday.
“I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA, to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move” to make their kickoff, he said.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it was prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.

U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons (55,340 metric tonnes) of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is that it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

Friday’s ground stop was also different than the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.

Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.
This story has been corrected to show the Sept. 11 attacks were in 2001.

title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
summary: U.S. air travel operations are still recovering after the nationwide ground stop
story: U.S. air travel operations are still recovering after the nationwide ground stop
Officials said they expect airline schedules to fully recover by the end of the day Sunday after a nationwide ground stop that was initiated out of caution caused massive travel disruptions.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.

Of the 41,000 flights scheduled Saturday, more than 6,600 were canceled, according to FlightAware. Just over 1,300 of the more than 26,000 flights scheduled for Sunday were canceled, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics firm. That amounts to about 5.2% of scheduled flights. Prior to Friday, the average cancellation rate for U.S. departures was 3.4%.
But officials said the U.S. airspace was safe and operational and would recover well ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack and no lives were at risk.
Here’s what to know:

Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said the system was stable Saturday. Several thousand flights were able to fly after the ground stop, but ultimately, some 12,000 scheduled flights were unable to take off Friday, he said.
Officials acknowledged the disruption but said safety was paramount.

Bedford offered an apology for stranded travelers and thanked air traffic controllers, pilots and flight attendants for managing the fallout. He said officials were confident the system is operating safely or else they would keep airplanes on the ground.

American Airlines said in a statement Saturday night that some individual flights might still be canceled as it continued working to fully restore its operations. It urged travelers to check their flight statuses.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight or a full refund if a flight is canceled.
Bedford said the administration was working closely with airlines and said they were waiving all terms and conditions.
Some airlines were allowing passengers to rebook if they had travel scheduled Friday or Saturday. Others extended the offer to people with reservations for Sunday or even Monday.
Bedford advised passengers to contact their airlines.

A contractor was replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fiber wire in a remote location Friday afternoon, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday. That kind of work has been happening across the country and across industries for decades, he said.

But on Friday, the router in that location started overloading the air traffic control system and causing intermittent disruptions to communications and radar feeds. When officials couldn’t quickly locate the cause of the overload, they grounded flights nationwide.
“We did that out of an abundance of caution,” Bedford said. “I’m sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons.”

Officials stressed that the ground stop was not the result of a system outage or nefarious activity by a foreign actor. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was the cause.

The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work. About 70% of copper wire has been switched to fiber already, officials said Saturday.

Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after its own massive outage. There was no indication the FAA ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Microsoft services offline Thursday, according to federal officials and a company spokesperson.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Users reported Microsoft 365 services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were interrupted.

title: US stocks waver as tech sell-off continues and Anthropic falls
summary: Stocks are wavering on Wall Street under the heavy weight of AI companies
story: Stocks are wavering on Wall Street under the heavy weight of AI companies
NEW YORK -- Stocks wavered in morning trading on Wall Street Friday under the heavy weight of falling AI companies.

The S&P 500 index was mostly unchanged in uncertain trading and is on track for a weekly loss of 5%. The benchmark index has lost ground for six straight days. Another day of losses would mark the longest such streak since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

More stocks were gaining ground within the S&P 500, but AI stocks with hefty market values have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which is much less exposed to big technology stocks, gained ground. It rose 457 points, or 1%, as of 10:07 a.m. Eastern time. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, fell 0.6%.

AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also run up against the recent midterm elections, where there has been a shift in power after the GOP, seen as more friendly to the industry, suffered an electoral sweep.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled on Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 7% to $90.55. It is still above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.99% from 5.04% late Thursday.

Oil prices fell 1.5% to $90.62 per barrel, despite continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.
Markets were lower in Europe and Asia.

title: Northeastern Florida faces flood threats from devastating storms
summary: Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday
story: Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday

Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida's Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday as forecasters warned flooding threats could stretch into next week when a major river is expected to crest well above record levels.

The National Weather Service posted flood warnings and watches stretching around 200 miles (320 kilometers) from just south of Melbourne to the Jacksonville area. Additional rainfall of 2 to 6 inches (5 to 15 centimeters) was expected through Saturday, while some areas could see an extra 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 centimeters).

“Severe, widespread flash flooding is expected,” the weather service said in a Friday morning forecast. “In addition, areas that normally do not experience flash flooding will flood. Furthermore, lives and property (are) in great danger.”

The St. Johns River, Florida's longest, rose above a record level Thursday near Cocoa that was set in 1953. The river is forecast to stay at least 2 feet (61 centimeters) above flood stage through early next week, the weather service said.

Also Friday, a nontropical low-pressure system was expected to form and could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding into early next week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

Parts of Florida's east coast have been deluged with rainfall totaling more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) in some spots since Tuesday, according to preliminary totals by the weather service. That's in addition to heavy rains that fell earlier this month. Several places have already seen their wettest November on record.

The storms shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of people and horses during what is supposed to be Florida's dry season that runs from October to May.
“Never seen such a thing like this in Florida,” said Jazmin Foster, whose Melbourne home was inundated with water for the second time in two weeks.

In Brevard County on Thursday, people with trailers braved knee-deep water to rescue dozens of horses and other animals at the Blue Lake Equestrian Center, an animal hospice and boarding facility in Cocoa. The animals were taken to a dry pasture elsewhere.

First responders conducted nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county, and those numbers continued to climb, Sheriff Wayne Ivey said. The city of Palm Bay conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of a mobile home community. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes.

Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help up and down the coast, the Division of Emergency Management said. Other responding agencies included about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

This week’s storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula. They're an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide.
Forecasters said El Niño conditions are expected to persist through the spring, meaning the soggy extreme weather in Florida and California will likely continue through the winter.

The California coast, from the Los Angeles to San Francisco areas, was also swamped with flooding in many areas this week, leaving neighborhoods under water and forcing some drivers to abandon stalled vehicles in floodwaters. A long stretch of the coastal Highway 1 was closed south of the Monterey Peninsula due to rock and mud slides.
Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California, and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.

title: Trump administration use of encrypted messaging apps like Signal is scrutinized by House Democrat
summary: A Democratic lawmaker is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees for official business
story: A Democratic lawmaker is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees for official business

WASHINGTON -- A top House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and the panel's incoming chairman, said in a series of nearly identical letters made public on Friday that he was concerned that President Donald Trump's administration was circumventing record-keeping requirements by using apps like Signal that can be configured to automatically delete messages after a certain time period.

Raskin noted in the letters, which were sent to top officials at the FBI, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the Bureau of Prisons and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the agencies were legally required to preserve all records related to their official business, policies and decisions.

But he said: “There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws. This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials.”

The Maryland Democrat cited as an example a Signal exchange that he said he had obtained between the FBI’s general counsel and an associate of the Republican president's oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., in which a potential or ongoing healthcare fraud investigation was discussed.

The Justice Department said in a statement Friday that it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.” The other agencies cited by Raskin did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

Signal is an app that can be used for direct messaging and group chats as well as phone and video calls. It uses end-to-end encryption for its messaging and calling services that prevents any third party from viewing conversation content or listening in on calls.
Encrypted messaging apps are increasingly popular with government officials, an Associated Press review from last year found.

Their prevalence was demonstrated in vivid fashion last year when journalist Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been inadvertently added to a Signal group chat of U.S. national security officials coordinating plans for airstrikes.

The White House and the Pentagon have said that disgruntled former employees were spreading false claims about the use of Signal, a commercially available app not authorized to be used to communicate sensitive or classified national defense information.

title: Rights groups urge sanctions after top UN court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
summary: Rights groups are urging military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court ruled that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in 2017
story: Rights groups are urging military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court ruled that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in 2017

UNITED NATIONS -- Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling, which orders Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.

Myanmar’s government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court’s demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya.
Khine Khine Soe, the president's spokeswoman, noted the International Court of Justice decision handed down Thursday had been the result of a nine-to-six vote of the judges.
“Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she told reporters in the capital Naypyitaw. “So it was not a decision made unanimously. I would say that it was unfair.”
While the World Court’s rulings are final and legally binding, it has no recourse beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.

The Security Council scheduled closed consultations on the ruling next Wednesday and a private meeting on Dec. 7 at the request of the United Kingdom, which expelled Myanmar's defense attache after Thursday's ruling.

But Daniel Forti, the International Crisis Group’s head of U.N. affairs, said it’s unlikely there will be any immediate action from the 15-member Security Council, which could impose sanctions on Myanmar. He said any action would likely be blocked by China and Russia, both permanent members with veto power.

“China has discouraged the Security Council from acting on the Myanmar file since 2021, as it is reluctant to cede any influence in its own backyard,” Forti told The Associated Press. “The ICJ ruling will not alter China’s calculations, and it is hard to imagine that either Beijing or Moscow would support any potential Security Council resolution that attempts to enforce the court’s recommendations.”

Forti said Gambia, which launched the court proceedings, may eventually pursue a resolution in the 193-member General Assembly calling on Myanmar to comply with the ICJ’s demands, even though its actions are not legally binding, unlike those of the Security Council.

Justice for All, an American human rights organization that advocates for the rights of Muslim minorities, called on the Trump administration to support a General Assembly resolution demanding Myanmar’s compliance with the judgment, and establishing international monitoring and follow-up.

Justice for All, which has a task force of 38 U.S. and Canadian Muslim organizations that have advocated for Rohingya rights since 2017, argued that sanctions should target Myanmar’s oil and gas sector and the networks that provide weapons and other support to its military.

Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnes Callamard urged governments not to welcome the president “on the international stage, especially as grave violations continue unchecked inside Myanmar.”

“Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar,” she said. “The U.N. Security Council should impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court.”
That court, however, is under U.S. sanctions along with many of its judges and staff, so any action by the Security Council would face an almost certain U.S. veto.

Prosecutors at the ICC requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing in late 2024 alleging he was responsible for crimes against humanity against the Rohingya. There has been no public announcement on a decision by judges at the court who would have to issue a warrant.
The court's Office of the Prosecutor did not immediately respond to a request Friday for comment.
Human Rights Watch urged governments to step forward to help the Rohingya.

“Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” Maria Elena Vignoli, the group's senior international justice counsel, said in a statement.

Justice for All called for global support for a Rohingya reparations fund and measures to advance their education, protection, pursuit of citizenship and safe voluntary return from Bangladesh, where some 1.2 million Rohingya now live in overcrowded camps.

Myanmar, which is majority Buddhist, has long claimed the Rohingya are “Bengali” migrants from Bangladesh, even though their families have lived in the country for generations. Nearly all Rohingya have been denied citizenship since 1982, effectively rendering them stateless, and they are denied freedom of movement and other basic rights.
Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who listened to the court ruling in The Hague, Netherlands, said the judgment “will only mean something if governments act on it.”
“So, I say to every U.N. member state, take robust steps to implement the ICJ judgment,” she said, starting with sanctions against the president.
“Make Myanmar pay reparations to the people it destroyed,” she said. “Give us back our lives. Give us a future. We want to be part of a stable, prosperous and thriving Myanmar.”
Associated Press writer Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands, contributed.

title: Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail
summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to shutter New York City’s notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032
story: Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to shutter New York City’s notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032

NEW YORK -- New York City's Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a plan announced Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars.
The city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.

For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing “ abnormal and unacceptable " conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms.

Mamdani, a Democrat, has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the longstanding plan to build new jails has met pushback, including from his predecessor, former Mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails.
“It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane."
The plan hinges on lowering the city's inmate population from the more than 6,500 people housed at Rikers to around 4,500.

The Mamdani administration is proposing a new slate of diversion and supervised release programs, expanding housing and social services to prevent recidivism, along with restoring an online bail payment system and reducing case delays through various measures.

“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers. Working alongside the City Council, Courts and nonprofit partners, we will meet it — for the people in our custody, the staff who serve them, victims of crime, and every New Yorker,” Mamdani said.

Instead of housing prisoners at Rikers — an island in the East River near LaGuardia Airport — the city will shift people to jails in the Bronx, Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan, as well as a handful of medical facilities for people who need healthcare or psychiatric treatment. The city also plans to reduce the number of beds for women, diverting them into community-based programs.
The borough jails are expected to open in Brooklyn in 2029; the Bronx and Queens in 2031; and then Manhattan in 2032, according to City Hall.
Criminal justice activists have pushed for decades to close Rikers Island, which has housed jail inmates since the 1930s.

In 2019, the New York City Council voted to close the jail complex and replace it with newer jails located in the city's boroughs, with local lawmakers invoking the names of former prisoners who died, including Kalief Browder, who took his own life at age 22 after being held for three years at Rikers.

At the time, city officials had also called for shrinking the jail population to accommodate the closure, but ran into opposition from critics who argued doing so would mean more violent criminals on city streets.

title: Reporter says Texas execution was like no other he's witnessed before
summary: There were immediate warning signs that something was amiss in the execution of Reinaldo Dennes, but no one could have predicted how the condemned killer would react to the injection of the powerful sedative pentobarbital
story: There were immediate warning signs that something was amiss in the execution of Reinaldo Dennes, but no one could have predicted how the condemned killer would react to the injection of the powerful sedative pentobarbital

HUNTSVILLE, Texas -- After covering capital punishment for The Associated Press in Texas since 1983 — and witnessing nearly 500 lethal injections — I've become accustomed to a certain routine in the procedure, although I'm reticent to describe any execution as “routine.”

It was 6 p.m. Thursday — a bell from a nearby church tolling the hour — when I and other witnesses climbed the concrete steps into the more than century-old Huntsville Unit of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. We were led into a reception office for what normally is a very brief period to await the short trek to the death chamber to watch condemned killer Reinaldo Dennes die.
A large state of Texas clock on a wall ticked off the moments. By about 6:20 p.m., we still hadn't moved.

I knew one of two situations was likely: Dennes was resisting the execution team's attempts to insert a pair of intravenous needles into his arms, or the execution team was having difficulty finding a suitable vein for the needles.

Thirty minutes later, as we were led into the chamber by corrections officers, Dennes appeared docile. His eyes were closed and his head was pointed toward the ceiling. His white prison garb was not disheveled and no additional restraints were applied to his head, meaning no evidence of a struggle.

Now I've seen over the years any number of final statements and reactions from condemned inmates who spoke in foreign languages, prayed, recited poetry, sang, cursed, expressed love, insisted on their innocence or acknowledged their crime and one who even told a joke.
Dennes was like no other.

Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Dennes talked about being “extremely blessed” by the love of “the father” and hoped his family and loved ones “get to know this great gift and great grace of God the father.”
He told the warden: “Go.” Almost immediately as the procedure began, his demeanor changed.
“The pain!” he exclaimed. “Go! Go!”
For nearly three minutes — and standing there furiously scribbling notes, I thought it seemed much longer — Dennes repeatedly moaned.

“Take me father! ... Take me into your arms! ... Take me father!” He occasionally interjected his cries with obscenities, a grunt and then groans. His right leg was “killing me,” he said, likening the sensation to a cramp.
“I don't think this is normal,” he said at one point.
On that, he was right. I've heard inmates say the lethal drug was hot or cold, that they could smell or taste it, or that it hurt.
At 7:08 p.m., after being examined by a physician, he was pronounced dead.

Texas prison officials said the execution team had difficulty finding suitable veins. Spokeswoman Amanda Hernandez said after repeated unsuccessful attempts — she couldn't say how many — the technicians found a vein in Dennes' left foot and another on the left side of his neck that were receptive to the IV needles.
I couldn't see. His feet were covered by a sheet and only the right side of his neck was visible to those of us who were witnesses.
The injection sites were in line with the prison system's procedures, Hernandez added. The alternate sites have been used in previous executions, although the need to do so is relatively rare.
Hernandez also suggested Dennes may have been faking, saying he had been complaining about pain from areas where no injections were attempted.
As a reporter, I'd like to find out the truth about the matter. But there's no way to know for sure.

title: A decade after shooting Harambe, the Cincinnati Zoo is reeling from Fiona's death
summary: The Cincinnati Zoo is once again facing the tragic death of a beloved animal
story: The Cincinnati Zoo is once again facing the tragic death of a beloved animal

CINCINNATI -- Months of international backlash cast a shadow over the Cincinnati Zoo after workers decided to fatally shoot a beloved endangered gorilla named Harambe in response to a little boy falling into his exhibit in 2016.

That outrage faded the following year with the premature birth of an adorable hippo named Fiona, this time bringing positive attention to the reeling zoo, which shared her miraculous survival story in videos and blog posts. They showed her taking a bottle, splashing in a pool and learning to run. She captured hearts around the world and helped restore the zoo’s image.
Now, though, the zoo is dealing with another tragedy: Fiona died Thursday more than a week after eating a visitor’s hat.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.

Fiona's death at age 9 led to an outpouring of grief as well as comparisons to the end of Harambe's life, as both were untimely and involved zoo visitors. Some social media users were quick to condemn the zoo, saying it needs to better protect its animals. Others called for compassion.

“As devastated as we are, we cannot begin to fathom the grief that Fiona’s keepers, veterinary team, and the entire Cincinnati Zoo family are experiencing today,” Dino Buddies, a local wildlife outreach company, said in a statement. “We hope that everyone extends these incredible individuals the compassion, kindness, and grace they deserve as they mourn the loss of an animal they loved so deeply.”

After Harambe was killed at age 17, the zoo reopened its gorilla exhibit with a higher, reinforced barrier. Tongue-in-cheek online petitions circulated seeking to add his face to Mount Rushmore and the dollar bill. There was also a more somber “Justice for Harambe” petition that sought to hold the mother of the boy who fell into the enclosure responsible for the gorilla's death. The county prosecutor determined there was no cause for charges.

Fiona swallowed the hat about 12 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air, it struck a ceiling fan and deflected into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the viewing windows. It was an accident, a zoo spokesperson said.

She was not the first zoo animal to die from eating a non-food item that found its way into a pen. Zoos around the world have been warning for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats.

Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
But the accidental nature of Fiona's death hasn't dampened the despair.
“The two saddest days in all my time here in Cincinnati come from the Zoo,” Facebook user Marianne King posted Thursday. The first was Harambe's death and the second was Fiona's, she said.

Joanne Prater, who lives in the Cincinnati suburb of Loveland, was attending a high school fundraiser Thursday evening and said every person she spoke to talked about how sad they were about Fiona's death and compared it to Harambe's.

“They are tokens of Cincinnati. You can’t say Fiona or Harambe without everybody knowing who that is here in Cincinnati," she said. "I guess both of their deaths could have been prevented, but unfortunately accidents do happen.”

title: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
