summary: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower...
story: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower...

WASHINGTON -- The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.

The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.
Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.
A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.

Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said.

Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.”
The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.
“I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

“In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government.
“Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.
The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
“We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said.

Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” adding that he hopes “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.
But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.

Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife.

“Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”

Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe's ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. “Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation,” he said.

Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.
“A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill,” Granholm wrote in a social media post. “But it would still need this president’s signature.”
Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure.

But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would “irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home.” He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment.
Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.

title: Fiona’s death gives parents a chance to teach kids about grief — and life
summary: A beloved 9-year-old hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo has died after swallowing a knit hat
story: A beloved 9-year-old hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo has died after swallowing a knit hat
For many children, the death of Fiona, a beloved hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, may be their first experience with losing an animal they have grown to love, even if they never met her in person.

Fiona, who was 9-years-old, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. Her death has sparked an outpouring of love from around the country for the Nile hippopotamus, with zoo visitors leaving flowers and cards by the statue outside the entrance.

Samantha Haines, a mother in St. Petersburg, Florida, said she initially kept the news that Fiona had swallowed a hat from her 10-year-old daughter, who loves hippos, because she “didn’t want to worry her.” But she told her daughter about Fiona’s death Thursday.
Psychologists and grief specialists say when animals die, the experience can provide opportunities for parents to help children understand death and navigate difficult emotions, including grief.

Haines said they cried together for about 20 minutes before she told her daughter she could add her Fiona-themed ornaments to the Christmas tree in her room. When her daughter emerged, she was distracted by a book about dragons and didn’t want to talk about the hippo.
“I think she just needs a distraction right now,” Haines said. “We have recently experienced a heavy death in the family and have been on the roller coaster of the grieving process already.”
Experts recommend using clear, age-appropriate language to explain that Fiona died and will not be coming back. Phrases such as “went to sleep” can confuse or frighten younger children.
Caregivers also do not need to have every answer. Acknowledging uncertainty and making space for questions can help children feel comfortable expressing their emotions.

Parents can also acknowledge their children’s feelings and share their own sadness with them. Experts say there is no single right way to grieve, and children may need time and repeated conversations to process the loss.

“People are so averse to talking about death and grief, but it is the one thing that is guaranteed: We are all going to die. We need to be open to talking about that,” Deirdra Flavin, CEO of the National Alliance for Children’s Grief, previously told The Associated Press.

Kaitlyn Hermsen, a mother of four in Oconomowoc, Wisconsin, says her 8-year-old daughter would visit zoos to see hippos, and became obsessed with Fiona’s story, especially because she and the beloved animal were close in age.
“Her love for hippos is so big that we traveled all the way from Wisconsin to Cincinnati to visit her,” Hermsen said.
She said telling her daughter about Fiona’s death was heartbreaking.
“Through the sadness, she found comfort in imagining Fiona in heaven with our dog, Loki, and her favorite cow, Betsy.”

Comments flooded a Facebook fan page for Fiona, with people expressing a mix of sadness and frustration. Some urged others not to direct their anger at the family of the visitor whose hat landed in Fiona’s enclosure, while others shared happy memories of visiting her.

Remembering Fiona through drawings, photographs, favorite videos or stories about her life can also provide comfort and a sense of closure. Such activities can help children celebrate the joy Fiona brought to others while beginning to understand that death is a permanent but natural part of life.
Mumphrey reported from Flagstaff, Arizona.

title: Judge tells prosecutors that terrorism case defendant can read violent religious passages
summary: A federal judge told federal prosecutors that the government must permit a man jailed on terrorism charges access to religious materials describing an important figure in Muslim history even if passages advocate violence
story: A federal judge told federal prosecutors that the government must permit a man jailed on terrorism charges access to religious materials describing an important figure in Muslim history even if passages advocate violence

NEW YORK -- A federal judge told federal prosecutors Thursday that the government must permit a man jailed on terrorism charges access to religious materials describing an important figure in Muslim history even if passages advocate violence because similar violent texts in the Bible would never be banned from distribution in jails.

Judge Colleen McMahon made the statement as she presided over a hearing where Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, repeatedly tried to speak directly to her, leading U.S. marshals to usher him quickly out of the courtroom at one point.
His lawyer, Andrew Dalack, said the government had denied al-Saadi access to a biography of a man who lived 1,300 years ago and who McMahon described as a “seminal figure in Muslim” history.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Jeffrey Coyle said the materials sent by al-Saadi's family contained passages that “justifies the blood revenge of enemies.”

McMahon stopped just short of issuing a ruling from the bench that religious texts do not pose a threat to the special administrative measure that severely limit al-Saadi's communications with the outside world. But she made her opinions clear.
“Excuse me,” she said, interrupting the prosecutor at one point. “There are passages in the Bible that could be read the same way.”
She cited “statements of immense violence” in the Bible, including the book of Joshua calling for killings “in the most vicious and disgusting way.”
The judge also said she didn't understand why he'd been denied newspaper articles about support for him in Egypt and a demonstration carried out on his behalf.
Al-Saadi was charged last week in a rewritten indictment accusing him of trying to pass secret messages to Iranian operatives planning an attack on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force.

The superseding indictment alleged that he had a role plotting to attack the Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, in western England, even though he’d been arrested last spring. A group of men were detained on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the air base where U.S. bombers are stationed.
Prosecutors say that al-Saadi used coded language in phone and video calls to his mother and sister in Iraq to pass messages encouraging associates to carry out the air base bombing.
Dalack said his client did not do it.
“Mr. al-Saadi denies that he’s using coded messages in communications with his family. If you look at what the government points to, it relies on pure surmise and speculation,” Dalack said.
Coyle said the government is not letting al-Saadi have any more calls with his family.

According to the indictment, al-Saadi was among three men who conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terror attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.

In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. He called himself a “prisoner of war.” He has been held without bail since.

Both Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say al-Saadi was a Kata’ib Hizballah commander.
Al-Saadi tried several times at Thursday's hearing to speak directly to McMahon. Speaking through an Arabic interpreter, his first outburst came as he was being arraigned on the new allegations.
Asked to enter a plea, he said: “I’m a statesmen. not a businessman.” Then, he added: “I'm innocent of the charge.”
“I'll take that as a not-guilty plea,” the judge responded.
During another outburst, McMahon told him: “It's really not a good idea for you to talk to me today.”
Shortly afterward, he was hurried out of court by marshals as he began shouting toward the judge that he wanted his lawyers replaced by attorneys that his family will retain.
After his current lawyers met with him, Dalack said al-Saadi had decided to return to jail rather than come back into the courtroom.
“He's obviously quite frustrated,” Dalack said.
The judge said she was adjourning proceedings in his case to give his family time to search for lawyers. She set a Feb. 10 date for him to return to court.

title: Everyone is a friend: Trump's meetings in Asia show his varied approaches to shifting world order
summary: President Donald Trump has engaged in two significant geopolitical meetings during his Asia trip
story: President Donald Trump has engaged in two significant geopolitical meetings during his Asia trip

WASHINGTON -- U.S. President Donald Trump huddled with leaders from longtime partners Japan, Australia and India in a resort conference room in Manila, Philippines, this week to strengthen a partnership called the Quad that is meant to counter China.

Two days later, Trump warmly greeted Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in an unprecedented, trilateral summit of countries that have been long considered rivals to take on “new opportunities and approaches on a range of very important issues."

Trump effusively described all these leaders as friends, but the meetings highlighted some key differences. The two geopolitical gatherings on the same whirlwind Asia trip reflect the U.S. president's varied foreign policy approaches at a time when the world order is shifting.

“The Quad, comprising four democracies that uphold the rule of law, represents the post-World War II international order,” said Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow focused on Asia at the Hudson Institute. “The trilateral, meanwhile, raises the prospect of a very different order — one in which three great powers stand above the rest, recognize each other’s spheres of influence and refrain from interfering in each other’s core interests.”

In a no-frills hotel conference room in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, Trump sat down with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Covered in blue cloth, four long tables formed the appropriate shape of a quadrilateral, with each government taking one side. The leaders were flanked by their Cabinet members. There were no decorations but a mandatory display of national flags.
Before the meeting, the four leaders took a photo together, where Trump took questions from reporters and joked around with his counterparts.

Calling the leaders “friends of mine," Trump turned to Albanese and patted him on the back, as the Australian premier nodded. Trump then threw his thumb toward Modi and joked, “And by the way, he’s a very tough man,” before pointing to Takaichi and saying, “and she may be even tougher.”
Modi didn’t crack a smile, but Takaichi chuckled. Trump turned back to Albanese: “And we? We’re OK, too,” to which the Australian laughed.
Moments earlier, Modi, apparently impatient, gestured to end the press conference to no avail as Trump kept taking questions.

The scene was much grander but far less spontaneous two days later when Trump joined Putin and Xi at a massive ring-shaped table with a burst of pink flowers in the middle at a state-owned resort in Shenzhen, China. The room was spacious with marble flooring, crystal chandeliers and jade sculptures.

Three leaders were alone at the table, seated some distance from one another. Xi read from a prepared script, with hardly any expression on his face. Putin looked at the documents in front of him, while Trump sat back with a slight smile on the opposite end of the table.
In Manila, Trump said at the Quad meeting that “we're all friends” and suggested that the leaders from Japan, Australia and India can reach him directly.
“We talk a lot when they have a problem, when they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open and the Oval Office is always open to you,” Trump said.
Talking to reporters, Trump praised his fellow Quad leaders, calling them “phenomenal people."
“And they’re friends of mine, so that helps,” the U.S. president said.

On Thursday, Trump described Xi and Putin similarly, addressing both as his “friend." At the airport in Shenzhen, Trump got a rare greeting there from Xi and even an unusual hug from the Chinese leader.

At a welcoming ceremony for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation grouping, Putin joined Xi and Trump on stage. He and Trump shook hands and held each other briefly by the arm, with Xi looking on and smiling.
At the trilateral meeting, Trump argued that differences among countries should not forestall talks.
“Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And, uh, we feel the opposite,” Trump said.

The joint press release from the Quad leaders called the group “a force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability, and prosperity" and laid out areas for cooperation, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and maritime surveillance.
The Chinese, U.S. and Russian governments issued a statement committing to reforming the United Nations, planning to increase petroleum supplies and affirming opposition to nuclear wars.

While the Quad statement was substantive and reflective of the alignment of the four nations, the trilateral statement was largely symbolic. Still, it offered more detail than expected, said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia.
With language about nuclear weapons and future dialogue, “it is a major concession by China,” said Kagan, now a senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

title: Iran war costs surpass $48B as lawmakers demand unreleased estimates on base damage
summary: The Iran war’s costs have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13
story: The Iran war’s costs have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13

WASHINGTON -- The costs of the Iran war have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13, but because that total does not include damage to U.S. bases attacked in the Middle East, lawmakers are pushing for the Pentagon to provide those figures.

Arthur Miller, a Pentagon budget official, provided the latest overall cost estimate Thursday to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering his nomination to be Navy comptroller. The $48 billion figure includes the costs of military operations, as well as for replacing equipment and munitions.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut pressed Miller for an estimate on damage to U.S. installations, which Miller said he didn't have. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the committee’s chair, directed Miller to try to provide an answer as soon as possible.
An Associated Press analysis found that Iran attacked aircraft hangars, systems that detect incoming strikes, warehouses, troop housing and more, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.

The war's price tag has been a flashpoint in Congress, with debates over costs intensifying as the Trump administration asks lawmakers to pass a $1.5 trillion defense budget. After the unpopular war and its economic effects contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections, financial battles over the conflict will only escalate once Democrats take control of Congress in January for the remainder of President Donald Trump's term.
The Pentagon has faced growing calls from Democrats to release estimates on the damage Iran has done to American bases in the Middle East through missile and drone attacks.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on the costs of the war at his confirmation hearing Tuesday for the permanent job.

Citing independent estimates and media reports, Warren said the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian shipping costs about $32.5 million a day, while an Iranian attack on the Navy’s regional headquarters in Bahrain did at least $400 million in damage.

Cao confirmed the figure for the blockade but said he could not offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because “it’s a nonpermissive area for us to go." Cao told a reporter months ago that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”

title: Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO ever. What that means, by the numbers
summary: Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking past the record for money raised as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to reach an initial public offering
story: Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking past the record for money raised as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to reach an initial public offering

Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking all records for money raised on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company.
The price tag on its shares was enough to put the value of the San Francisco company well beyond $1 trillion.

That kind of number was once unheard of for a company's first moments trading on the stock market. But an acceleration in corporate wealth — and most recently the AI boom — has changed that. Anthropic is the second business to debut with a value over a trillion dollars (following SpaceX just months ago), and will join a handful of other tech giants that measure their wealth by figures reaching 13 digits.

Time will tell how Anthropic ultimately fares on the public market. The Claude maker decided to proceed with its IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, fears of a possible AI bubble and growing unease among the public about the technology's risks overall.
Here are some numbers to help understand Thursday's IPO.

That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of Thursday's trading, it offered 980 million shares priced at $83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about $75 billion in June.
The next biggest IPO hauls went to South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix ($26.5 billion in July) and oil giant Saudi Aramco ($25.6 billion in 2019).

The initial price per share was set at $83. But that spiked more than 30% to open at $111.50 a share — pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to $2.01 trillion just before noon ET.

By market close Thursday, Anthropic finished its first trading day at $97.17 per share. That's still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly $1.75 trillion.
In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of $2.1 trillion. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to $1.95 trillion.

Apple currently leads the pack at $5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft ($3.8 trillion) and Nvidia ($3.6 trillion), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S&P 500 index yet.
Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over $1 trillion. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018.
That would surpass the roughly 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) between Earth and the sun.
The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. $1 trillion is a thousand times greater than $1 billion. And a million times more than $1 million.
There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the U.S. Census Bureau. If $1 trillion was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost $122.

title: Prosecutor declines to charge white officer who fatally shot Black man in Wisconsin
summary: A Wisconsin prosecutor is not filing criminal charges against the police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July
story: A Wisconsin prosecutor is not filing criminal charges against the police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July

MADISON, Wis. -- The Madison police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in July, sparking racial justice protests and renewed calls for police reform, will not face criminal charges, a prosecutor announced Thursday.

Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, a white officer with more than a decade of experience in law enforcement, fired the shots that killed Corey Ruiz on July 22. Baitinger-Peterson was one of four officers who responded to calls about someone checking out parked cars and an alleged burglary attempt, police said. They surrounded Ruiz, who was on a bicycle.

“I conclude it was reasonable for the officer to use deadly force when this person resisted officers, produced a knife, and was not affected by multiple attempts to use Tasers while officers attempted to take him into custody,” Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne said in a statement announcing his decision.

The Wisconsin Department of Justice said immediately after the shooting that two officers attempted to use a Taser on Ruiz but weren’t successful. Ruiz “brandished a knife and injured” Baitinger-Peterson, the department said.

Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents Ruiz’s family and had called for the officer to be charged, said in a statement that there was nothing in the videos that the district attorney showed them on Thursday to justify the shooting.

“The medical examiner told the family that if the officer had not fired that shot to his head, Corey would have survived,” Crump said. “It was clearly an excessive use of force. This police killing in Madison, Wisconsin, was unjustifiable, unreasonable, unnecessary, and unconstitutional.”

Ozanne said he reached his decision after reviewing evidence that included police reports, diagrams, surveillance videos, police squad car videos and citizen videos. Madison police officers do not wear body cameras.
“In the video you see they tackle him, they tase him, they kick him and then the police officer executes him,” Crump said during a news conference. “The video is the objective unbiased witness here.”
“That is an execution,” he said. “When you are shooting a man who is on the ground, three (times). It hits him in his chest and the kill shot hits him in his head.”
Crump said the medical examiner told the Ruiz family he would have survived had the third shot not been fired and hit him in the head.
Ozanne said his decision was a correct interpretation of the law.

“A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law, however I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand,” the prosecutor said. “The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not.”
Baitinger-Peterson has not replied to an email seeking comment.

Executive Director Jim Palmer of Wisconsin Professional Police Association, the police union, said in a statement the decision that the officer's use of deadly force was legally justified “is supported by the evidence and consistent with the legal standards governing the use of force by law enforcement officers.”

It was the third time since 2012 that Madison police had shot and killed someone in the same neighborhood. The killing sparked days of protests and forced the city to reckon with calls for police reform to address racial justice issues.
Baitinger-Peterson and the other three officers who interacted with Ruiz that day have been on paid administrative leave since the shooting.

While bystanders captured the confrontation on video, there is no body camera footage because Madison police officers don’t wear them. All Madison police officers could be equipped with body cameras by the end of 2027 thanks to a $350,000 donation from a local nonprofit that city officials announced in September.
The donation will help cover operational expenses, while other costs are being funded through grants and other means.
Associated Press journalist Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed.

title: Illinois man pleads not guilty over thwarted mass shooting at Hindu temple
summary: A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Chicago-area Hindu temple has pleaded not guilty to all charges
story: A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Chicago-area Hindu temple has pleaded not guilty to all charges
CHICAGO -- A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Chicago-area Hindu temple that officials say was only thwarted when his gun jammed pleaded not guilty to all charges Thursday.

Alexandros Paporakis was indicted by a grand jury earlier this month on nine charges, including terrorism and armed violence, both felonies. Paporakis also faces weapons-related charges, including possessing a firearm without a serial number.
Those charges could carry a maximum sentence of life in prison, his attorney, Fedor Kozlov, told reporters. Kozlov said he filed a demand for a jury trial.

Authorities say Paporakis planned to attack a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, on Oct. 11, the first day of the Hindu holiday of Navaratri. Paporakis drove to the temple’s parking lot and tried to fire at a person outside, court documents show. Police say the gun jammed.
Police say Paporakis, who was arrested later that day, told a co-worker that he would try again.

Prosecutors say Paporakis wrote in a document that he was a neo-Nazi and white supremacist who fantasized about killing non-white people. The indictment alleges he wrote that he intended the shooting to terrorize Indian immigrants.
Police say they recovered a rifle, ammunition, a tactical vest and a patch “displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism” from his house.
Paporakis has not been charged with a hate crime, despite calls from local and national South Asian leaders for state and federal authorities to do so.
Paporakis briefly appeared in court Thursday in a tan jumpsuit alongside Kozlov, who announced his not guilty plea. He is due back in court on Jan. 7.
He remains in detention after a judge ruled his release would pose a threat to the community. Kozlov said Paporakis is being held in a medical facility in the Cook County jail.
He is aware of the gravity of what he is accused of, and is “taking it day by day,” Kozlov said.
“He sees the world as a 19-year-old, in my mind, child," Kozlov added. “It’s hard to describe and understand how he feels and how he processes it.”
Prosecutors declined to comment following Thursday's hearing.

Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Central Park's horse-drawn carriage drivers sue NYC over incoming ban
summary: Central Park’s horse-drawn carriage drivers have sued New York City to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry
story: Central Park’s horse-drawn carriage drivers have sued New York City to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry

NEW YORK -- Hold your horses: Central Park's horse-drawn carriage drivers sued New York City on Thursday to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry.
The law — approved after the death of a teenager last spring — is set to stop the carriage rides by June 2028.
But the union representing carriage drivers filed a federal lawsuit in Manhattan attempting to have the ban struck down, arguing the city is taking away their livelihoods.
“The City’s approach can be summarized in twelve words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” the lawsuit reads.

The lawsuit is the latest turn in a long fight over the carriage rides, as animal welfare activists and industry supporters have tussled over whether the carriage rides amount to animal cruelty or are simply a romantic throwback to the city's past.

At a bill signing ceremony at City Hall on Thursday, Mamdani lauded the role of horses in the city’s development but said the animals should no longer be hauling tourists around a perpetually busy Central Park among joggers, cyclists and other passersby.
“Our city has changed and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” said Mamdani, a Democrat.

City lawmakers reignited their push for a ban earlier this year in response to the death of 18-year-old Indian tourist Romanch Mahajan, who died after jumping from a runaway carriage in what appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park.

Over the years, horses have collapsed or gotten startled and run off into cars or other objects. In response, the city has put various safety regulations in place for the industry, including veterinary checkups, vacation time for horses and a retirement age for the animals.

City Hall has promised to release a career transition plan for those in the carriage industry next April that includes job training, educational pathways and stipends, though drivers argue their future remains uncertain.

"Despite the good intentions of the mayor, the protections he outlined recently should have been written into the legislation," said John Samuelsen, head of the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage drivers.
The union's lawsuit argues the law is unconstitutional and that the city violated local legal procedures when it approved the law. It names the mayor and various other city officials as defendants.
A spokesperson for the city's law department said it is reviewing the case.

title: Maine parents sue town over autistic daughter's metal rooster statues
summary: A fight over whether giant metal roosters in Maine are illegal advertising or artwork that comforts an autistic child has landed in federal court
story: A fight over whether giant metal roosters in Maine are illegal advertising or artwork that comforts an autistic child has landed in federal court
A fight over whether giant metal roosters in Maine are illegal advertising or artwork that comforts an autistic child has landed in federal court.

David and Sara LeBlanc sued the town of Ogunquit this week, alleging that enforcement of its sign code violates their First Amendment rights. They want to display the roughly 6-foot-tall (1.8 meters) ornaments for their daughter, Pyper, but the town considers them advertising for the couple's adjacent restaurant, the Omelette Factory.
“The roosters are a symbol of one thing: How much we love our daughter,” David LeBlanc said in a statement. “But the town made up an entirely different meaning for them.”

After issuing multiple fines, the town granted the couple a disability variance that allows them to keep two roosters but specifies that they must be attached to a railing. More fines followed when the couple declined to build a railing and chained them to two posts instead. They have since removed all of the tin statues, according to the lawsuit, which points out that other local businesses display lobster buoys, antique farm equipment and large tiki statues without incurring fines.

"This is governmental discrimination based on the content of speech and the identity of the speaker," the lawsuit states. “Such discrimination is presumptively unconstitutional, and the Town cannot justify it.”

The LeBlancs are represented by the Institute for Justice, which won a similar case in New Hampshire in 2025 when a judge sided with a bakery owner in a dispute over a large mural high school students painted on his building. The town of Conway had argued the mural featuring doughnuts and other baked treats was a regulated sign, but the judge found the town infringed on the bakery owner's free speech rights.

Ogunquit's town clerk, Christine Murphy, did not respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday. Meanwhile, many of the LeBlancs' original roosters have been adopted by local residents and businesses, and their supporters around the world have been buying their own to display.
“Every time Pyper spots another rooster in someone's yard, her face lights up,” Sara LeBlanc said in a statement. “This town has embraced her. We wish the town government would, too.”
____ Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

title: UK, EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, reshaping post-Brexit relationship
summary: UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship
story: UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship
BRUSSELS -- UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.

A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.

Burnham said the two sides would agree to a “pragmatic” set of deals that will make it easier for food products and young people to move between Britain and the bloc, but leave big questions about the relationship unanswered. Months — likely years — of negotiations lie ahead on everything from student fees to manufacturing rules.
“The deal is done,” a British government spokesperson said, adding that details would be published in a joint statement later.

Burnham was scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.

Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
“The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” he said this week.

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.”
Burnham pitched the package of agreements expected to be agreed Friday as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people.”
He said “a closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe.”
The deals are set to include an agreement for up to 100,000 young adults from Britain to live and work in EU countries for up to three years, and the same number of Europeans to come to the U.K.

There will also be an emissions trading agreement and a deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products that will make things cheaper and easier for British exporters to Europe. Burnham said Friday the deals could add 0.5% to Britain’s economy — he'd previously set it at 0.4%.

But nothing in U.K.-EU relations is ever quick or simple. An EU official said the package is contingent on the two sides reaching agreement on university tuition fees in the next six months. EU negotiators want European students to pay domestic fees if they study in Britain rather than the higher fees for foreign students, something the U.K. has resisted. The official said negotiations had not been easy but they sensed good will to resolve the issue.
The official was designated to brief reporters about the summit but only on condition that they not be named.
Talks are also continuing on Britain's desire to have access to the bloc’s “made in Europe” rules for manufacturing.
To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain’s independence.

“I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again,” Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told the BBC. He said “it’s perfectly clear that this very, very soon becomes a debate about: do we rejoin or do we stay out?”

The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.’s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

“Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential,” Costa said ahead of the meeting. “By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond.”

Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country’s intentions.

Ireland’s ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, “there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant.” If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants.”
Lawless reported from London.

title: Number of people seeking unemployment aid ticks higher yet still low historically
summary: Slightly more people applied for U.S. unemployment benefits last week, though layoffs remain low and most American workers enjoy solid job security
story: Slightly more people applied for U.S. unemployment benefits last week, though layoffs remain low and most American workers enjoy solid job security
WASHINGTON -- Slightly more people applied for U.S. unemployment benefits last week, though layoffs remain low and most American workers enjoy solid job security.

The Labor Department said Thursday that jobless claims ticked up to 203,000 from a revised 202,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, rose 2,000 to 197,750.

Applications for unemployment aid are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. This year, claims have remained at a historically low level below 220,000.

The report suggests that most companies are confident enough in the economy and their sales to hold onto their workers. At the same time, hiring has been sluggish, resulting in a “low-hire, low-fire” job market.
Even so, job creation has improved in the past few months. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists forecast, while the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, from 4.2%.

The U.S. economy is expanding at a solid pace as consumer spending has remained resilient despite elevated inflation, which has eroded Americans’ inflation-adjusted earnings. Investment in data centers is also powering the economy.

Yet the growth has spurred only limited hiring. Many economists are watching job data closely to evaluate whether artificial intelligence is displacing workers, but so far it hasn’t led to a pickup in layoffs. Some companies may be delaying hiring as they implement the technology.

The economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, up from just 2.2% in the previous three months. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta forecasts that it will expand at a similarly healthy 3.2% pace in the final three months of the year.

title: Sen. Tim Kaine says he will force votes on human rights consequences of US policies in Russia
summary: Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia says he will force a vote on the Senate floor to require President Donald Trump's administration to calculate the human rights consequences of its policies in Russia
story: Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia says he will force a vote on the Senate floor to require President Donald Trump's administration to calculate the human rights consequences of its policies in Russia

WASHINGTON -- Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine says he will force a vote on the Senate floor in the coming weeks to require President Donald Trump's administration to calculate the human rights consequences of its policies in Russia.

Kaine is introducing the resolution on Thursday under an arcane provision of a foreign policy law that allows any senator to trigger a vote requiring a report on a country’s human rights practices. His measure would request more information about the effects of a diesel deal with Russia that was struck by the Republican president in October and that waived sanctions against Moscow and allowed for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel.

The measure would also require the State Department to report on the consequences of other U.S. policies as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the Pentagon delayed the delivery of Patriot air defense interceptors and that U.S. intelligence that warns of incoming Russian attacks against his country had been interrupted.

Trump said in announcing the deal on Oct. 9 that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote on social media. He did not address the sanctions or Russia’s war but said, “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority.”

If passed, the resolution would ask the State Department to calculate how Trump's policies have affected Russia’s ability to wage war in Ukraine and if they have caused or worsened human rights abuses. It also asks for an update on the current status of negotiations to end the war, which Russia launched in February 2022.
Kaine says he hopes the resolution, which he calls a “test of good faith,” can pass with bipartisan votes.

“If they were to give us a nonstarter human rights report that whitewashes Russia’s record, that will tell us a lot and that will tell the American public a lot," the Virginia senator said in an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday.

The resolution — coming as Trump had just wrapped up a meeting in China with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping — is part of Senate Democrats’ strategy since the beginning of Trump's second term to force votes on reversing parts of his agenda. Kaine has led efforts to force multiple war powers votes, including several on the war in Iran.

Kaine also triggered a vote last year on a resolution to require more transparency from the Trump administration about the human rights effects of deportations to El Salvador. The Senate, controlled by Republicans, voted along party lines to block it.

The strategy has proven effective for Democrats as they have taken floor time from majority Republicans and forced them to go on record on the Iran war and other issues ahead of this year’s midterm elections, in which Democrats ultimately won control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a decisive rebuke of Republican governance in Washington.

Kaine said he will continue to find ways to trigger votes even when Democrats take the Senate majority next year. Unlike most bills, the privileged resolutions he has introduced under the Foreign Assistance Act, the War Powers Act and other foreign policy laws prompt a quick vote within weeks and bypass committees.
Getting past a presidential veto will be hard, Kaine concedes, but, “I want to make everybody here own what’s going on” and be accountable for their votes.
“We have to put bills on the president’s desk,” Kaine said.

title: Mental competency at issue in US criminal case against Meghan's father
summary: A judge scheduled a mental competency hearing for the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex
story: A judge scheduled a mental competency hearing for the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex

TAMPA, Fla. -- A judge scheduled a mental competency hearing Thursday for the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, two weeks after he was arrested in Florida and charged with storing child sexual abuse material in California.

Thomas Markle was released after his arrest at a senior care center but was ordered to jail four days later, on Nov. 10, when authorities accused him of cutting off his electronic ankle monitor. A judge also ordered him to be examined by a mental health professional.
A hearing was set for Thursday afternoon in federal court in Tampa, Florida. Prosecutors declined to comment Wednesday. Markle's lawyer did not reply to an email seeking comment.

Markle’s arrest in Lakeland, Florida, followed the seizure of approximately 78 items from storage units in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, the FBI said in a court filing.
Some images appear to depict him with children, the FBI said.
Markle had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S. and settle in Florida.

The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half brother found child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. The discovery led to a search of the two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.

Meanwhile, in the Philippines, Markle is under investigation for possession and intent to distribute images. The Women and Children Protection Center, a branch of the Philippine National Police, filed a formal criminal complaint against Markle on Monday, police spokesperson Brig. Gen. Allen Rae Co said in a written statement.

The complaint was filed with the prosecutor’s office following an investigation into digital devices found at Markle’s former home in Cebu City, the statement said. The prosecutor’s office will assess the case for possible charges.

Markle did not attend his daughter Meghan’s 2018 wedding to Prince Harry at Windsor Castle. She said at the time he needed to tend to his health. Meghan is an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits.”

title: Iowa residents brace for a lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals
summary: Residents are raising concerns about plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals at an ammunition plant in southeast Iowa
story: Residents are raising concerns about plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals at an ammunition plant in southeast Iowa

DES MOINES, Iowa -- Plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that have become unusable and might explode if moved have residents in southeast Iowa worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.

The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is set for Friday, and officials recommend that residents of a neighborhood in nearby Middletown begin vacating the area that morning. If they can’t leave their homes, they should stay inside and keep windows and doors closed.

“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure.”
Officials also have released maps showing the potential for lead dust to drift north toward other communities. Some schools in the path of the plume have canceled classes.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but there are thousands more in the track of the plume.
The vibrations from the two blasts will be quick but could break old windows in town. The resulting dust is expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said.
While the Army recommends washing cars and cleaning windowsills and outdoor surfaces, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough.

Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered.

"The safety of our people and our neighbors is non‑negotiable,” Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production.

The Army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November. The Environmental Protection Agency on Nov. 13 approved an emergency permit, paving the way for Friday's detonation.

That permit required the Army to track the potential air and dust dispersion and notify the public five days in advance, prompting Sunday's notification to communities as far as 100 miles (160 kilometers) away.

Less than 20 miles (32 kilometers) northeast in Mediapolis, city officials were approached about allowing soil, water and air testing late last month. But they only learned of their potential exposure from the planned detonation Sunday, when the map put them dead-center in the dust exposure area.

Mediapolis Community School District announced Tuesday that the “uncontrollable variables” prompted the decision to close school Friday, with no events or sports practices. The public library also is set to close, and the local fire department will hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles.

The EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample the air, soil and water during and after the detonation, according to city officials. But the city will do its own testing as well to try to assure concerned residents.
“This is probably a first for me. I believe it’s a first for a lot of our citizens,” said Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker. “The biggest issue we’re having is the lack of information.”
Even Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office was first briefed Monday on the public advisory, her office said.

News of the planned blasts also caught the attention of environmental and public health officials in Illinois. They urged the U.S. military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state following the detonations.

The barrels of lead azide had been stored at the ammunition plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, public affairs specialist at the Army Sustainment Command.

During a routine check earlier this year, they found that some of the water had evaporated, causing the lead azide to crystallize. That makes it more sensitive to friction and shock, thus “creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation,” according to an emergency permit approved last week by the EPA.
Moving or relocating it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, officials said. Barati said that possibility increases in cold weather.
“We’re really concerned about the weather situation,” Barati said on moving forward with Friday’s detonation. “We’re really concerned that it will detonate on its own.”
The Army said it put together a panel of experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with the detonation plan.
The barrels are surrounded above, below and on all sides with concrete, which is buried under soil. Sand barriers are stacked two stories high around the soil.
During the detonation, the soil will be sprayed with water and the air will be misted to try to keep the majority of lead on Army property, Barati said.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, said it is encouraging to see that the Army and the EPA are doing all they can to minimize the dust, but it's still unknown how much will end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces.

Lead is a neurological toxicant that can decrease brain activity and development, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy said. He is particularly concerned for toddlers who are at the age of putting everything in their mouth.

According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the contents of the drums using other chemicals were considered. But officials said any plan that involved handling the drums would increase the probability of accidental, fatal detonation.
Hill reported from Las Vegas and Montoya Bryan from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Florida set for record-breaking 20th execution same day as Texas lethal injection
summary: Florida is set to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband, while Texas plans to execute a man convicted of killing a Houston jeweler during a $3.6-million diamond heist
story: Florida is set to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband, while Texas plans to execute a man convicted of killing a Houston jeweler during a $3.6-million diamond heist

Florida is set Thursday to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas plans to execute a man convicted of killing a Houston jeweler during a $3.6-million diamond robbery.

Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, is scheduled to receive a three-drug injection at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison in Raiford. Reinaldo Dennes, 70, is set to receive a lethal injection an hour later at a prison in Texas and become the ninth person executed by that state this year. The planned executions of the two septuagenarians in one day reflect the aging of the U.S. death row population.

Overton was convicted of killing Michael and Susan MacIvor and their unborn child during an August 1991 break-in at their Florida Keys home. Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his office on Jan. 24, 1996.

Florida has carried out more than half of the nation’s 37 executions this year under outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. Thursday's scheduled executions come amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the United States following Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in October.

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wants to bring justice to families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty’s reinstatement in 1976. Thursday's execution would surpass the 2025 total, with two more Florida executions scheduled in December.
Appeals in the cases in Texas and Florida were pending.

The MacIvors were found dead in their Tavernier, Florida, home on Aug. 22, 1991, according to court records. Autopsies determined both had been strangled and that Susan MacIvor, who was eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner also said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.

Investigators collected DNA evidence from the scene, but initially found no match with any samples in the state's database. But then Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors' home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996. Authorities said a sample taken from him matched the sample collected at the MacIvors' home, and he was charged with their killings.
Overton was convicted in 1999 of two counts of first-degree murder and received a death sentence for each. Defense attorneys had argued that investigators had planted the DNA evidence.

Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes had arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours. According to court records, she opened the door for him and his brother the night of the shooting and also distracted the security guard at Dennes’ request.
The guard, who was shot twice but recovered, identified Dennes as his disguised attacker.

Later that evening, police were called to the building and found the jeweler's body upon entering his office, according to court filings. The documents said officers found the jeweler's safe was empty with no signs of the diamonds or the $200,000 in cash he was supposed to have on hand.
The diamonds have never been recovered.
Dennes’ attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove that he killed Szucs.
Prosecutors noted in a recent court filing that Dennes, who came to the U.S. from Cuba with his family as a child, admitted guilt during a Spanish-language interview with Telemundo in 2022.
“I did those things, so I am guilty," Dennes told Telemundo, adding that he regretted taking a man’s life, the prosecutor's filing said.
A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.

title: Charges dismissed against boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. over bad check in Las Vegas
summary: A Las Vegas court has dismissed felony charges against Floyd Mayweather Jr. related to allegations that the boxer wrote a bad check to purchase a watch
story: A Las Vegas court has dismissed felony charges against Floyd Mayweather Jr. related to allegations that the boxer wrote a bad check to purchase a watch

LAS VEGAS -- A Las Vegas court dismissed felony charges against Floyd Mayweather Jr. on Wednesday at the request of prosecutors, following allegations the boxer wrote a bad check to purchase a watch, according to court records.
A hearing in the case that had been scheduled for Thursday was canceled.
Mayweather, 49, was charged in April with theft and passing a check without sufficient funds with intent to defraud.

Prosecutors in Clark County had alleged Mayweather wrote the $200,000 check to Las Vegas designer resale store Gold and Beyond in December 2024 despite having insufficient funds in his account, according to the criminal complaint.
The Associated Press left emails, voice and text messages this week seeking comment with Mayweather’s attorney, Clark County prosecutors and an attorney for Gold and Beyond.

Mayweather, a former five-division world champion, announced his retirement in 2017 with a 50-0 record. After saying earlier this year that he was coming out of retirement, he was scheduled to be in Athens, Greece, for the “Battle of the Legends” boxing match in June. The event was canceled due to a legal dispute with CSI Sports.

CSI sued Mayweather in the Southern District of New York district court alleging breach of contract for allegedly failing to fight Mike Tyson in a separate event. Mayweather denied the allegations in court documents.
Earlier this year, Mayweather was sued in New York over his alleged failure to pay rent at a Manhattan apartment and was in financial disputes with multiple jewelers.
He also filed a lawsuit in New York against his former business manager, alleging a yearslong fraud scheme.

title: Helicopter that crashed, killing 1 and injuring 2, was flying 'extremely' low: NTSB
summary: Investigators say a helicopter that crashed earlier this month in Biscayne Bay had been flying so low that it hit the water on a turn
story: Investigators say a helicopter that crashed earlier this month in Biscayne Bay had been flying so low that it hit the water on a turn

MIAMI -- A helicopter that crashed earlier this month in Biscayne Bay, killing one person and critically injuring two others, had been flying so low that it hit the water on a turn, the National Transportation Safety Board said Wednesday.

The Robinson R44 II helicopter went down Nov. 4 near Bill Baggs State Park off Key Biscayne while on a trip to film a powerboating event offshore, the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said. The pilot died, and a photographer and videographer on board were injured.

The helicopter was making low-altitude turns “extremely” close to the surface of the water, according to the safety board's preliminary report. Some of the helicopter's doors had been removed to facilitate photography and videography. On one turn, the rotor blades hit the water and brought down the aircraft.

The photographer told investigators the helicopter flew low and parallel to a boat's right side, then turned and got ahead of it for a “good shot” as the boat passed underneath, according to the report. Then the videographer observed the rotor blades strike the water.

Television news video of the crash showed the helicopter upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing.

Witnesses in nearby boats made distress calls, and a good Samaritan tried to help one of the victims, Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said. Rescue workers from several local agencies, as well as the U.S. Coast Guard and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, responded to the crash.

title: Book excerpt: "We Thought They'd Never Leave" by Tony Shalhoub with Josie Adams
summary: The Emmy- and Tony Award-winning actor and his daughter collaborate on a book featuring reflections on food and extended family, including their yearly ritual of a week-long summer reunion.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

Emmy- and Tony Award-winning actor Tony Shalhoub's new book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave: Musings on Food and Family" (written with daughter Josie Adams, and published by Gallery Books), offers reflections on food and his extended family, including their yearly ritual of a week-long summer reunion.
Read an excerpt below, and don't miss Tracy Smith's interview with Tony Shalhoub and Josie Adams on "CBS Sunday Morning" November 22!
Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.
Origin Story
What kind of lunatic family willingly gathers fifty-plus people in one place for seven days straight with no catered food, no outside help, and no exit strategy? Mine.

Every July, we converge in Wisconsin like salmon returning to spawn. Only with more card games, more garlic, and slightly less grace. Outsiders never believe it when I explain it to them. Nearly all my relatives, across four generations, cooking every meal from scratch, cleaning up the fallout, negotiating sleeping arrangements, and arguing over who's on the hook for Tuesday breakfast. No, we don't get paid. Yes, we do it every year. And the most bewildered question I'm always asked is ... Why?!

I used to respond with logistics. I'd explain how each family takes a night to cook, how we rotate the duties—head chef, sous chef, cleanup crew—as if we were on a ship, alone at sea with no port in sight. I'd describe how the menu is posted months in advance, how someone inevitably forgets the garlic, how someone else then inevitably overbuys the garlic, how someone else altogether inevitably burns the garlic, and how, miraculously, it all gets eaten anyway.

I'd outline the sleeping arrangements: the cousins packed in bunk beds like sardines, the uncles snoring in recliners, the blow-up mattresses that never survive the week. But logistics only explain how it works, not why it works. And that's the real question, isn't it? Because if you drill down, this reunion is objectively insane. Most sane people spend their summers escaping family obligations—jetting off to beaches, renting cabins far away from their in-laws, finding any excuse to avoid the awkward conversations and mismatched expectations that come with extended kin. We, on the other hand, run toward them—voluntarily spending seven days each summer marinating in each other's quirks, grievances, and toum sauce.

Truth is, a reunion should not be confused with a vacation. It's work. It's heavy lifting—sometimes literally, when you're carrying cases of tomatoes up the steps or hauling coolers of ice across the lawn. It's emotional labor, too: smoothing over past grudges, refereeing card games, and determining which conversations are "on the table" and which are simply "tabled."

Which is why, to explain why we do this, to understand this ritual of ours—the chopping and bickering and feeding of too many people until the table groans—I need to go back a hundred years, to another table on another continent, where the question wasn't how to make food for fifty, but whether there would be bread enough for one.

title: Here are the GTA 6 songs you'll hear cruising around Vice City
summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 players carry out missions to songs by artists such as Cardi B, Lana Del Rey and Travis Scott.
story: Grand Theft Auto 6 relies on a murderer's row of musical hitmakers to provide the backbeat for cruising around Vice City.

The latest installment in the video game franchise, which officially launched on Thursday, features 34 original songs from a range of artists, including Cardi B, Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen. The game's official album was created in partnership with Atlantic Records, and will be available on music platforms such as Spotify and Apple Music beginning on Nov. 20.
Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA series, is also offering fans limited-edition vinyl and CDs featuring the original tracks.
Music is an essential part of the GTA experience for players like 34-year-old Kansas City resident Cameron Logan Cox, who credits the game's music over the years with helping springboard his career.
"I went on to become a filmmaker and director for a hip-hop label," he told CBS News. "I really don't think I would have had that musical affinity if not for GTA."

In addition to the official GTA 6 soundtrack, gamers will be exposed to countless other tracks through "in-game radio," a feature in GTA 6 that allows players to listen to songs from fictional radio stations while they carry out their missions. They can turn on a station while they drive through Vice City, or via their phone.
"My favorite thing in GTA has never been a mission," Cox told CBS News. "It's the car, the radio and nowhere I have to be."

GTA 6 offers 22 stations, according to industry media outlet GameStop. Some have DJ personas, such as the Cocoteo FM station, which is hosted by characters voiced by Puerto Rican singers Bad Bunny and RaiNao, according to Rolling Stone.

GameStop has a list of some of the songs in Vice City. Among the hundreds of tracks are old hits like "Let Your Love Flow" by the Bellamy Brothers and "Pour Some Sugar on Me" by Def Leppard, as well as more recent hits like Chappell Roan's "HOT TO GO!".
