title: Nvidia forms export control panel amid concerns over China sales
summary: Chipmaker creates new committee amid growing concerns that it has allowed restricted products to reach China.
story: Nvidia on Tuesday said its board has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls, a step that comes amid heightened scrutiny of the chipmaker's sales practices to some Southeast Asian companies.

The move comes days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO over revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company. The woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation), had worked for a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, which had bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips.

Nvidia also faces mounting pressure in Washington, D.C., with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressing concern that China is gaining access to the company's advanced chips, which are critical to developing AI models. The U.S. has barred sales of Nvidia's highest-end chips to China due to national security and competitive concerns.
On Monday, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
Congressional pressure grows

Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee, according to a statement on Tuesday from the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," the committee chairs, Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said in the statement.
Nvidia said its existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the new committee and its interim CEO, Colette Kress.

"Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said in a statement.
The company added that the decision to create the committee reflects the board's commitment "to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight."

Nvidia shares have dropped 16% following news of Huang's extramarital relationships and his departure from the company, which has shed more than $700 billion in value in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's business could also take a hit if new U.S. restrictions on sales of semiconductors and chipmaking equipment affect its sales to China, according to Wall Street analysts.

"Any new leadership will be very wary of drawing the ire of either the U.S. Congress or the U.S. Treasury and will consequently err on the side of caution when it comes to authorizing any non-U.S. sales," Louis-Vincent Gave, CEO of investment adviser Gavekal, said in a report.

The spotlight on Nvidia also comes at a delicate time for U.S.-China relations, especially as the countries compete in AI. President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with China's President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.
Chinese government officials warned the U.S. last week against imposing additional guardrails on chip exports, which China said would disrupt global supply chains.

title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
summary: Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, is barreling ahead with its public offering despite mounting concerns about AI going rogue.
story: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector.
In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide.

"We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.

The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025.
Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment.

"We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history."
Referendum on AI

The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established.
Anthropic shares will list on the Nasdaq stock exchange, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT."

More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services.

"This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast."

The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on.

Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year.

"Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing.
Potential obstacles to growth

Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout.

To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI.

"If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing.

AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people losing control of the technology, potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water.
Barreling ahead despite safety concerns

Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out rival OpenAI, which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity.

Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and carry out cyberattacks. In September, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development after one of his company's former researchers said that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade.
In an interview with CBS News, Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI.

title: Hawley, Durbin introduce Roblox safety bill ahead of hearing
summary: The legislation would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration.
story: Missouri Republican Josh Hawley and Illinois Democrat Dick Durbin are introducing new legislation targeting sexual abuse on Roblox and online gaming platforms, CBS News has learned.

The legislation, titled the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration. Roblox is being sued by dozens of families and state attorneys general who claim online predators have been able to groom, extort and exploit kids they meet on the platform.

The measure is being rolled out ahead of an inaugural congressional hearing Tuesday into the popular gaming portal. The hearing, chaired by Hawley, will feature witness testimony from two abuse survivors and a pair of experts.

"I am investigating allegations that Roblox, a popular online gaming platform for kids, has become a breeding ground for sexual predators," Hawley said in a statement. "This week, as my Subcommittee holds the first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox's practices, Senator Durbin and I will introduce new bipartisan legislation to give survivors justice. We must hold these platforms accountable and ensure no child is left vulnerable to exploitation online."

The bill would close loopholes to ensure a child's rights aren't limited in click-through agreements, allow class-action lawsuits and let survivors and families choose whether to bring a claim in public court or through confidential arbitration.

"In the digital age, predators can target our kids from anywhere—including online gaming platforms like Roblox. And sadly, the numbers show that they have," said Durbin. "Therefore, an 'agreement' buried in the terms of service shouldn't limit a child's or family's rights to bring their claim before a judge or jury. I'm proud to partner with Senator Hawley on this bipartisan issue, and I won't stop until this bill—and other key measures to protect children online—are signed into law."
CEO Dave Baszucki was invited to testify at Tuesday's hearing but has declined to appear.

"The claims being made about Roblox are fundamentally misleading and ignore the rigorous safeguards we have in place to help protect users," a Roblox spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. "Roblox's mandatory age checks for chat, age-based content, prohibition on sharing photos or videos via chat, and continuous monitoring and filtering of chat, help set the standard for youth protection online."
In August, Hawley and Durbin launched a joint investigation by the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism into child safety on Roblox.

"Roblox appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over the safety and well-being of our children, and the alleged criminal activity on Roblox warrants congressional scrutiny," the Senators wrote in a letter to the company at the time.

Roblox has 138 million daily active users, ranging in age from five to over 25, according to its latest shareholder letter released at the end of October. The company currently faces nearly 200 lawsuits in federal court and has reached settlements with at least six states over online child safety issues.

This month, Roblox chief safety officer Matt Kaufman wrote that the company continues to partner with law enforcement and "aggressively look for bad behavior and report it through the appropriate channels."

Last year, the company announced it would strengthen its age verification protections for minors. Roblox CEO David Baszucki described the guardrails in an interview with "CBS Mornings" as "what we believe will become the gold standard for safety and civility on the internet."

title: Nvidia's board of directors opposes restoring Jensen Huang as CEO
summary: Nvidia's board isn't considering rehiring Jensen Huang as CEO despite an online petition that has drawn more than 180,000 signatures.
story: Nvidia board members are not interested in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO or in any other role at the chipmaker, according to a source directly familiar with their thinking.

Huang stepped down from Nvidia on Thursday amid an investigation into his extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. His departure from the chipmaker he co-founded more than three decades ago came within days of the relationship becoming public.

At the same time, thousands of Nvidia employees and technology executives, including Elon Musk, have signed a petition asking the chipmaker to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, with the organizers arguing that he "may have been forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case."

The push to reinstate Huang comes as the company named Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as its interim CEO and said it would seek a permanent replacement. Nvidia's stock has tumbled in the past week amid the controversy, chopping more than $500 billion from its market valuation.

"For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," according to the petition, which described itself as an "independent, volunteer campaign" that is "not affiliated with, authorized by or endorsed by Nvidia Corporation or Jensen Huang."

The petition added, "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes ... That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now."

The petition has gained more than 180,000 signatures, including from what it says are more than 9,000 Nvidia employees representing about one in five company workers. Executives, including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke, have also signed the petition, according to its website.
"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X on Friday.
At the same time, Huang is said to be discussing his return to Nvidia with allies, the Financial Times reported on Sunday.
President Trump suggested to reporters on Monday that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.
"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook as Nvidia's next leader.
Long-shot bid

Huang's return to Nvidia is a long shot, according to Wall Street analysts. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for the chipmaker to hire its next CEO from outside the company, arguing that the company needs a major leadership shakeup amid questions about whether sales of its chips to companies in Singapore and other Asian countries circumvented U.S. export controls and ended up in China.
"We will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore," Bessent said on Fox News on Sunday.

Given Bessent's push for Nvidia to look outside the company for its next leader, Huang's return appears unlikely, according to Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli, who told investors in a research note that the "odds of him being reinstated seem quite low."
Dan Ives, a well-known tech stock analyst at Yorkville Ives, downplayed the likelihood that Huang would resume his duties at Nvidia.

"Any talk of a damaged Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles," he said in a note to investors. "For the company, the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette [Kress]."
Prediction market users aren't giving much credence to the idea of Huang's return, with Kalshi traders assigning only a 10% chance of the former CEO returning to that role.
Nvidia shares are poised to continue their decline on Monday, with the stock down $2.39, or 1.5%, to $160.46 in early trading.
Investors will be tuning into Nvidia's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon to hear more about the company's guidance in the wake of Huang's departure.

"The critical question in the immediate term is what management has to say about the 70% sales growth guidance for next fiscal year — does Nvidia reiterate confidence in that or withdraw it given uncertainty about export rules in Washington," Crisafulli said.

title: Here's how Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation unfolded at Nvidia
summary: Jensen Huang's shocking exit as CEO of Nvidia unspooled suddenly, yet signs of trouble had emerged much earlier.
story: Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia caps a tumultuous week for the chipmaker, with his resignation coming less than a week after his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy became public.

But the seeds for Huang's downfall were planted much earlier. The woman with whom he had a relationship, Alice Huang (no relation), arrived on the tech scene in 2023, when she became the managing director of Singapore-based data center Megaspeed International.

Megaspeed, which says it has complied with U.S. laws, would proceed to buy billions of dollars in Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, has been photographed and recorded socializing with Jensen Huang, prompting questions in May from one quizzical investor about their "uncomfortably close relationship."

In a statement on Sunday, Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025, and it denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Below is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's startling resignation:
November 2015

Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, joins investment firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who became her husband, according to the Wall Street Journal.
March 2023

7Road International, originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, is renamed Megaspeed, and ownership of the "neocloud" company is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an enterprise controlled by Alice Huang. She becomes its managing director.
June 2023
Cloud-computing company Shanghai Century Litong is founded. A company linked to Alice's sister, Huang Yu, held an ownership stake.
October 2023
Nvidia designates Shanghai Century Litong as a preferred cloud partner, giving the Chinese company priority access to Nvidia's chips, according to The Information.
Around November 2023
Megaspeed's shares were transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata, and Alice Huang ceased to be listed as a director of the company, according to news site Caixin Global.
June 7, 2024
Information technology firm NetThunder posted a picture on social media of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other tech executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.
End of 2024
Megaspeed's assets exploded from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, according to financial filings reviewed by Reuters.

Shipment records from December 2024 through early 2026, analyzed by short-selling firm Culper Research, suggest that Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported about $4 billion in products from a company that builds equipment with Nvidia chips.
Early 2025

Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, jointly pitched Chinese investors on a Southeast Asia data center project, reportedly telling them they had "no problem securing GPUs" — the graphics processing units Nvidia specializes in — and citing Alibaba as a customer, according to the Financial Times.
Jensen Huang meets with President Trump at the White House. It marks their first of many White House encounters in Mr. Trump's second term.
February 2025
Singapore opens an investigation into Megaspeed and several other companies over suspected false declarations related to the purchase of servers and other offenses, according to Bloomberg News.
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are recorded on video together at a dinner at San Liu Shi Fu restaurant in Taipei, around the time of the Computex tech conference in Taiwan.
July 2025

Jensen Huang says the technology giant has won approval from the Trump administration to sell its advanced H20 computer chips, used to develop artificial intelligence, to China, a reversal of prior administration policy.
"It's so innovative and dynamic here in China that it's really important that American companies are able to compete and serve the market here in China," Huang said at the time.
That same month, Nvidia becomes the first public company to be worth $4 trillion.
February 2026
Chinese police detained Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband and business partner, in connection with suspected stock manipulation, sources told Caixin.

That same month, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country after she downplayed her role at Megaspeed amid the country's investigation into its operations, according to a Bloomberg News report.
Jensen Huang boards Air Force One in Alaska to accompany Mr. Trump on a two-day trip to Beijing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Mr. Trump about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The briefing, which occurred before Jensen Huang joined the trip, was the second briefing Mr. Trump had received from U.S. intelligence about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, the Times reported.
Jensen Huang attends Mr. Trump's state dinner for China's Xi Jinping at the White House.
Jensen Huang attends an AI event at the White House and signs a set of voluntary AI safety standards amid calls for tighter guardrails on the technology.

Jensen Huang writes a message to Nvidia employees admitting that he had an extramarital affair. The same day, Nvidia's board said it had launched an independent investigation amid reports that its CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
The New York Times on Nov. 8 reported that U.S. government surveillance suggested Alice Huang was feeding information directly to Beijing.

At an impromptu press conference at the White House, Mr. Trump said he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the tech exec had indicated he was unaware of Alice Huang's links to China's intelligence services. Mr. Trump also described the Nvidia CEO as an "honorable man" who's "definitely suffering."
Mr. Trump didn't address questions about when he first learned about the spy allegations, only saying, "not too long ago" and that "it didn't make much of an impact on me."
The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a subordinate at Nvidia.
Nvidia's board of directors announces that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately.

title: SpaceX pulls off first Starship recovery from orbit in spectacular fashion
summary: It was the first recovery of a Starship from orbit, a major milestone for a rocket SpaceX founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower launch costs.
story: After a 22-hour stay in space, a SpaceX Starship rocket plunged back to Earth Saturday, enduring the blazing heat of reentry while homing in on its Texas Gulf Coast launch site, flipping vertical at the last moment and settling into the grasp of two huge mechanical arms on its launch gantry.

Throngs of SpaceX employees gathered nearby cheered and applauded as the rocket restarted three of its six methane-fueled Raptor engines to flip upright, rapidly slowing to a near hover as the robot arms moved in for a mechanical embrace, catching the rocket a moment before engine shutdown.

"This is so incredible to see!" said SpaceX commentator Jessie Anderson. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes. Congratulations to our teammates at SpaceX, and to everyone who supported the Starship program."

It was the first such recovery of a Starship from orbit — previous test flights ended with planned ocean splashdowns — marking a major milestone in SpaceX's drive to develop the first fully reusable orbit-class rocket, a vehicle company founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower the cost of launching payloads to Earth orbit, the moon and, eventually, Mars.

The Starship was launched atop a Super Heavy booster Friday using the same pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility on the Texas coast. Standing 407 feet tall, the two-stage rocket is the most powerful launcher ever built, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust at liftoff from 33 first-stage Raptor engines.
After propelling the Starship upper stage out of the lower atmosphere, the Super Heavy first stage attempted its own return to the launch site for capture by the gantry's mechanical arms.

Going into the giant rocket's 15th test flight, SpaceX had successfully recovered the first-stage boosters used in three previous launches. But the Super Heavy launched Friday was diverted to an offshore splashdown because of a guidance problem. The vehicle ran out of fuel and exploded moments before hitting the water.

While a disappointment to the SpaceX team, Musk said in a posting on the social media platform X the problem was a "slight underperformance of engines," adding that "these early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand."
"This booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights," he said.
The Starship upper stage did not disappoint.

Beaming down crystal-clear views from cameras mounted on its steering fins, the spacecraft's belly, covered in heat-shield tiles, glowed red as the ship heated up in a fireball of atmospheric friction.

Crossing the Baja Peninsula and then northern Mexico, the big rocket rapidly descended before flying just north of the launch site, banking and dropping belly first out of low clouds, restarting its engines to flip upright and then falling at an angle toward the gantry, slowing to a near standstill as the arms closed around it.

"The room behind me going absolutely insane," SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said from the mission control center. "These people have done so much to earn this. ... I mean, that was the missing link. That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

But SpaceX will need to successfully launch and recover a large number of Super Heavy-Starships to demonstrate the statistical reliability needed for crewed flights. And the company will need to demonstrate its ability to autonomously refuel Starships in Earth orbit and keep their propellants from boiling away in the space environment.

While the system is designed to be fully reusable, the Starship upper stage uses most of its propellant getting into Earth orbit. NASA wants to use a variant of the Starship to carry astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and multiple Super Heavy-tanker flights will be needed to refuel the lander in Earth orbit before it can head for the moon.

SpaceX plans to begin orbital fueling tests in the next several Super Heavy-Starship flights. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it's open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready in time.

title: Microsoft says it "restored service" after major worldwide outage
summary: A Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams impacted many users, companies and government services.
story: Microsoft said early Saturday it had restored its services after a worldwide outage which involved services like Outlook and Teams impacted users, companies and government operations around the world.
In a post on X, the company said: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions."

The disruption, which lasted over 24 hours, affected a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.
Microsoft said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity, and apologised for the incident.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said Friday on X. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

The outage affected Microsoft's suite of business products, as well as those tailored for personal use by individuals, students and families. Users in more than 70 countries and territories experienced disruptions, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks technology outages.

"Microsoft in a Friday the 13th moment as global outage [causes] a very bad day in Redmond," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives said in an X post Friday. "There will be major questions for MSFT in this global outage."

Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said in a social media post Friday that "technical challenges and failure modes" made the recovery process "more difficult than normal."

"I'm working closely with the engineering team to complete the full post-mortem," Lamanna said in the post. "We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future."
Widespread impact
Microsoft first flagged technical issues just before 1 p.m. ET Thursday. The company updated users about its recovery progress through a series of posts on its Microsoft 365 Status X account.
More than 130,000 users reported issues with Microsoft on Thursday, Downdetector's website shows. However, those reports started to wane by Friday morning as Microsoft worked to restore its services.
The outage disrupted email for hours, hampering work activity for some employees.
"It's just challenging sending reports or things that needed to be approved," one woman told CBS News Los Angeles.
However, some took delight in the slowdown, with social media users posting videos celebrating the freedom of not having access to email.
It's unclear how many people were impacted. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft's website.
Companies worldwide report issues

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported problems connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call on its quarterly earnings because of the outage.
In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024.
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

"They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Texas-based cybersecurity company CrowdStrike blamed a bug in an update that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer computers, setting off a global tech outage in July 2024 that grounded flights, took TV broadcasts off the air and disrupted banks, hospitals and retailers.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, it could "impact the production timeline," he said.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on social media that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage had affected some of its operations, including email responses.
In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were "keeping a close eye on the developments."

title: Audacious California train thieves film multimillion-dollar robberies
summary: The FBI estimated cargo theft losses in the U.S. and Canada reached nearly $725 million in 2025.
story: A ring of thieves allegedly targeted dozens of freight trains in Southern California, stealing more than $22 million in merchandise — and brazenly filming the robberies themselves — before their arrests following a 14-month investigation.

It's just one example of the growing problem of train heists in the U.S. The FBI estimated cargo theft losses in the U.S. and Canada reached nearly $725 million last year — up 60% from the year before. The Department of Homeland Security estimates cargo theft costs the U.S. between $15 billion and $35 billion a year.
Police say these thefts disrupt supply chains, potentially leaving customers with delivery delays and higher prices.

The alleged thieves in California targeted at least three dozen freight trains over more than two years and stole millions of dollars' worth of goods including Nike sneakers, electronics and power tools, federal prosecutors say.

The crew coordinated their robberies through Instagram, the prosecutors said. Then they would board a moving train, cut air hoses or brake hoses to force emergency stops, and haul stolen goods to nearby stash houses.

Almost every step of the thefts was filmed. One video shows a suspect sawing into a cargo container above a moving train, then multiple men moving merchandise. One man even poses for the camera as the theft is carried out.
The stolen items would then be sold on the black market.

Fourteen men were arrested for their involvement in the theft ring. They face charges including conspiracy, theft of interstate railroad cargo, possession or receipt of stolen interstate railroad cargo, and violence against railroad carriers, according to a news release from the Department of Justice. Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman referred to the case as "the granddaddy of all train cargo theft prosecutions in L.A. County."
During a news conference, LAPD Deputy Chief Alan Hamilton remarked that criminal investigations are "always easier when they post their own stuff on social media."

Law enforcement agencies nationwide are stepping up efforts to curb these kinds of theft rings. In October, CBS News took an exclusive look behind the scenes of a first-of-its-kind national blitz where federal agents, railroad police and law enforcement in more than two dozen states worked together to track thieves targeting cargo trains.

During the operation, officials used infrared drone technology to track heat signatures along train tracks and in rail yards. Cmdr. Michael Ware, who leads the Cook County Sheriff's Police Organized Retail Crime and Cargo Theft Task Force, told CBS News the technology is "like a third eye in the sky" that gives law enforcement "an advantage" and collects evidence. He showed CBS News video of one example of two men breaking the seals on a cargo container holding $35,000 worth of electronics.

"A lot of times we apprehend the guys and they come out like there's no way we have no proof. I wasn't in a container and they see the drone footage like 'you got me.' So it's a game-changer," Ware said.

title: 6 reasons stocks are falling, and what you should do about it
summary: The S&P 500 is on track for a seventh consecutive day of losses, marking its longest losing streak since February 2020. Here's what's taking the shine off stocks.
story: The stock market is having its roughest patch since the early days of the pandemic.

Stocks wavered on Friday after tumbling the previous day, with the S&P 500 on track to mark its seventh consecutive day of losses. That would mark its longest losing streak since February 2020, when investors fled the market amid the panicked early days of the pandemic.
The S&P 500 slid 70 points, or about 1%, to 7,105 in early trading, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index tumbled 2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3%.
Here are six factors souring investors' mood, and what experts say you should do about it.
Fears that AI investments might not pay off

Investors are increasingly concerned that the enormous spending on data centers and other infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence may not deliver the hoped-for returns. Anthropic, the first AI lab to go public, has shown rapid revenue growth, but its regulatory filings also point to massive losses — about $104 billion for the first nine months of 2026 alone.

"Those figures explain both the frenzy and the nerves," said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory group. "From here, the market will judge whether the software layer can turn breathtaking growth into lasting profit, and Friday's wobble shows the judging has already begun."
Anti-data center laws could take root

With Democrats set to gain the upper hand in Congress, investors are bracing for new laws that could restrict data center construction when newly elected officials take office in January. Although the shifting political winds aren't expected to halt that buildout, even a modest slowdown could impact the financial results for a range of big tech companies investing heavily in AI.
"The Blue Tidal Wave win and fears about an anti-AI/anti-data center DC" are contributing to the selloff, said Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, in a report on Friday.
The Fed raising interest rates

The Federal Reserve is expected to hike interest rates at its December meeting, as inflation remains well above the central bank's 2% annual target. Raising rates tamps down inflation, but it also makes borrowing more costly, tempering consumer spending and business investment.
"The evidence does not suggest we are on a path back to 2%" without intervention from the central bank, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday.
A crackdown on chip exports

The revelation that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a spy for the People's Republic has sparked calls for stricter export rules to China. The ensuing turmoil at Nvidia, including Huang's resignation, has prompted the Commerce Department to move to restrict sales of advanced AI chips to China.
"The chip industry globally is witnessing a far larger impact from Washington's new export restrictions than initially expected," Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge, said in a report.
Fears over Trump's saber-rattling

Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. That's raising fears that new hostilities could cause a renewed spike in oil prices, adding to inflationary pressures.
"The Iran war remains in a dangerous liminal stage," Crisafulli said.
Government shutdown risks

Lawmakers face a Dec. 11 deadline to extend funding for most federal agencies and prevent a U.S. government shutdown. But there's a risk that efforts in Washington, D.C., to broker a deal could break down, as some congressional Democrats are pushing to block any funding bill that doesn't restrict funding for the Iran war.

Shutdown risks could also intensify next year under a divided government, according to Oxford Economics. The Democratic-controlled Congress could "bring bruising fights over shutdowns and the debt limit, while doing little to curb tariff, immigration and geopolitical uncertainty," analysts with the investment adviser said in a report this week.
What experts advise

Investment pros say that while it's important to stay informed, it's best not to sell stocks in a panic, as that can lead to losses that are tough to recover from. For instance, investors who sold in February 2020 may have lost out on the sharp market gains that followed as the economy recovered from the pandemic.

"We have seen so many peaks and valleys over the decades, with many investors asking us over the last few weeks, is this a March 2000 moment (pre-dot.com bubble) or Fall 2007 vibe (financial crisis buildup)," Ives wrote. "This is a painful tech sell-off that is heavily discounting [that] this 4th Industrial Revolution thesis will take place over the next few years, and that is the wrong move in our view."

title: More than 140 sick on cruise ship that departed Fort Lauderdale, CDC says
summary: The Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess departed Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11 on a 12-night journey.
story: More than 140 passengers and crew on board a cruise ship that departed from South Florida last week have reported becoming sick with a mystery gastrointestinal illness, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says.

According to information provided by the CDC, the Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess departed Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11 on a 12-night journey. The outbreak was then reported days later on Nov. 15.
At least 134 of 2,936 passengers and 14 of the 1,132 crew members have reported symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea, according to the CDC.
In response to the outbreak, Princess Cruises and the crew on board the ship said there have been increased cleaning and disinfection efforts according to their outbreak and response plan.
In addition, passengers and crew who are sick have been isolated.

"Norovirus is often the cause of gastrointestinal illness outbreaks on cruise ships, but we don't always know the cause of the outbreak when we begin an investigation," the CDC said on its website. "Finding the agent that caused an outbreak (causative agent) can take time."
So far, the cause of the illness is unknown.

"Princess Cruises can confirm that a limited number of guests aboard Caribbean Princess have reported mild gastrointestinal illness," the cruise line said in a statement to CBS News Miami. "Our crew responded promptly by implementing enhanced sanitation protocols across the ship, including comprehensive cleaning and disinfection measures."
The statement says that while most guests remain unaffected by the illness, it is continuing to monitor the situation.
According to the CDC, cases of illnesses that have been reported are totals for the entire voyage.
"It does not mean all people are sick at the same time, such as when they arrive or leave a port or ship," the CDC continued.
The Caribbean Princess departed Fort Lauderdale on a round-trip, 12-day Panama Canal trip that is expected to return on Nov. 23.

title: New UFO files show contractor planned vault for "exotic material"
summary: The Pentagon's latest batch of UFO files includes a report from a government contractor detailing plans for an underground vault to store "exotic material or tissue" it was seeking.
story: Washington — The Pentagon released a new batch of UFO files on Friday, including one report from a government contractor detailing plans for an underground vault to store "exotic material or tissue" and recovered "hardware" it hoped to obtain.

The report was among 43 files included in the eighth release of UFO, or UAP, documents. The records mostly consisted of historical documents from the Air Force and CIA dating from the 1950s, with others describing more recent events.
What's in the new UFO files?

The July 2009 report was produced by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies as part of a Defense Intelligence Agency program, funded by Congress at the urging of then-Sen. Harry Reid, to study potential future aerospace threats.

The 538-page document said the company identified the need for "a highly secure underground vault" to store "hardware and biological samples from the corporate world and/or from private individuals and groups located elsewhere, including Brazil." It would be located in Nevada.

"It was recognized by the BAASS administrator that there was no highly secure facility at BAASS to store exotic material or tissue that the organization could obtain," the report said. "Accordingly, the BAASS administrator designed an underground facility to be located in North Las Vegas at the Bigelow Aerospace facility."
The facility would be buried under 15 to 20 feet of dirt and feature a 5,000-square-foot vault with "3 foot thick walls" and a thick steel door.
"Any surface structures protruding from the ground will be extensively camouflaged," the report said.

There's no public record that the vault was ever built. Subsequent BAASS reports the Pentagon has released make no mention of it. A Defense Intelligence Agency official found the company's reports had "limited value" several months later, and the Pentagon's research project ended in 2012. Bigelow Aerospace, BAASS's parent company, laid off its entire workforce in 2020.
A copy of the BAASS report appeared online last year, but Friday's release is the first time the Pentagon has made it public.

Friday's documents also include files and videos of more recent UAP encounters. Three clips captured by the military and submitted to the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office show white dots moving across the screen.
Another file details strange detections captured by a civil air-surveillance radar in 2023. Eight detections were picked up over 84 seconds between 55,000 and 70,000 feet in the sky.

"If the detections were associated with a single continuous track, their cumulative point-to-point displacement would be approximately 38.5 miles, yielding a minimum mean horizontal ground-speed estimate of 1,650 mph," the Pentagon said.
The slide notes that the available data was "not sufficient" to establish that all eight detections were caused by the same object.

The older files in Friday's release include one account from 1953 by Clarence "Kelly" Johnson, the chief engineer for Lockheed who later designed the U-2 and SR-71 spy planes. Johnson told the Air Force that he spotted a dark, elliptical object hanging motionless against a "gold and red" sky while watching the sunset at his California ranch.

"I wondered why this one object was so dark, considering that the sun was behind it. I immediately thought that some aircraft had made an intense smoke trail; so I studied the object closely. It was apparent, after my first few seconds of consideration, that the outline of this object did not change," Johnson wrote.

He said he watched the object through binoculars before it sped off "in a long shallow climb." At about the same time, a Lockheed test crew flying offshore reported chasing what looked like "a very large flying wing" that shrank to "a mere speck."
An Air Force record included in the file categorized the sighting as a lenticular cloud.

UFO
UFO

title: Stocks plunge as investors take cover amid growing uncertainty
summary: The Dow tumbled 1,100 points, while other stock markets also swooned, as Wall Street frets over AI growth and other market risks.
story: Stocks crumbled on Thursday as investors confronted a number of headwinds that could hurt corporate profits and heighten economic uncertainty.

The Dow tumbled 1,101 points, or 2.2%, to close at 49,097, while the S&P 500 slipped 2%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.3%. The swoon in markets was broad, with more than 90% of S&P 500 stocks nosing down.
Stocks were mixed when trading opened on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 370 points, or 1.5%, early in the session, the S&P 500 dipped 0.4% and the Dow gained 0.6%.

Wall Street analysts said no single catalyst accounted for the plunge, but rather pointed to a slew of factors weighing on investor sentiment. Those include ongoing concerns about whether the heavy spending on AI will boost profits, renewed fears that the U.S. and Israel are planning attacks on Iran, and the specter of a potential government shutdown as early as December.

"The slump has set off a scramble of headline searching as people scour the wires to find the most negative sounding news flash," Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge, said in a research note. "People just don't have much enthusiasm for this market, and rallies tend to bring out sellers instead of chasers (there is still a lot of hesitation when it comes to being long AI-linked names, especially picks-and-shovels, and the defensive stuff is quite extended after the recent rally)."

For weeks, investors have fretted about the financial strength of the AI sector amid concerns that the torrent of capital pouring into data centers may not deliver the productivity and profit growth companies are counting on.

More recently, investors were shaken by the resignation earlier this month of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after the revelation that he had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Some lawmakers have increased scrutiny of Nvidia's sales to China and to companies in southeast China, while the Commerce Department this week signaled it plans to tighten export controls on AI chips.

Despite those concerns, Anthropic had a successful stock market debut, with its shares rising as much as 34% in Thursday trading after the company staged the largest initial public offering in history.

On Thursday, shares of AI-related stocks went from morning gains to afternoon losses. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared amid the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8% before swinging to a 1.8% loss. CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents access to them to customers via the cloud, went from a 10.5% morning gain to a 5.5% drop.

Nvidia erased an early gain of 4.7% and flipped to a loss of 2.7%. The chip company has been the face of the AI boom, and its stock has struggled with the worries that have been dogging the entire industry.

It wasn't only tech stocks that tumbled on Thursday. Williams-Sonoma dropped 15.3% after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was just below Wall Street's forecast.
Walmart sank 1.2% even though the retailing giant reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts' expectations.

title: Flooding prompts hundreds of water rescues in Florida
summary: The St. Johns River in Florida reached a new record high, crossing over 18 feet for the first time ever.
story: Extreme flooding in central Florida has led to hundreds of water rescues due to more than 2 feet of rain over the past two days in some locations — and the threat is not over.

There have been more than 100 water rescues in Brevard County, where the St. Johns River reached a new highest level, over 18 feet, breaking a record set 70 years ago. Many of those rescues have come in the city of Cocoa.

"While we may have substantial property damage, we've got vehicles that are damaged, businesses that are damaged, right now we have absolutely no one that has lost their life from this storm," Brevard County Sheriff Wayne Ivey said at a press conference Thursday. "Very minimal injuries across the board. That's the most important thing."
The heaviest rain is now moving north of the Space Coast, hitting Daytona and Jacksonville before heading to the Carolinas this weekend.
The entire block where Robert Spinning lives is underwater.
"I'm worried to death," Spinning told "CBS Mornings." "I don't have flood insurance. I can't afford it."
A flood watch remains in effect for all of Florida's east coast through at least 7 p.m. for another 6 to 8 inches of rain on Friday before things dry out over the weekend.

The St. Johns River will continue to rise through Friday evening and could reach 18.6 feet, which would be a foot higher than the old record from 1953. It's forecast to remain at record height through at least next Tuesday.
Floodwaters wiped away part of the Port Malabar Boulevard Bridge in Palm Bay for the second time this month. The town had just held a reopening ceremony on Monday.

Melbourne is now experiencing its wettest November on record, with over 17 inches of rain so far this month. Cape Canaveral has received more rain than that in just the last 48 hours, checking in at 26.9 inches. Oak Hill, which is north of Cape Canaveral, has received 17.3 inches in the past two days.

The same storm impacting Florida will move north along the East Coast and could develop limited tropical characteristics. It currently has a 50% chance of being named Subtropical Storm Kyle on Sunday, according to the National Weather Service.

title: Mayor Mamdani announces plan to shut down Rikers Island
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled his strategy to shut down Rikers Island and replace it with four smaller jails across the city.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled his strategy to shut down Rikers Island and replace it with four smaller jails across the city.
The city is legally required to close the troubled jail complex by August 2027. The administration closed one Rikers facility earlier this year, but the rest of the complex remains open.
Under Mamdani's plan, the first replacement jail won't open until 2029.
In the meantime, his administration is putting millions toward reducing the jail population and improving conditions.

The plan announced Friday includes $50 million for job training, education, mental health counseling and drug treatment. Another $76 million will go toward community programs and supervision to keep more people out of jail while awaiting trial.
The city also wants to speed up court cases and expand hospital care for people with serious medical and mental health needs.
"We'll work across city agencies to speed up the exchange of evidence and address court backlogs. We do not want any New Yorker to spend a day longer in detention than necessary," Mamdani said.
Department of Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards said the effort is personal. He was once incarcerated at Rikers and said both the inmates and staff have been overlooked.
"At Rikers, out of sight, out of mind is the norm for both people in our custody and our staff," he said.
Richards also said unnecessary pretrial detention can "increase the likelihood of eviction, job loss, and ultimately, rearrest in the future, while case delay harms victims calling for justice."
Another challenge is capacity.
The four new borough-based jails are designed to hold about 4,100 people. That's far fewer than the roughly 6,700 people reported in custody at Rikers in June.
Some community leaders are pushing back.
Jan Lee, the founder of a group called Neighbors United Below Canal, said the plan does not address residents' concerns with construction of new jails.

"It still allows nighttime drilling, still sends heavy trucks through our narrow streets after dark, and still puts the burden of the City's construction schedule on our elderly neighbors and families living just feet from the site," Lee said.
Violence and safety concerns have plagued the facility for years.
Mamdani said assaults at Rikers happen at eight times the rate of similar jails, and inmates are held there nearly four times longer than the national average.

story: An early-morning 4.2-magnitude earthquake rattled the Los Angeles area on Friday.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the earthquake struck about a half-mile north-northwest of Commerce, California, which is about 7 miles from downtown Los Angeles.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass posted about the quake on social media, saying it likely woke up many Angelenos.
"While unsettling, there are no immediate reports of damage or operational impacts, including at LAX," Bass wrote. "The LAFD and City teams will continue to monitor and update as needed."
People reported feeling the quake as far away as Lancaster, California, about 80 miles north of downtown L.A., and Poway, California, about 115 miles to the south, the USGS said.

Shortly after 5:30 a.m., the LA Fire Department provided an update that no significant infra/structure damage or injuries were noted. The spokesperson added that the LAFD Earthquake Mode is complete and normal operations will resume.
"Use this event as a reminder to prepare for inevitable earthquake activity in our region," the LAFD said.

title: Meet Anthropic's 7 co-founders, now worth about $20 billion each
summary: Dario Amodei and the company's other six co-founders instantly joined the ranks of America's richest citizens with the AI giant's initial public offering.
story: Anthropic's seven co-founders are in for a massive payday.

Each of Anthropic's co-founders is now worth about $20 billion, based on their stock holdings and the initial price of its record-setting initial stock offering. Their individual wealth, at least on paper, will put them in the same ranks as Rupert Murdoch and his family, worth a combined $20 billion, and famed inventor James Dyson, who is worth $19.9 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Anthropic, the AI developer behind the popular Claude chatbot, started trading shortly before noon on Thursday on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT." Its shares were priced at $83 each, well above the targeted range of $70 to $78 apiece, suggesting strong investor demand.
That came to pass as its price quickly surged to nearly $115 once trading began. Shares later lost some of their early gains and wound up at $97.17 — still 17.1% higher.
The IPO was the largest in U.S. history, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion public offering in June.

The IPO also turned many Anthropic employees into instant millionaires. The typical worker at the company could be worth more than $40 million after the initial stock sale, CNBC reported, citing regulatory filings and investors.
Here's what to know about the seven Anthropic founders.
Dario Amodei: $19.7 billion

CEO Dario Amodei, 43, co-founded Anthropic in 2021 after working at OpenAI, its chief rival in the race to dominate the artificial intelligence space. He has said he was prompted to launch Anthropic because he wanted to build an AI model aligned with broader human goals, such as advancing scientific knowledge.
His 237.3 million Class A shares are worth about $19.7 billion, based on the $83 per-share price reserved for Anthropic insiders and early investors.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco's Mission District with his sister, Daniela, another co-founder set to realize billions in wealth. Their father was a leather craftsman, while their mother managed public library renovations, according to the New York Times.

Amodei, who earned a Ph.D. in biophysics from Princeton and a bachelor's degree from Stanford, also completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford's medical school, and also worked at Google Brain, the search giant's AI research lab.
Daniela Amodei: $19.8 billion
Daniela Amodei, 39, co-founded Anthropic with her brother after also working at OpenAI, where she held positions including vice president of safety and policy.
Her 238 million shares will be worth about $19.8 billion, based on the $83 per-share IPO price.

Amodei, who holds a bachelor's degree in English literature from the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Stanford University's business school that she hadn't planned to focus on AI. "I really think of myself as a generalist," she said.
She told Stanford that she and her brother decided to leave OpenAI to form Anthropic based on their values.

"We were running towards something versus running away from something. We had this vision in our heads of wanting to create an organization where the values that matter to us around safety and around responsibility were at the forefront of what we were doing," she said.
Tom Brown: $20 billion
Tom Brown, 39, another of the seven co-founders of Anthropic, serves as the company's chief compute officer.
His 240.8 million shares are valued at $20 billion, based on the $83 per-share IPO price.

Before co-founding Anthropic, Brown led the engineering of GPT-3 at OpenAI, according to his company bio. He has a master's degree from MIT, where he majored in computer science with a focus on how it applied to cognitive science.
Jack Clark: $19.8 billion

Clark, 37, co-founded Anthropic with Dario and Daniela Amodei, and now serves as the head of the Anthropic Institute, which the company describes as a think tank focused on researching the societal implications of AI.
Clark's 242.3 million shares are worth about $19.8 billion.

Clark served as policy director of OpenAI before co-founding Anthropic, and is a former tech journalist who covered supercomputers, neural networks and advanced technology for publications including BusinessWeek.
Jared Kaplan: $19.8 billion

Kaplan, 42, serves as Anthropic's chief science officer and is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University, where he has taught courses on the foundations of deep learning, according to his company bio.
His 239 million shares are worth $19.8 billion, based on the IPO price.

Kaplan, who has a Ph.D. in physics from Harvard University and a bachelor's degree in physics and math from Stanford, spent the first 15 years of his career in academia as a theoretical physicist, according to Anthropic. He was also "instrumental in building GPT-3 and Codex at OpenAI," his bio states.
Sam McCandlish: $19.9 billion
McCandlish, 36, is Anthropic's chief architect, focusing on large-scale AI model training, leading pretraining and research productivity, according to his company bio.
His 240 million shares are worth about $19.9 billion, based on the IPO price.

Before co-founding Anthropic, he led a team at OpenAI, where he focused on the science and scaling of machine learning. He has a Ph.D. in theoretical physics from Stanford University and a bachelor's degree in math and physics from Brandeis University.
Christopher Olah: $19.9 billion
Olah, who is in his early 30s, is the interpretability research lead at Anthropic. Olah previously led interpretability research at OpenAI, according to his company bio.
His 239.5 million shares are worth about $19.9 billion, based on the IPO price.

title: Can Democrats force an end to the Iran war when they take Congress?
summary: With Democrats set to take decisive House and Senate majorities, some members want to pressure the Trump administration to end the Iran war. The exact plan is not clear.
story: Washington — For months, Democrats have made ending the Iran war a core part of their pitch to midterm voters, promising that if they win control of Congress, they'll push President Trump to end an unpopular conflict that they blame for price increases.

Now, with Democrats set to take decisive majorities in the House and Senate next year, some members want to use the power of the purse to pressure the Trump administration to wind down the war, using must-pass bills as leverage. Exactly when — and how — they plan to act are less clear.

Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut told CBS News before the election that she would support "cutting off the funds for the Iran war." DeLauro is set to chair the powerful House Appropriations Committee, which has the ability to block funding.
"If they want money, they have to get congressional approval," DeLauro said.

The first pressure point could arrive in a matter of weeks, before Democrats take control of Congress. Lawmakers face a Dec. 11 deadline to extend funding for most federal agencies and prevent a government shutdown. Several Democrats have argued the party should block any stopgap bill that doesn't restrict funding for the Iran war.
But some top House Democrats who will control key committees next year are backing away from that approach, warning it could lead to a shutdown.

DeLauro is part of government funding negotiations and favors a short-term extension until February if full-year appropriations measures are not passed by the deadline. She indicated that she is against using a continuing resolution as leverage.

"I think that the American people would like to see us end the war," she told reporters Wednesday. "I also believe that the American people may not believe that shutting the government down ends the war."
In a statement to CBS News on Thursday, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York said he would oppose a continuing resolution "if I believed shutting down government helped us actually achieve that."
"But I believe it would only shut down parts of government that Americans rely on," said Meeks, who is the incoming chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

The party's House and Senate leaders — Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer — support ending the Iran war but have not specified what their approach will be, including whether they're open to attaching language to a stopgap funding bill.
Jeffries said Tuesday the House and Senate appropriations committees are in "active conversation" about how to fund the government.
"I don't want to get out ahead of that process," he told reporters at a news conference. "What is clear is that the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran needs to end. It should end today."
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who is challenging Schumer for majority leader, has argued the party should use the Dec. 11 deadline to force restrictions on the Iran war.

Van Hollen said in a statement last week that any funding deal "must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran." It was cosigned by Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and more moderate Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado.

Some Democrats also plan to offer amendments to any government funding deal to block war funding until the conflict is authorized by Congress, including Bennet, Duckworth, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Schumer-allied Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York.
Senate Democrats discussed how to proceed during a closed-door lunch meeting on Tuesday. Van Hollen told reporters they "had a very good discussion," but there was "no final decision."

Reps. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona and Ro Khanna of California said they would also vote against any funding package that "does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran."
What could Democrats do next year?

After Democrats formally take control of the House and Senate in January, they could have several opportunities to attach Iran war-related language to must-pass legislation, in addition to voting on standalone bills and resolutions to restrict the war.

Lawmakers will likely need to extend government funding again, and they will need to raise the debt limit at some point next year. The appropriations process for the 2028 fiscal year and the annual National Defense Authorization Act are two other possible points of leverage.

Schumer told reporters earlier this month that "we are going to end the war," and said, "the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people."
Still, blocking the president from taking military action in Iran could be a challenging task.

"It is a complicated thing to force the president to stop using military force, and does require an alignment of political opportunity, savvy legislating, coordination that just is going to take time and political capital to implement," said Scott R. Anderson, a former State Department attorney and Brookings Institution senior fellow.
Mr. Trump has vowed to use his veto power liberally. Democrats would need support from several Senate Republicans and dozens of House Republicans to override his veto.

Beyond that, Mr. Trump and other presidents have claimed sweeping authority to direct the military. The president did not seek congressional authorization for the Iran war. Instead, he told lawmakers shortly after the war began that he "acted pursuant to my constitutional authority as Commander in Chief," in a notice issued under the War Powers Resolution, which requires the president to notify Congress of military hostilities within 48 hours.

That 1973 law also limits hostilities to 60 days — with an extra 30-day grace period to withdraw troops — unless lawmakers pass an authorization for use of military force, and it allows Congress to pass resolutions directing the president to terminate hostilities before then.

House and Senate Democrats have used that law to vote to terminate hostilities several times this year, drawing support from some moderate or anti-interventionist Republicans. One war powers resolution cleared both chambers in June. But the Trump administration has brushed off those votes, arguing the War Powers Resolution is unconstitutional. On Thursday, the Senate blocked another House-passed resolution, losing Republican support for reining in Mr. Trump on Iran.
Jeffries said Tuesday that House Democrats are discussing whether to force more votes on war powers resolutions this year.

"It's something that's under discussion right now, and we'll take a look at vehicles that we have available to us," he said. "But it certainly is the case that early on in the new Congress, we're going to aggressively move to end the reckless Republican war of choice in Iran."
Later in the day, during an interview at the Atlantic Summit in Washington, Jeffries indicated that Democrats would vote next year on a resolution "that has the force of the law."
The resolution that cleared the House and Senate in June was passed under a procedure that did not require the president's signature.
Jeffries said the goal is to send a war powers resolution to Mr. Trump's desk, essentially daring him to veto it. The war remains deeply unpopular with Americans.
"There's nothing more powerful than putting that bill on the president's desk," Jeffries said.

Meeks told CBS News that starting in January, "I will introduce a War Powers Resolution, support legislation that cuts off funding for this war, and require the administration to take diplomacy seriously by sending real diplomats, not the president's golf buddy and son in law."

Other Democrats have backed using funding bills as leverage. Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia said in one recent interview that if the Trump administration doesn't follow already-passed war powers resolutions, "our only choice is to use the appropriations process to forbid funding for war operations, unless the president gets the legally required authorization by Congress."

Asked about Democrats' plans, a White House official told CBS News: "As President Trump and Secretary Rubio stated, our economic pressure campaign is devastating Iran to such an extent that the President does not have any need to conduct major combat operations."
"The Democrats continue to prove that have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to baselessly obstruct the President's agenda," the official said.
What could restrictions on the Iran war look like?

There is some history of Congress constraining the president's ability to make war. In 1973, the House and Senate overwhelmingly passed legislation blocking the government from using funds for hostilities in Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. Then-President Richard Nixon signed it into law.

Anderson told CBS News that if lawmakers want to force an end to the Iran war, they could pass legislation that either prohibits hostilities with Iran outright or bars the president from using federal funds to pay for the war, or both.
"You need some sort of affirmative bar to block the president from acting," he said. "Even then, there's kind of a question of, 'Does the president listen? How enforceable is it?'"
Another open question: What specific military actions Democrats might try to ban.

The U.S. has not conducted large-scale offensive operations against Iran in recent months, but the conflict has remained at a simmer. The two countries have exchanged occasional strikes — typically after the U.S. military alleges imminent threats from Iran — and the U.S. has enforced a blockade on Iranian ports and escorted oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Anderson says Congress could try to bar the Trump administration from resuming offensive bombings, and the blockade on Iran could also be restricted. Defensive operations are likely to be exempted, though the bill would need to be worded carefully.

In the past, Anderson notes, presidents have argued the Constitution inherently gives them the power to carry out operations to defend U.S. nationals, regardless of any legislative complications — an argument President Gerald Ford used to evacuate Saigon and order some other operations around the tail end of the Vietnam War.
"If you do an absolute funding cutoff, what do you do when you have U.S. vessels traversing the Strait of Hormuz and they do get shot at by Iranians, or American sailors get captured?" he said.

Democrats have yet to publicly lay out a plan for how they plan to counter the administration if it defies Congress on ending the war. If Democrats believe the administration isn't complying with its obligations, the House or Senate could sue, but the outcome could be hard to predict.
Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the incoming chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, has argued that impeaching Mr. Trump over the war should be an option.
"How are we going to stop him? What law are we going to pass when he chooses not to obey the law?" Smith said in an interview with CNN last month, prior to the election.

Smith told The New Republic earlier this month that even if Democrats forbid any funding for the war, "the legal language and the loopholes — the ways that Trump can sort of jump out of it — those will all continue to be challenges."
"We are headed into uncharted territory here," Smith said.
Anderson said he believes Democrats are serious about passing restrictions on the Iran war, but it could take multiple attempts and plenty of "political fighting and legal maneuvering."
"People do need to be patient," Anderson said. "There is this expectation that Democrats won and the Iran war will end tomorrow. That is not what is going to happen."

title: Beloved hippo Fiona dies days after swallowing hat
summary: Fiona the hippo, who survived being born prematurely and rose to global fame, has died, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced Thursday.
story: Fiona the hippo, who survived being born prematurely almost a decade ago, and whose story captured hearts around the world, has died, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced Thursday.
"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a news release. "We did not expect this outcome.  She fought until she couldn't anymore."

Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, had ingested a knit hat that ended up in her enclosure by accident last week, the zoo said, and despite the team's efforts to get it out of her system, "it was ultimately too much to overcome."
A Cincinnati Zoo spokesperson confirmed to CBS News that the hat Fiona swallowed had been tossed in the air by a zoo visitor, then catapulted it into the enclosure by a ceiling fan.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her.  They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said.  "She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many."

Before Fiona's death, veterinarians closely monitored her health, turning to an unconventional method to try to help her pass the blockage by borrowing a vibration plate from a horse farm. They had Fiona stand on the device several times a day, hoping the vibrations would help move the material through her digestive system.

Fiona would have been 10 years old this January. Her birth in 2017 drew the attention of millions on social media after she was born prematurely, weighing just 29 pounds, far below the typical 55–120 pounds for a newborn Nile hippo. Fiona was the first Nile hippo born at the zoo in 75 years.
To support baby Fiona, zoo staffers worked around the clock to care for her, including bottle-feeding her and helping her learn to swim.
In August 2022, Fiona's little brother, Fritz, was born at the Cincinnati Zoo.
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called Fiona "a true icon" of the zoo, saying in a social media post that she "captured the hearts of Ohioans and those around the world, bringing joy to millions."

"Fiona was a symbol of perseverance and joy in Cincinnati," Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval wrote on X. "She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world.   Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."
The Cincinnati Bengals even paid tribute to Fiona, saying: "Rest in peace, Fiona. The queen of the Queen City."
