title: Meet the 19 new senators set to be sworn in to Congress
summary: From a former wheelchair basketball Paralympian to a Methodist pastor and one senator returning after defeat, the new class hails from different backgrounds and parts of the country.
story: Washington — Nineteen new senators are preparing to take their seats in the 120th Congress in January — the largest class in almost five decades — after Democrats flipped a slew of seats in the midterm elections, and some incumbents chose to retire.

From a former wheelchair basketball Paralympian to a Methodist pastor and one senator returning after defeat, the new class hails from different backgrounds and parts of the country. But mostly, they're much younger: With several freshmen in their 40s and one in his 30s, the Senate's average age is dropping by a couple of years — to 63.
These are the new senators:
Abdul El-Sayed, D-Michigan

Abdul El-Sayed, 42, is a former Michigan health official who defended an open Senate seat in Michigan after Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek reelection. El-Sayed, a Democrat, defeated former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, running on a leftist platform including "Medicare for All." He won a bruising campaign, despite reservations about his appeal to Jewish and Black voters over his opposition to U.S. support for Israel and his progressive platform. At the same time, top Republicans, including President Trump and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz called him a "jihadist" and sought to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood, and even implied that electing him could be deadly to Americans.
With his victory, El-Sayed will become the first Muslim senator in U.S. history.
Adam Hamilton, D-Kansas

Adam Hamilton, 62, is a fifth-generation Kansan and pastor. He defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, flipping the seat for Democrats for the first time in nearly a century. Formerly a Republican, Hamilton ran on an affordability-focused agenda, while appealing to a cross-party coalition to take on Marshall. As a pastor, Hamilton led the U.S.' largest United Methodist church and is a well-known author and speaker.
Andy Barr, R-Kentucky

Republican Andy Barr, 53, has represented Kentucky in the House since 2013, and won the Senate seat after Sen. Mitch McConnell announced he would retire. Barr, an attorney, had the president's endorsement, and billed his Democratic opponent in the race as too extreme for the Bluegrass State. In the House, Barr served as co-chair of the Congressional Horse Caucus and the Congressional Bourbon Caucus, two of Kentucky's defining interests.
Annie Andrews, D-South Carolina

Democrat Annie Andrews, 46, is a pediatrician who defeated Trump-endorsed incumbent GOP Sen. Darline Graham, who had been appointed to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, after his sudden death in July. Andrews campaigned on healthcare access and affordability, along with fighting corruption in Washington. With her victory, she became the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the Senate, and the first Democrat elected to represent the state in the upper chamber since 1998.
Barry Moore, R-Alabama

Republican Barry Moore, 60, has represented Alabama in the House since 2021. A member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, Moore ran as a staunch supporter of Mr. Trump and touted being the first elected official to endorse the president in 2015. He won the seat after Sen. Tommy Tuberville launched a gubernatorial bid, rather than seeking reelection. Moore and the state's other senator, Katie Britt, both hail from Enterprise, Alabama, and attended the same high school.
Chris Pappas, D-New Hampshire

Democrat Chris Pappas, 46, has represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019 and defended an open Senate seat in the Granite State after Sen. Jeanne Shaheen opted not to seek reelection. Along the campaign trail, Pappas billed himself as an independent voice for the state and ran on his record in the lower chamber, where he's a member of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus. With his victory, Pappas is set to become the first openly gay male senator in the chamber's history.
Harriet Hageman, R-Wyoming

Harriet Hageman, 64, a Republican, has represented Wyoming as the state's at-large representative in the House since 2023. Hageman's Senate victory came after GOP Sen. Cynthia Lummis, a first-term senator, announced she would not run for reelection. Hageman grew up on a ranch and attended college on a livestock judging scholarship. A former litigator and staunch supporter of Mr. Trump, Hageman first came to Congress after defeating former GOP Rep. Liz Cheney.
James Talarico, D-Texas

James Talarico, 37, is a Texas state representative, former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who flipped the Senate seat for Democrats in the Lone Star State. Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who had bested incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the primary. The Texas Democrat calls himself a progressive Christian, and ran on fighting corruption and lowering costs, overcoming widespread GOP criticism that he was too extreme for the state, as they pointed to comments he's previously made on issues like veganism and gender. Derided as "Tofu Talarico" by Republicans, he toasted Democrats' victory on election night with Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa at a Whataburger.
Josh Turek, D-Iowa

Josh Turek, 47, is a state representative and former wheelchair basketball Paralympian. A Democrat, he flipped Iowa's Senate seat after Sen. Joni Ernst opted not to seek reelection, defeating GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson. On the campaign trail, he touted his background in the state legislature representing the most conservative district held by a Democrat in the state, and he pledged to work — including with Mr. Trump — to deliver for Iowans.
Julia Letlow, R-Louisiana

Julia Letlow, 45, has represented Louisiana in the House since 2021, when she became the first Republican woman to represent the state. She won the Senate seat after defeating incumbent Sen. Bill Cassidy in the primary, following Mr. Trump's endorsement. Letlow, who previously worked in education, initially came to Congress after winning a special election for Louisiana's 5th Congressional District following the death of her husband, who died in 2020 from complications related to COVID-19 before he could be sworn into office.
Juliana Stratton, D-Illinois

Juliana Stratton, 61, is a former state representative and Illinois lieutenant governor who launched a Senate bid after Dick Durbin, the No. 2 Senate Democrat, announced his retirement. Stratton, a fellow Democrat who ran on a progressive platform, is the fifth Black woman ever to be elected to the upper chamber, where she and Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland will make history, with three Black women serving simultaneously for the first time.
Kevin Hern, R-Oklahoma

Republican Kevin Hern, 64, has represented Oklahoma in the House since 2018, and joins the Senate's ranks after Sen. Alan Armstrong was appointed as a placeholder following Markwayne Mullin's departure to become Homeland Security secretary earlier this year. Hern, a former aerospace engineer and businessman, who at one time owned 24 McDonald's franchises, chaired the conservative House Republican Policy Committee in the House. He's set to be sworn in later this month, due to Armstrong's temporary appointment to the position.
Kurt Alme, R-Montana

Kurt Alme, 60, a Republican, is a Harvard-trained former U.S. Attorney for the District of Montana, nominated to the position twice by Mr. Trump. Alme comes to the Senate after GOP Sen. Steve Daines opted not to seek reelection, in a move that sparked controversy when Daines made the announcement just before the filing deadline and endorsed Alme, blocking any major challengers. Alme, who has also served as Montana's budget director, said he plans to target government spending, telling supporters on election night, "My first bill will say, if Congress can't balance a budget, Congress doesn't get paid."
Peggy Flanagan, D-Minnesota

Peggy Flanagan, 47, is Minnesota's lieutenant governor and a former state representative. She held on to an open seat for Democrats after Sen. Tina Smith opted not to seek reelection. Flanagan defeated the GOP candidate, former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya, after winning the Democratic primary in August against a more moderate candidate. Flanagan ran on progressive priorities like Medicare for All and secured endorsements from top progressives. With the victory, Flanagan is set to become the first Native American woman in the U.S. Senate.
Mary Peltola, D-Alaska

Mary Peltola, 53, is a former congresswoman who became the first Democrat to represent the state in the House in 50 years in 2022. She ultimately lost her reelection bid for Alaska's sole House seat in 2024, before going on to defeat incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan this cycle. Peltola, who framed herself as an independent voice for the state, is set to become the first Alaska Native to be elected to the Senate. Republicans accused Democrats of foul play after another candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Dan Sullivan, joined the race and advanced to the ranked-choice November election. But as it turned out, Peltola won by more than 12,000 votes, and the second Dan Sullivan won just about 4,800, far less than the margin of victory.
Roy Cooper, D-North Carolina

Roy Cooper, 69, is a popular former two-term North Carolina governor who flipped the Senate seat for Democrats after Sen. Thom Tillis decided not to seek reelection. Cooper faced off against former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley in the race, making an affordability message central to his campaign, like with his "Make Stuff Cost Less" tour throughout the state. Cooper is also the longest-serving state attorney general in North Carolina's history, where he's become known for his love of diet soda. The self-identified "diet soda sommelier" is fond of Diet Sun Drop and said he dreamed of drinking it from the Stanley Cup if the Hurricanes won (they did win).
Scott Colom, D-Mississippi

Democrat Scott Colom, 43, is a district attorney and seventh-generation Mississippian who defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a major upset that few saw coming this cycle. Colom, who will be the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction, campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues, while pledging to deliver for the Magnolia State in places that he argued Hyde-Smith fell short. Colom may have taken the political world by surprise with his victory, but when he arrives at the Capitol, he's sure to be recognized from what may have been the catchiest ad of the midterms cycle — the "Pick Another Senator" spot that seized on Hyde-Smith's response to rising beef prices.
Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio

Sherrod Brown, 74, is a former three-term Democratic senator who lost his reelection to Ohio GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno in 2024. But he's back, after defeating incumbent Sen. Jon Husted in November. Brown's strong working-class brand in the Buckeye State resonated with voters, as issues like affordability and data centers were the dominant concerns. Husted was appointed to fill Vice President JD Vance's Senate seat last year until this past special election. Now, Brown will take his seat and serve out the remainder of Vance's Senate term, which will end in early 2029.
Troy Jackson, D-Maine

Democrat Troy Jackson, 58, is a fifth-generation logger who was previously president of the Maine state Senate. He ousted GOP Sen. Susan Collins, who had survived several challenges to her reelection in her nearly three decades in the upper chamber. Jackson, who became the Democratic nominee after Graham Platner exited the race, billed himself as a champion of the working class on the campaign trail. And though he first ran for office more than two decades ago as a Republican, his politics have since shifted leftward, with backing from prominent progressives like independent Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts.

title: Russia missiles pummel Ukraine and hit NATO soil in Poland
summary: Missiles flew into Poland overnight as Russia hit Ukraine with "one of the largest attacks" since the war began, killing at least 8 people.
story: Poland's government said Russian missiles landed in the country overnight as Vladimir Putin's forces hammered Ukraine with what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called "one of the largest attacks" since the war began. The strikes on Ukraine killed at least eight people, according to Zelenskyy.
The prime minister of Poland, a NATO member, decried the Russian weapons landing in his country as "an intentional provocation" of the U.S.-led military alliance.

"We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia. Therefore — ⁠and this is not just my own assessment, but ‌also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an ‌accident," Prime Minister ⁠Donald Tusk said. "It ‌appears that we ⁠are dealing with an intentional ⁠provocation."

"Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror," Zelenskyy wrote, adding that Putin's attempt to "redraw the world" with his Chinese and U.S. counterparts during their summit Thursday in China had been a "failure."
"Hard to regard it as a coincidence"

Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine overnight and early Friday, including cluster munitions, Zelenskyy said in a fiery social media post. Some of the Russian weapons hit the Austrian embassy and landed near the Netherlands embassy in Kyiv, prompting France to call for a meeting of the United Nations Security Council.
"Russia will have to answer for this," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot wrote in a social media post.

Poland's defense minister said three Russian weapons, believed to have been two missiles and a drone, entered southeast Poland's airspace on Friday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and Patriot anti-missile systems in the country's southeast were activated, but no injuries were reported.
Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.
The Article 5 collective defense clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in a Friday social media post that he had spoken with Tusk "about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight" and stressed that the alliance stands "in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend."

"This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," Rutte said. "I condemn Russia's attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine."

NATO's Supreme Allied Commander for Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, was in "close contact with Poland's chief of defense and minister of defense as Poland's investigation into the overnight airspace violations continues," his spokesperson Martin O'Donnell told CBS News on Friday.

Thousands of troops from 11 European countries that support Kyiv, members of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, are currently in Poland taking part in a major military exercise framed as training for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine, about 60 miles west of where the Russian weapons landed Friday.

"It is hard to regard it as a coincidence that the time and place of the violation of Polish airspace coincide with the Coalition of the Willing's exercises," Deputy Polish Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote in a social media post.

The escalation comes a day after President Trump sat with Xi and Putin —   whom he greeted warmly and called his friend — in Shenzhen, China, for a rare face-to-face meeting that seemed to achieve little.

The presidents discussed the Ukraine war, which Mr. Trump has long pushed to end through negotiations, but soon after the 90-minute meeting, Putin ruled out direct talks with Kyiv, citing a strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces that severely damaged a highly symbolic bridge linking Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.

"We will respond to these strikes," Putin warned Thursday. "I want everyone to know this. I believe that our retaliatory actions … will be far more painful than what the Kiev regime did to the bridge."
At least 8 killed, dozens wounded in Ukraine

Ukrainian forces managed to intercept 79 of the 110 missiles Russia launched overnight, Zelenskyy said, but none of the 27 ballistic missiles, which he attributed to Kyiv's lack of interceptors. He has been pleading with the Trump administration to help Ukraine replenish its missile interceptor stocks for months, saying the shortage is being paid for in civilian lives.

Russia's attack targeted Kyiv and nine other regions, leaving more than two dozen people wounded in addition to the eight confirmed to have been killed, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
"Missiles hit critical infrastructure in the capital, including bridges," he said. "A water supply facility, office and commercial buildings were damaged."

A hospital in Kharkiv was damaged, as well as businesses in the Mykolaiv, Odesa and Chernihiv regions, and residential buildings in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia, Sumy, Chernihiv and Lviv, which is in the far west, close to Poland, Koretskyi said, adding that energy infrastructure was also hit.
Some nuclear plants were forced to reduce power generation after the attacks, according to an energy ministry official.

"The tactics of the strike this time were particularly vile," Zelenskyy said in his post on social media, noting that there had been "several groups of missiles with pauses of 20-30 minutes to complicate extinguishing the fires, clearing the rubble and recovery."

"A clear response from the world to all this is also needed," he said. "It is important that there are not only statements from partners about supporting Ukraine and Ukrainians, but also the implementation of specific agreements on air defense … We very much hope that the Pentagon will release the supply that we expect."

title: U.S. and Israel considering new assault on Iran, sources say
summary: Israel wants a new joint operation with the U.S. against Iran, but it's unclear whether President Trump is willing to resume military action, and if so, to what extent.
story: Tel Aviv — Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, according to sources familiar with the matter.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration is concerned about how rapidly the Iranians are rebuilding their ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and the pace at which Iran is working to shield its military and nuclear infrastructure from attack by moving it underground, the sources told CBS News.
President Trump also said this week that Iran may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, though he provided no evidence to support the claim.

Months of indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have failed to bring a ceasefire deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has refused to even discuss its nuclear program unless the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and accepts six other key conditions.
Israel's military is prepared for a new round of fighting with Iran and is in peak defensive posture to respond to any first attack by Iran, the sources told CBS News.

The Netanyahu administration would prefer to launch a new joint operation with the U.S., but the sources told CBS News it remains unclear whether Mr. Trump wants to order new military action, and if so, what kind. The war was a key factor in the Republicans' defeat in the recent midterm elections and it remains deeply unpopular with Americans.
The U.S. has significant firepower in the region, including tens of thousands of forces and two aircraft carriers with their associated strike groups, amounting to dozens of warships and aircraft.

For both Mr. Trump and Netanyahu, who jointly launched the war with Iran almost nine months ago with a massive round of strikes on the Islamic Republic, the window for any new collaborative action may be closing.

Netanyahu could lose his position as prime minister in the coming weeks due to the results of Israel's national election late last month. Mr. Trump's Republican party will lose control of both houses of the U.S. Congress in January, meanwhile, giving his political opponents far greater say over financing of the war.

Neither Netanyahu's office nor Israel's military responded to CBS News' requests for comment on the planning for any renewed attacks on Iran, which would be the third round of major hostilities. The White House and U.S. military declined to comment on the current thinking within the administration, but American military commanders have long said they are prepared to execute any orders Mr. Trump gives. With the assets already in place a new offensive operation could be mounted within two to four days, if such an order were given.

Mr. Trump has said repeatedly that Iran is keen to make a deal to end the war, but Tehran has rejected any ceasefire to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, or any talks on its nuclear program, unless the U.S. agrees to seven key demands, including an end to hostilities on all fronts in the Middle East and an end of the U.S. blockade of Iran's ports and vessels.

Alongside the rising concern over Iran's growing capacity to produce conventional weapons — which the regime has boasted of itself —   President Trump also raised the possibility of the Islamic Republic working to obtain biological or chemical weapons.
"They're looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear," Mr. Trump told a Fox News reporter in China ahead of his meeting with his Russian and Chinese counterparts.

Iran's foreign ministry rejected the allegations on Thursday, comparing it to U.S. claims that Iraq was developing weapons of mass destruction before the invasion launched by then-President George W. Bush in 2003.
"We find ourselves facing ominous new allegations and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script," Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X.

President Trump has offered no clear signal about whether he intends to order major new military action against Iran. He told Fox News on Wednesday that he still wanted to reach a deal with Iran, but one that he feels will last, and also renewed his threat to use force.
"I'm going to finish it off," Mr. Trump said of the war. "Yeah, soon. I mean, one way or the other, we'll finish it off."
On Thursday, however, he told Israel's Channel 12 that he's "not rushing into any decision," indicating a willingness, not for the first time, to let the stalemate drag on into 2027.
"We will see what happens after the beginning of the year," he told the television network.

U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper, who oversees American forces in the Middle East, met with top Israeli security officials at Israel's defense ministry Wednesday for what the Israeli military called a "joint, comprehensive situational assessment."
Israel's most senior general, Eyal Zamir, as well as the director of the Mossad intelligence agency, Roman Gofman, were among the senior Israeli officials who met with Cooper.
Israeli authorities confirming the Mossad director's attendance at the meeting was unusual, and many in the country have taken it as a sign that Iran was a key topic of discussion.
Gofman met U.S. officials in Washington last week, including CIA Director John Ratcliffe, according to people familiar with the matter.

"The head of the Mossad, who hardly leaves the country, didn't go for a brief in and out, but for a couple of days. It's a serious matter on the table," said Erez Winner, chairman of the Israel Defense and Security Forum, an Israeli think tank with close ties to the Netanyahu administration.
If the decision is made to take Israel back to war with Iran, it would come at a politically sensitive time for Netanyahu.
His political rivals, in the wake of last month's election, have been tasked with forming a government, potentially leaving him in power for just a few more weeks, possibly less.

Since losing his majority in Israel's parliament, Netanyahu has made the argument to his rivals, and to the Israeli public, that a unity government is required to deal with the country's pressing security threats. He has long accused Iran of having ambitions to build nuclear weapons, and placed that at the pinnacle of those threats.

Iran has always denied any desire to build nuclear weapons, though after President Trump pulled the U.S. out of a previous international nuclear agreement during his first term, it has enriched uranium to a point far beyond the needs of civilian nuclear programs.

International monitors believe Iran still has a stockpile of about 900 pounds of uranium enriched to 60% purity somewhere under the rubble of its heavily damaged nuclear facilities. At that level, the material is just a short technological step away from being enriched to weapons-grade.

Despite the concerns, some of Netanyahu's political rivals believe he is trying to take the country back to war to avoid losing power. In recent days, he has held security briefings with some of those rivals — an unusual step that analysts say may hint at the possibility of imminent military action.
President Trump endorsed Netanyahu before the Israeli election, and he said he also would prefer to pair up with the right-wing Israeli leader in any new attack on Iran.
The speculation about a major new operation comes amid a renewed tit-for-tat exchange of fire between Iran and the U.S.

The U.S. launched a strike on Iran's strategic Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, which American officials categorized as self-defense in response to Iranian strikes targeting U.S. assets in Bahrain, which the U.S. military said were intercepted. Iran has also launched strikes against Kuwait this week, with officials saying they caused no damage.
The Iranian regime has been preparing, publicly, for renewed hostilities, and it has warned that its response to any new attack would reach farther than its previous actions.

Iranian government and military officials, including senior members of the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, have threatened to widen retaliatory attacks to target not just Israel and U.S. military infrastructure in Persian Gulf states, but U.S. bases in Europe, Gulf energy infrastructure and undersea internet cables.
A recent statement attributed to Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said in the event of a return to open hostilities, "there would be no geographical limit for Iranian missiles."

title: Putin says Russia won't negotiate with Ukraine after bridge strike
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin said Russia will not negotiate any limited ceasefire now with Ukraine, citing a Ukrainian strike on a highly symbolic bridge this week.
story: President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies.

The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day.

Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge.

"Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."
Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported.
While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless.

It's not clear how much Ukraine came up in Mr. Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin on Wednesday, or in the meeting with both Putin and Xi on Thursday. Last week, the White House said Ukraine wouldn't be a topic of discussion, but before he left for Asia, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would be discussing the war. The White House readout of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was sparse on detail, and did not mention Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff have been in Germany to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders of Germany, France, the U.K. and other European nations — a group known as the Coalition of the Willing — about Ukraine and other topics.
Kushner said they discussed the "latest efforts to achieve a just, lasting and durable peace in Ukraine."

"We are grateful for his leadership, constructive engagement, and close partnership as we work together toward our shared goal of ending this terrible war and building a secure and prosperous future for Ukraine and Europe," Kushner posted to X.
Merz, speaking to reporters after the meeting, called the China summit a photo-op and said the trilateral format "will not bring peace" in Ukraine.
As he went to shake Putin's hand before an earlier meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Mr. Trump referred to the Russian leader as "my friend."
"Who is he?" the president said, pointing at Putin and smiling. "He's my friend."

title: Trump meeting with Putin and Xi in China appears to achieve little
summary: The U.S., Chinese and Russian presidents said they agreed during a rare meeting to boost oil production and "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war."
story: President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.

The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.

The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.

Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.

The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."

They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the "International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
"A great relationship"

The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.

"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Focus on Ukraine
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.

"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."

Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."

Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."

Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons, with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.

Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program, ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year.

China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi, however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence.
Global trade and AI

The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."

Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed, is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.

Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.
Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence.

"We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements."

Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year.

Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future.

During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth.
Foreign conflicts loomed large during the Trump-Putin-Xi talks. Iran is one contentious area, given China's status as one of the largest customers of Iranian oil, and Russia's ties with Iran.

The White House previously said the war in Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said he expected the issue to come up, calling it "my favorite subject."

Taiwan is another frequent discussion topic between the U.S. and China. During the U.S. president's visit to Beijing in the spring, Xi reportedly delivered a stern warning about the island, which he has long vowed to reintegrate with mainland China, floating potential "clashes and even conflicts" if the issue isn't "handled properly."
And Mr. Trump was expected to press Xi to release two detained Americans during his visit to China, CBS News has reported. Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, U.N. top court rules
summary: The U.N.'s top court ruled in a landmark judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.
story: The Hague, Netherlands — In a landmark judgment, the United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

International Court of Justice President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar "has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention."
The 15-judge panel of the World Court rejected Myanmar's defense that the 2017 campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents.

Iwasawa said that "the court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers."
The decision marks the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide.

"This is a great day for the Rohingya, and it is a great day for all oppressed people, everywhere, who have been told that their suffering does not count and that no one is listening," said Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the court's ornate, wood-paneled Great Hall of Justice for the three-hour reading of the ruling.
The intent to destroy a group in whole or in part is a key element in establishing whether crimes amount to genocide under international law.
The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya.

The Muslim-majority African nation of Gambia launched the proceedings at the International Court of Justice in 2019, asking it to rule that Myanmar breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order the nation to end any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.
The judgment comes as the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the Gaza conflict and the war in Ukraine.

"Genocides have similarities in how they are committed so this decision will have an impact on other cases," said Melanie O'Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia.

In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya "in whole or in part."

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox's Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Gambia has asked for reparations for the Rohingya, including ordering Myanmar to grant them full citizenship and the right to return home.
The court's rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.

In a previous judgment in 2007, the court said that Serbia "violated the obligation to prevent genocide" in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town.
Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to weigh in on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the Genocide Convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya human rights activist who fled Myanmar as a young child with her mother in the 1990s, said the demands in the Myanmar case are rooted in her community's desire for recognition and dignity.

"Because so far, we've just been pushed around into this limbo state," she said. "It's been almost 10 years now that Rohingya have been living in very, very precarious conditions across the Asia-Pacific."

In March 2022, then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said Myanmar's treatment olf the Rohingya amounted to genocide, in a declaration intended to generate international pressure and lay the groundwork for potential legal action.
"The day will come when those responsible for these appalling acts will have to answer for them," Blinken said at the time.

title: Danish lawmakers OK Greenland security deal with U.S.
summary: Denmark's parliament unanimously approved a hard-wrought agreement with Greenland and the U.S. to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
story: Copenhagen — Denmark's parliament on Thursday unanimously approved a hard-wrought agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The vote follows months of pressure by President Trump seeking to control Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of Denmark, a NATO ally.

The trilateral deal among Mr. Trump and Danish and Greenlandic leaders paves the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Mr. Trump's repeated calls for the vast, mineral-rich island to become part of the U.S.
The 109-0 vote in the Folketing amounts to a final step: The deal was expected to enter into force once Denmark and Greenland had signed on.
Greenland's parliament approved the deal earlier this month, also with no opposition.
The deal isn't technically a treaty so doesn't need a green light from the U.S. Senate.
The text of the agreement says it will become effective once Denmark and Greenland inform the U.S. "in a diplomatic note" indicating that their parliaments had completed all necessary steps.
The U.S. ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the "strong support" in the Danish parliament for ratification of the deal "paving the way for it to enter into force."

"The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of NATO," he wrote on X.
The aim is to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.

Mr. Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed the deal in September in New York, after months of quiet, behind-the-scenes negotiations to address his security concerns and Danish and Greenlandic fears of a possible U.S. takeover.

Under the deal, which builds on a defense agreement dating to 1951, the United States can expand its military presence on the island and "modernize and expand" its activities at the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest.

The U.S. can also set up "defense areas" at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east of Greenland, and can establish additional defense areas in the territory and strengthen its military operations or sites.

title: What to know about Trump's meeting with Xi in China
summary: President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday against the backdrop of a widening scandal.
story: Washington — President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, against the backdrop of a widening scandal over advanced U.S. chips reaching China and internal divisions within Mr. Trump's Cabinet about how to address it.

The bilateral meeting is taking place in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, known as APEC. Mr. Trump embraced Xi when he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday.

It's the third time the two world leaders are meeting face to face this year. The last time they met was in September, when Mr. Trump hosted Xi for a three-day summit at the White House. Mr. Trump is hosting Xi again for the G20 Leaders' Summit at Trump National Doral in Miami in December.
The Trump-Xi meeting will be followed by a meeting of Mr. Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Here's what Mr. Trump and Xi are likely to discuss.
Jensen Huang, Alice Huang and Nvidia

Mr. Trump told reporters as he left for Asia that he may bring up Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The Justice Department has been investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed for diverting semiconductor chips to China.
The president has cast doubts on assessments that Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset.

"I don't know that she is a spy," he said. "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country, that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the scandal is much bigger than Jensen Huang and his alleged affairs.

"It's really kind of unfolded into a much bigger, longer-term scandal that involves the question of how many chips did China get, how porous were export controls, and how did the Commerce Department enforce them?" McGuire said on a phone briefing with reporters Wednesday. "Which I think is a much more important, longer-term strategic question for the United States, for the U.S.-China relationship than anything involving Jensen Huang's personal affairs."
China and chips
Shortly before the president left for Asia, the Trump administration announced new interim trade rules that will restrict Chinese AI companies from accessing advanced U.S. chips remotely.

The move comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of slow-walking restrictions on Megaspeed, revealing a rift between Bessent and Lutnick. Bessent told CNBC that Mr. Trump had indicated that China should not have access to the chips, but suggested that Lutnick was resisting. The president didn't take sides in the Bessent-Lutnick debate, telling reporters before he left for Asia that the men have "two different views" where "one wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China."

"One view is you don't want to insult China," Mr. Trump said Monday. "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them. And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. Both can say either is wrong or right."

Ultimately, the Treasury Department and National Security Council, not the Commerce Department under Lutnick, wrote  the new interim rule cutting off Chinese companies from remotely accessing the most advanced AI chips in data centers abroad, though the Commerce Department issued the rule.

"This is a very significant action that really cuts off a lot of the avenues that China is using to get AI computing power," McGuire said. "There was a digital forensic study that was done recently that showed that every single advanced Chinese model is actually trained with the most advanced American chips, so even though these chips have been banned to China, the controls have not been effective. They've probably had some impact but not that much."

The actions taken on Monday, however, will have a "really significant" effect on China's access to computing power, which "could materially widen the lead" between the U.S. and China on AI, McGuire said.
AI safety

Mr. Trump has shown no signs of wanting to slow the United States' AI advancement in the race against China. After a September summit between Mr. Trump and Xi, the U.S. and Chinese governments pledged to set up a communication channel to share information when AI goes off the rails.

But talking about wayward AI incidents after the fact isn't nearly enough, said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow on technology with the Asia Society Policy Institute and a digital fellow with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.

Graylin will be interested to see if Mr. Trump and Xi can work past the negative news cycle, like the Jensen Huang scandal, to take more steps on AI safety collaboration by bringing together more technical experts for working-level discussions.
"I hope that we go beyond just having surface level discussion, and we start to actually create some enduring institutions around safety," Graylin said.
Taiwan
Before leaving for Asia, Mr. Trump was asked if he'll bring up Taiwan in his meeting with Xi.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," the president responded. "I won't have to raise it."
David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations — not the former White House AI czar David Sacks — said he thinks that's right.

"I think that it's very clear that every time Xi sees Trump, they do a little check-in on Taiwan, and Xi Jinping raises his concerns on Taiwan and his expectations of how President Trump will handle Taiwan and cross-strait dynamics," Sacks told reporters on the Council on Foreign Relations call.

A $14 billion arms package to Taiwan is still pending on the president's desk, Sacks said. Earlier this year, the Navy said the arms sale had been put on "pause" to make sure the U.S. military had enough munitions for the Iran war. Sacks said there will be "more pressure from Congress in the coming months to move that arms package forward."

"And so, if President Trump is determined to resist that, you know he will need, you know — Xi Jinping will hope to kind of stiffen his spine and say, 'You're on the right track, and if you approve this arms package, you're going to send cross-strait relations reeling.'"
The Trump-Putin-Xi meeting

Lyle Goldstein, the director of Defense Priorities Asia, told CBS News he is actually optimistic about a Trump-Putin-Xi meeting. Goldstein said he doesn't think any "major results" will come out of the sit-down, but the discussions might bear fruit in a future U.S.-China-Russia meeting.

"I actually think it could allow for some, not for breakthroughs, but for some movement on major issues," Goldstein said. "And this is the first time ever that you have this trilateral format for Russia, China, and the U.S. So I would like to see this continue."
Mr. Trump said he has a range of topics to discuss with both Xi and Putin when they meet, including denuclearization.

"We're going to talk about denuclearization," Mr. Trump said. "Tough subject, because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right? Especially since you do have other countries."

They'll also discuss Iran, the U.S. president said. On Tuesday, Mr. Trump said Iran would have a major price to pay if it detonates a so-called dirty bomb, after CNN reported U.S. intelligence indicates Iran may be developing plans to set off such a device in the nation's capital.

The White House previously said Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion in the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting, since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said Ukraine will be a topic for the three leaders.
"We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine," he told reporters.

title: Girlfriend of American killed in Costa Rica arrested
summary: The former girlfriend of Kurt Van Dyke, who comes from a legendary surfing family, has been arrested, along with another man, on suspicion of murder.
story: American surfer and businessman Kurt Van Dyke was found stabbed and strangled in his Costa Rica home earlier this year. Now, his girlfriend and another man are in custody on suspicion of murder.

Heavily armed Costa Rican police arrested the two in the dark of night last week, some nine months after the 66-year-old was found dead in the town of Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, where he owned a hotel. His 31-year-old girlfriend, whom police have only identified by her last name, Arroyo, survived the attack without any serious injuries, police said initially.

The other person arrested was identified as a 34-year-old man with the last name Gutiérrez. Police allege he and Arroyo "planned a robbery targeting the American with the intent of obtaining the PINs for bank cards" linked to the hotel.
Van Dyke's brother, Peter Van Dyke, told CBS News the revelation that police suspect she was involved in Kurt Van Dyke's death is "shocking."
He said the fact that she was found alive following the attack struck him and his family as "extremely odd," but said he "didn't want to make any speculations."
"We had our suspicions," he said.
Kurt Van Dyke had lived in Costa Rica since the '80s. He comes from a legendary surfing family that pioneered the sport in Santa Cruz, California.
Now that arrests have been made, Peter Van Dyke says the focus is on justice.

"I can't say the word 'happy' because this is not a happy situation," he told CBS News. "We're just satisfied with the outcome so far. I have faith in the Costa Rican law enforcement. It took them nine months, and I totally understand why."
Kurt Van Dyke had three children, and his family said his eldest son plans to be in Costa Rica for the eventual murder trial.

title: Florida pastor convicted in plot to kill Haitian president
summary: A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship has been convicted of U.S. charges related to the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.
story: A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted Wednesday of U.S. charges arising from the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on all charges, including conspiring to kill Moïse, after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges, the most serious one being conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
Sanon, who faces up to life in prison at sentencing, showed little reaction as the verdict was announced in a federal courtroom in Miami.
An attorney for Sanon, Zeljka Bozanic, said in a statement, "We respect the jury's decision, but strongly disagree with the verdict and will file an appeal."

Federal prosecutors said at trial that South Florida was a hub for planning and financing a plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators' choosing. The prosecutors said Sanon was the conspirators' initial choice for Moïse's replacement. They also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.

Sanon had acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but said the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the U.S. as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the Midwest.

Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a nighttime raid at their home on July 7, 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.

Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from U.S. government programs that were intended to help businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to court records. U.S. prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in South Florida with a former Haitian senator and several U.S. businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies — Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU — for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.

CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.

By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian Supreme Court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

title: Voyager 1 sets distance record of 1 "light day" from Earth
summary: Voyager 1 and its sister ship Voyager 2 are still beaming back data from interstellar space as they near their 50th anniversary next year.
story: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, launched nearly a half century ago in 1977 to provide the first close-up views of Jupiter, Saturn and their assortment of moons, reached a distance from Earth early Wednesday of one light day — more than 16 billion miles — the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from the home planet.

Its sister ship Voyager 2, on a different trajectory, added Uranus and Neptune to the outer planets "Grand Tour" before following its sibling out of the solar system and into interstellar space in 2018, six years after Voyager 1.

Both spacecraft continue to beam back data about the magnetic fields, charged particles and plasma waves in the space between the stars as their power steadily declines and their signals grow weaker and weaker.

As of 5:16 a.m. EST Wednesday, Voyager 1, sailing through space at nearly 38,000 mph, was expected to pass the one-light-day milestone, so far away that radio signals, traveling at 186,000 miles every second, need 24 hours to reach flight controllers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
That means the 13-member team will have to wait until Thursday for Voyager 1's first post-light-day signal to confirm the achievement.

And what an achievement it is: No other space agency in the world has matched or even attempted a mission rivaling Voyager, one that many believe ranks with the Apollo moon landings as one of the greatest feats of American space flight.

"It's difficult to describe, difficult to put into words," said Voyager Interstellar Mission Manager Kareem Badaruddin, one of just three full-time team members keeping the aging Voyagers healthy and their antennas aimed at Earth. "I feel like this mission is one of the great things that people have ever done, that humans have ever done.
"All of us, every person, whether they've worked on this mission or not, can take some pride in it and can feel like this is a part of what our civilization has accomplished."

It's not known how long the Voyagers will continue to function as the plutonium in their nuclear power packs steadily decays. With luck and clever management, engineers hope to keep the data flowing for several more years before the signals finally stop.

Voyager 1 started out with about 470 watts of power. That's down to a little more than 210 watts now, enough to run just two of its 10 instruments while keeping the spacecraft properly oriented so it can beam magnetometer and plasma wave data back to Earth. Voyager 2 has a slightly more powerful generator and is operating on a bit more than 230 watts, enough to keep three instruments running.

But even after the power is exhausted, both Voyagers will continue on their way, expected to remain roughly intact, if powerless, for a billion years or more, almost certainly outlasting human civilization.

On the remote chance any aliens might one day stumble upon a Voyager in the cold reaches between the stars, both spacecraft are carrying what amount to messages in a bottle, gold phonograph records encoded with the sights and sounds of planet Earth.

The records include greetings in 55 languages, 115 photos of Earth's people, wildlife and technology, representative natural sounds and carefully selected art and music from multiple cultures, everything from J.S. Bach to Navajo chants to Chuck Berry singing "Johnny B. Goode."

"If Voyager should, sometime in its distant future, encounter beings from some other civilization in space, it bears a message, a phonograph record ... with instructions for use," Carl Sagan, the late astronomer who led the golden record project, said in the 1980 "Cosmos" television series.

"And on this record are a sampling of pictures, sounds, greetings and an hour and a half of exquisite music, the Earth's greatest hits, a gift across the cosmic ocean from one island of civilization to another."

Now beyond the confines of Earth's solar system, the stream of ones and zeros describing the interstellar environment leaves Voyager 1's 12-foot-wide dish antenna with less than half the power used by a typical 40-watt refrigerator bulb.

By the time the signal reaches Earth 24 hours later, its strength is a tiny fraction of a trillionth of a watt, vastly less than the power needed to run a wristwatch — a signal so weak that giant 230-foot-wide antennas in NASA's globe-spanning Deep Space Network are needed to pull in the faint whispers.

Commands from flight controllers at JPL now take a full day to reach the spacecraft with another 24 hours required to find out if the commands were received and acted upon. Fixing a problem is a glacial, nail-biting affair.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager at JPL, said in a web posting.
Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are powered by electricity generated through the decay of radioactive plutonium 238 in compact nuclear power plants known as radioisotope thermoelectric generators, or RTGs.

Both spacecraft have slowly but steadily lost power as the plutonium in their RTGs has decayed. Flight controllers closely manage the available power and the resulting heat needed to keep fuel lines from freezing so thrusters can fire when needed to keep the spacecraft — and their dish antennas — locked onto Earth.
Badaruddin said the small flight control team feels the weight of responsibility for keeping the Voyagers alive.

"If ever you get that sense that oh, I made a mistake, I'm the one who caused a problem for the spacecraft, that's crushing," he said. "Every one of the team members feels they're committed to doing everything in our power to do our best for these spacecraft. We're doing everything we can to keep them going for as long as we can."

Only three of the 13 Voyager team members are full-time JPL employees. Two are retirees who worked on the project at launch and came back to help during the interstellar voyage while the rest split their time between Voyager and other projects.

"I've been at JPL for 32 years, and everybody loves their spacecraft, and everybody feels like it's a family member and gives everything they've got for it," said Badaruddin. "And Voyager is no different in that regard. And these two retirees have come back and given a tremendous amount of effort and time."

The Voyager program was approved in the early 1970s when the outer planets were lined up in a way that would permit a so-called "Grand Tour" of them, enabling spacecraft to make velocity-boosting flybys to jump from one planet to the next, shaving years off the time needed to explore them all.
But to reduce costs, the project was only funded for flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 2 was launched first, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 followed on Sept. 5.

Voyager 1 was on a faster trajectory and reached Jupiter first as planned, flying past the giant planet in 1979, sending back spectacular images of its Great Red Spot — a storm that has been churning for centuries, the planet's turbulent atmosphere and its major moons, including detailed looks at Europa, where an icy crust is thought to shield a global ocean, and Io, found to be the most volcanic world in the solar system.

It then flew on to Saturn, wowing astronomers with fantastically detailed photos of the solar system's most spectacular planet, sending back never-before-seen views of its rings, small moons that shepherd the ring particles along, the planet's atmosphere and, as it departed, cloud-shrouded Titan.

With the successful Titan flyby and the completion of the mission's major objectives, NASA approved sending Voyager 2 on a gravitational slingshot past Saturn and on to Uranus and Neptune in 1986 and 1989, respectively.

On Valentine's Day 1990, Voyager 1's cameras were used a final time to take a family portrait of the six largest planets — Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — from a distance of 3.7 billion miles. Earth appeared as little more than a blue dot in the pinkish glow of reflected light within the camera.

"Consider again that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us," Sagan said of the photo. "On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives ... on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam."

He concluded by saying "there is perhaps no better demonstration of the folly of human conceits than this distant image of our tiny world. To me, it underscores our responsibility to deal more kindly with one another, and to preserve and cherish the pale blue dot, the only home we've ever known."
Voyager 1's cameras have been powered down ever since.

In 2012, Voyager 1 flew through the outer edge of the bubble around the solar system defined by the solar wind and the sun's magnetic field, sailing out into interstellar space. It is now in what Carolyn Porco, a well-known planetary scientist and member of the Voyager imaging team, calls "the realm of deep time."

In about 18,000 years, she writes on her Substack page, Voyager 1 will reach another major milestone: passing through a distance of one light-year from Earth, roughly 5.8 trillion miles, only a quarter of the way to the nearest star and "still well within the zone where the sun is the dominant gravitational influence."

But in a million years, the silent spacecraft will have passed well beyond the confines of the solar system, reaching a distance of 56 light-years while "remaining within the sun's local interstellar neighborhood — a low density region filled with diffuse hydrogen and helium gas and scattered stars: most are very dim, some are sun-like, and comparatively few are luminous."

In 100 million years, Voyager 1 will be about 2,000 light years from Earth as the spacecraft and the distant solar system are carried along by the galaxy's rotation. "Still not very far," Porco writes. "But at this time, it will find itself among cold, dense molecular clouds, star-forming regions and nebulae and supernova remnants formed by the deaths of stars."

Finally, 1 billion years from now, the spacecraft will have sailed about 20,000 light-years from home, making four trips around the galactic core in the process. "By then, the sun's growing luminosity will have sufficiently heated the Earth to destroy atmospheric carbon dioxide, halt oxygen production and exterminate plant life and the complex lifeforms that depend on it."
"By that time, both robot and maker will be extinct."

The cosmic travelogue concludes with a personal observation: "The foretelling of Voyager's galactic wanderings leaves one to contemplate the impermanence of all existence and the preciousness of life. And that just might be Voyager's greatest gift of all."
