title: Mysterious illness tied to breast implants shares symptoms with MS, but key questions remain
summary: Christina Applegate suspects her breast implants could be behind joint pain and other symptoms, saying she plans to discuss it with her doctors.
story: Diana Zuckerman, Ph.D., president of the National Center for Health Research and a breast implant safety advocate in Washington, D.C., said breast cancer illness has been taken more seriously in recent years.
Weeks after Christina Applegate revealed she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), the actress has shared a suspicion that her breast implants could be to blame for her symptoms.

On a Nov. 10 episode of the podcast "MeSsy," which she co-hosts with actress and MS advocate Jamie-Lynn Sigler, Applegate — who underwent a double mastectomy in 2008 after a breast cancer diagnosis — said she believes she is overdue to have her implants replaced.
Applegate also said she recently saw a study suggesting that implant-related symptoms could resemble MS.
CHRISTINA APPLEGATE'S MS MISDIAGNOSIS AFTER 5 YEARS OF TREATMENT EXPOSES ALARMING MEDICAL REALITY
"And I swear, over the last five years or whatever, I thought, ‘What if they’re leaking, and they’re like poisoning me?’" she said.
Applegate said she plans to discuss the possibility with her doctors. She did not say that her implants had been confirmed as the cause.

Weeks after Christina Applegate (pictured in 2022) revealed she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, the actress has shared a suspicion that her breast implants could be to blame for her symptoms. (AFP via Getty Images)
Some of her symptoms have included joint pain, difficulty lifting her right arm and pain that can make it hard to get out of bed, she shared during the episode.
"I don’t know what’s going on in my joints, but I can’t move my right shoulder at all now," she said. "I can’t lift my arm."
NYC MARATHON RUNNER, 24, DIES JUST 2 MILES FROM FINISH LINE AFTER SENDING DAD CHILLING TEXTS
Other possible conditions that could contribute to these symptoms include rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and Lyme disease, Applegate said.

"We’re going into square one, just doing some testing and going one by one [through] the sister diseases to MS," she added. "It’s overwhelming because there are so many different things that could be going on and this pain stuff."
What is breast implant illness?

Diana Zuckerman, Ph.D., president of the National Center for Health Research and a breast implant safety advocate in Washington, D.C., said that breast implant illness hasn’t always gotten a lot of attention, but is being taken more seriously in recent years.

"It’s a range of symptoms, and not everybody has the same symptoms," she told Fox News Digital. "And some of them are pretty common, such as joint pain or chronic fatigue. Some women talk about feeling like they've had the flu for [months]."
Research has shown that in some cases, if the implants are taken out, women recover "almost miraculously and immediately and dramatically," a health expert said. (iStock)
Brain fog, memory issues, anxiety, insomnia, muscle pain and weakness are additional symptoms that could potentially overlap with various viruses or conditions.

Women with breast implant illness tend to have many symptoms all at once, Zuckerman said. "They're often very young women who are in their 20s, and suddenly they feel like they're in their 50s — that's how they describe it."
Research has shown that in some cases, if the implants are taken out, women recover "almost miraculously and immediately and dramatically," Zuckerman said.
A difficult diagnosis
Jonathan Kaplan, M.D., a board-certified plastic surgeon at Pacific Heights Plastic Surgery in San Francisco, agrees that breast implant illness symptoms are real.

"While patients may have abnormal blood tests to support their concerns about having some type of illness, these lab tests would not predict ahead of time if the patient is more or less likely to have issues if they choose to get implants," he told Fox News Digital.
"The cause could be due to breast implants, but the only way to confirm that is to remove the implants and see if the patient improves."

For those experiencing symptoms such as fatigue, joint or muscle pain, and cognitive concerns, Kaplan recommends starting by looking for other treatable causes, which might include MS or effects of medications.

"The cause could be due to breast implants, but the only way to confirm that is to remove the implants and see if the patient improves," he said. "If they do not, then they may have unnecessarily undergone a surgical procedure that did not benefit them."
MYSTERIOUS DISEASE SENDING YOUNG, HEALTHY TEXAS WORKERS INTO KIDNEY FAILURE
For women who are considering explant surgery, Kaplan asks them how they would feel if they removed the implants and the symptoms persist.

"If they've run out of other options or causes of their illness, they may feel like it is worth the risk of having a procedure even if it doesn't help their illness," he said. "There's no evidence at this time that MS would be affected by the presence or absence of implants."
In 2021, the FDA issued strict new labeling rules requiring a boxed warning and a mandatory patient decision checklist for all breast implants. (iStock)
Kaplan shared that he once had a patient who received breast implants and then several years later experienced fatigue and had abnormal bloodwork suggestive of kidney failure.

"Once she removed her implants, she felt better and labs returned to normal," he said. "But we couldn't have gotten any lab ahead of time that would have predicted her risk of breast implant-associated illness."
What the research shows

Patricia McGuire, M.D., a St. Louis-based plastic surgeon and chair of the Breast Implant Emergency Task Force, noted that over 100 symptoms have been reported by patients in association with breast implant illness.
"They have no abnormal labs or physical findings, and there is no diagnostic criteria," she told Fox News Digital. "It is a diagnosis of exclusion and is not a currently recognized illness."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Symptoms can occur with all types of implants, she noted – silicone gel, saline, smooth and textured implants, by all manufacturers.

"We do not know the cause," McGuire said. "The suggestions have been heavy metals from the implants entering the body, bacterial biofilms, fungal infections, allergic reactions, immune response to a foreign body and neuropsychiatric conditions."
"We also know that some patients may get better with implant removal."

In a prospective, blinded study that McGuire co-led with Dr. Caroline Glicksman, researchers found no biological differences — such as heavy metals, bacteria or inflammatory blood markers — between women reporting breast implant illness and asymptomatic control groups.

Instead, the research revealed that while patients experienced genuine symptom relief after implant removal, the condition was strongly linked to elevated anxiety, somatic symptom patterns and a heavy reliance on social media for medical information, she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"To be honest, we were disappointed that we did not find an easily reversible cause, or that we did not find a blood value that could be used to make a diagnosis or point to the cause of symptoms in these patients," McGuire added.
"We have a couple of pilot studies in the works, hoping we can find something definitive."
What patients should know
In 2021, the FDA issued strict new labeling rules requiring a boxed warning and a mandatory patient decision checklist for all breast implants.
The warning explicitly lists systemic symptoms, such as fatigue, memory loss, rash, "brain fog" and joint pain, and notes that symptoms may resolve after removal.

For those experiencing symptoms such as fatigue, joint or muscle pain, and cognitive concerns, a surgeon recommends starting by looking for other treatable causes, which might include MS or effects of medications. (iStock)

Breast implants are not considered lifetime devices. The FDA recommends routine MRI or ultrasound screenings starting five to six years after surgery (and every two to three years after) to check for "silent" ruptures.
However, implants do not have a strict 10-year expiration date if they are intact and the patient is asymptomatic.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Anyone with breast implants who experiences symptoms should undergo a full medical work-up to rule out reversible causes before having surgery, McGuire advised.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"For a patient considering implant removal, they should see a board-certified plastic surgeon who has experience in breast surgery," she added.
Fox News Digital reached out to implant manufacturers requesting comment.

title: Popular alcoholic drinks linked to sudden kidney damage in 14-year study
summary: Beer and hard liquor drinkers face a sharply higher risk of acute kidney injury, a UK Biobank study finds, while red and white wine showed no such link.
story: Josh Gowin explains how research has shifted the understanding of alcohol's health risks, including its association with reduced brain volume, as drinking habits and social norms continue to change.

People who regularly drink beer or hard liquor face a significantly higher risk of sudden kidney damage than light drinkers, while wine drinkers do not show the same increased risk, according to a large British study.
Researchers at Anglia Ruskin University analyzed health and lifestyle data from 250,791 adult drinkers in the UK Biobank database, tracking them for an average of 14 years.
Over that time, 10,335 participants developed acute kidney injury, a serious condition in which the kidneys suddenly stop filtering waste from the blood properly.
IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE
The study, published in the journal Scientific Reports, challenges a longstanding medical assumption that alcohol harms the kidneys mainly as a secondary consequence of liver disease.
The elevated risk among beer and liquor drinkers continued even after researchers considered liver disease and a wide range of other health and lifestyle factors.

The elevated risk for beer and liquor drinkers persisted even after accounting for liver disease, suggesting alcohol may damage the kidneys directly through inflammation rather than solely as a secondary effect of liver harm. (iStock)

"Acute kidney injury is a serious condition that can lead to chronic kidney disease, kidney failure and an increased risk of dying early," lead author Rudolph Schutte, an associate professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Anglia Ruskin University, said in a university news release.

"While alcohol has traditionally been linked with kidney injury through its impact on the liver, our research suggests that spirits and beer may contribute directly to kidney damage through inflammatory pathways."
HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK
To compare drinking habits, the researchers divided participants into three groups based on their average weekly consumption of each type of alcohol.
In the U.K., one unit of alcohol equals 8 grams of pure alcohol — a little more than half of a standard U.S. shot of liquor or about half a pint of lower-strength beer.
"Acute kidney injury is a serious condition that can lead to chronic kidney disease, kidney failure and an increased risk of dying early."

Among liquor drinkers, those in the lowest consumption group drank an average of 1.22 units per week. Compared with that group, people who averaged 2.69 units per week were 8.1% more likely to develop acute kidney injury.
Those in the highest tier, averaging 8.73 units per week, had a 25.5% higher risk.

Beer drinkers showed a similar, though smaller, pattern. Compared with light beer drinkers averaging 2.67 units per week, people who drank an average of 6.81 units had a 5.7% higher risk of acute kidney injury.
Those in the highest group, averaging 23.6 units per week, faced a 14.8% higher risk
Regular consumption of beer or hard liquor is linked to a significantly higher risk of sudden kidney damage, whereas wine shows no significant overall association. (iStock)
Researchers found no significant link between red or white wine consumption and a higher risk of acute kidney injury overall.
The authors noted that higher levels of internal inflammation appeared to drive the increased risk seen with other drinks.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"The results provide important population-level evidence supporting laboratory research that has suggested alcohol can directly affect the kidneys," Schutte said.
Beer drinkers saw a smaller increase in risk, rising by 5.7% at an average of 6.81 units per week and 14.8% at 23.6 units per week compared to light beer drinkers. (iStock)
Because the study is observational, it can only identify links between drinking habits and kidney injury, and cannot prove that beer or liquor directly caused the damage.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The authors also warned that the findings do not prove wine protects the kidneys, noting that drinking above 14 units per week, the U.K.’s recommended limit, was tied to higher risk across all drink types, including wine.

Additionally, participants relied on memory to report their average weekly alcohol intake, which can lead to inaccurate estimates or underreporting.
The study also only included adults ages 40 to 69, meaning the results may not apply to younger or older people.

title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' mania comes with serious health risks, doctors warn
summary: Experts warn Grand Theft Auto VI marathon sessions can trigger eye strain, sleep deprivation and problematic gaming amid the PlayStation 5 launch.
story: Psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert addresses concerns surrounding major video game releases, noting that while violent games do not cause real-world crime, excessive screen time can strain health and relationships.

As millions of players prepare for the long-awaited release of "Grand Theft Auto VI," mental health and medical experts are warning that marathon gaming sessions, skipped sleep and obsessive playing habits could have physical and psychological effects.
The latest installment in the blockbuster franchise launches Thursday, Nov. 19, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, according to New York-based maker Rockstar Games.
"Grand Theft Auto VI" is an action-adventure game set in the fictional state of Leonida, which includes Vice City. Players follow a story while exploring the game’s world and taking on missions.
SKIPPING SLEEP MAY PACK ON POUNDS FASTER THAN YOU THINK, NEW STUDY FINDS
The release is prompting questions about how much time players may devote to the game — including during the workweek.
According to a survey of 1,000 full-time employed U.S. gamers conducted by gaming and esports media company GameSquare, 10% plan to skip work for the game’s launch.
The latest installment in "Grand Theft Auto" launches Thursday, Nov. 19, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, according to New York-based maker Rockstar Games. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)

Another 30% are considering taking time off, and 36% said they would call in sick rather than use planned vacation days. Meanwhile, 42% expect to be less productive at work because of the release, according to the survey.
TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS

Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist based in New York and Washington, D.C., compared the excitement around major game releases to overnight lines for new smartphones, saying fans want to be part of the moment.
DOCTOR REVEALS 4 HIDDEN HEALTH RISKS OF SPENDING TOO MUCH TIME INDOORS

"Video games and social media can be a great distraction from the stress of real life and relationships, but it shouldn't become real life," Alpert, author of "Therapy Nation," told Fox News Digital. "In other words, it shouldn't dominate. It should just be an escape."
Health risks of extended play

"Grand Theft Auto" is an open-world game, meaning players can freely explore a large virtual environment rather than follow a set path from one level to the next. Cleveland Clinic says that freedom, along with the game’s fast-paced action and rewards, can make it hard to stop playing.
"It shouldn't dominate. It should just be an escape."
That constant stream of stimulation can raise a player’s threshold for excitement, making ordinary offline interactions feel flat by comparison, according to Alpert.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Pulling an all-nighter to explore Vice City can also take a toll on the brain. According to the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute, sleep deficiency impairs concentration, slows reaction times and makes it harder to regulate emotions.

While a single late night is unlikely to cause lasting harm, Alpert said, repeated sleep loss can leave players more vulnerable to anxiety, irritability and difficulty completing basic tasks at school or work.
Sitting at a screen for eight or more hours can trigger neck and back pain, as well as digital eye strain, experts warn. (iStock)

Extended gaming sessions can take a physical toll. Sitting at a screen for eight or more hours can contribute to neck and back pain, repetitive-motion injuries and eyestrain, according to Mayo Clinic.
Research cited by the clinic found that eyestrain affects up to 56% of competitive gamers. Symptoms can include headaches and blurred vision.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Prolonged, uninterrupted sitting can reduce blood flow to the brain and legs, while also affecting blood-vessel function.
"People can get sick if they are sitting at a computer for eight or more hours a day playing games," Alpert cautioned.
Signs of problematic play

The American Psychiatric Association lists nine proposed symptoms of internet gaming disorder, a condition included in the DSM-5-TR for further study. A proposed diagnosis requires five or more of the following symptoms within a year.

Becoming preoccupied with gamingFeeling irritable, anxious or sad when unable to playNeeding to spend more time gaming to feel satisfiedMaking repeated unsuccessful attempts to cut backLosing interest in other activitiesContinuing to play despite problemsLying to family members or others about time spent gamingUsing games to escape or relieve a negative moodJeopardizing or losing a significant relationship, job or educational opportunity because of gaming

Roughly 10% of full-time employed U.S. gamers plan to skip work outright for the "Grand Theft Auto VI" launch, while 42% anticipate being less productive. (iStock)

"When I look at addictions or people spending too much time online, I look at how [it] has impacted relationships, their work, school, family relations, their health and their finances," Alpert said. "So, when we start to see those suffering, there's a problem."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Adolescents and young adults may be more vulnerable to problematic gaming, while anxiety and depression can co-occur with it, according to Cleveland Clinic.
Ensuring safe play
To participate in launch week in a healthy way, experts recommend setting the following boundaries.

Take regular movement breaks: Stand, walk or stretch for at least five minutes every hour to restore circulation and ease muscle tension, Alpert suggests.Set firm time limits: Alpert advises parents to keep consoles out of teenagers’ bedrooms and limit play to an hour or two after homework is finished. For adults, he recommends prioritizing work and relationships over late-night sessions.Create a mental buffer: After logging off, take a brief breather before jumping back into daily responsibilities.

Set firm time limits: Alpert advises parents to keep consoles out of teenagers’ bedrooms and limit play to an hour or two after homework is finished. For adults, he recommends prioritizing work and relationships over late-night sessions.
Create a mental buffer: After logging off, take a brief breather before jumping back into daily responsibilities.
"You almost have to do a gut check and a reset and remind yourself that what you just saw is fantasy and what you're experiencing now is reality," Alpert added.
Sitting at a screen for eight or more hours can contribute to neck and back pain, repetitive-motion injuries and eyestrain, according to Mayo Clinic. (iStock)
The psychotherapist added that concerns about gaming’s physical effects should be separated from claims that violent games lead to real-world violence.

"Millions of people play violent video games, and they don’t go out there and commit crimes," he said, adding that there is no evidence linking gameplay to real-life violence.

title: Flu activity rises across US as 6 states reach high levels, CDC data shows
summary: Cases of the flu are spiking early nationwide, with the CDC reporting Louisiana at very high activity and influenza A (H1N1) the top virus this season.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses rising flu activity across the U.S. and advances in fertility treatment after actress Hilary Swank reportedly announced her third pregnancy at 52.
Cases of the flu are already cropping up across the country in an early spike.
In its weekly influenza update, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has alerted that seasonal flu activity is "higher than typically observed at this time of year."

About 11% of specimens tested for flu at clinical labs were positive in the week ending Nov. 7, with that percentage rising. The CDC also reported more than 3% of doctors’ office visits were due to flu-like symptoms.
WANT TO DODGE THE FLU THIS YEAR? EAT THESE SECRET-WEAPON IMMUNITY-BOOSTING FOODS
New York, Massachusetts and Hawaii were in the CDC map’s moderate category for influenza-like illness in the week ending Nov. 7 (week 44).

The CDC’s Outpatient Respiratory Illness Activity Map uses reports from ILINet, the agency’s national network of outpatient health care providers, to show how often patients are visiting doctors for respiratory illness symptoms. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)

California, Tennessee and Oregon were in the high category for influenza-like illness, along with South Carolina and Texas. Louisiana was the only state in the very high category, according to the CDC’s Week 44 map.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The CDC noted that an earlier increase in activity does not predict a higher seasonal peak or overall severity.

While it’s too early to know which flu viruses will be most dominant this season, in the week ending Nov. 7, the most frequently reported virus was influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, a descendant of the strain that caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic and has circulated seasonally since.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The CDC estimates that there have been 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations and 2,100 deaths tied to flu infections so far this season. Five flu-associated deaths among children have been reported to the agency.
Cases of influenza are already on the rise across the U.S. this November. (iStock)
In an October media briefing, Dr. Anna Durbin of Johns Hopkins University stated that the flu hospitalization rate in mid-October was the highest it’s been in 15 years.
"Because the flu season is starting a bit earlier, I think it's really important for everyone to get a flu vaccine as soon as possible," she advised.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Dr. Fred Lopez, an infectious diseases specialist at the LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans, told the Associated Press that flu season is "taking off in a direction that’s only likely to increase in the next month or two."
"If you haven’t been vaccinated, you should get vaccinated now," he added.
The CDC recommends an annual seasonal flu vaccination, available for people 6 months and older. (iStock)

The CDC recommends an annual flu vaccine for everyone 6 months and older. Prescription antiviral drugs can treat flu and should be started as early as possible, especially for people at higher risk of complications.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
With Thanksgiving approaching, doctors expect flu and other respiratory viruses to spread as people travel and gather with friends and family.
Last winter, flu activity surged in late December. At the time, New York City health officials described the season as the city’s most intense in 20 years, according to the AP.

title: Alzheimer’s blood marker could predict cognitive decline risks, Mayo Clinic says
summary: A Mayo Clinic study finds a p-tau217 blood test may predict cognitive decline risk within five to 10 years, offering a less invasive option than PET scans.
story: Clifford Jack Jr., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist, speaks about a blood test that detects a protein linked to Alzheimer’s disease, which could help predict whether older adults will develop cognitive decline within five to 10 years.

A blood test that detects a protein linked to Alzheimer’s disease could help predict whether older adults will develop cognitive decline within five to 10 years, according to a new Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology.

The study looked at levels of phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) in 2,178 cognitively unimpaired adults, ranging in age from 60 to 90. It also considered age, gender and whether participants carried the APOE ε4 genetic variant, which is associated with Alzheimer’s risk.
The participants, drawn from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, underwent blood biomarker testing, genetic testing and multiple cognitive assessments.
ALZHEIMER'S WARNING SIGNS COULD EMERGE YEARS BEFORE MEMORY LOSS, STUDY FINDS
While APOE ε4 had a modest association with risk after accounting for p-tau217, older age was associated with greater risk, according to the researchers.
For example, at the same elevated p-tau217 level, a 65-year-old faced a 6% estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment, compared to a 37% risk for an 85-year-old.
A blood test that detects a protein linked to Alzheimer’s disease could help predict whether older adults will develop cognitive decline within five to 10 years. (iStock)
Alzheimer’s disease is marked by plaques and tangles that accumulate in the brain, senior author Clifford Jack Jr., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist, noted.

"The test tells you, just by taking a blood sample, whether someone has that pathology in the brain," he told Fox News Digital, adding higher levels of the pathology are associated with a greater risk of progressing from normal cognition to impairment.
10 HEALTH CONDITIONS MAY BE LINKED TO ALZHEIMER'S YEARS BEFORE DIAGNOSIS

Detecting p-tau217 in blood may be "less invasive and potentially more scalable" than using PET scans to measure amyloid burden, a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease that is associated with future cognitive impairment.

"The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology," first author Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher, said in a news release.
Alzheimer’s disease is marked by plaques and tangles that accumulate in the brain. (iStock)
If investigational treatments are found to be effective at preventing or delaying cognitive decline, this blood test could take on greater significance, according to the researchers.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment," Jack noted.
Study limitations
The risk estimates were developed in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, which is drawn from a specific geographical area.
"The older population in southeast Minnesota is not representative of the entire United States," Jack said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
While the study’s methods could be applied to other populations, the researcher said the findings need to be replicated outside the region.
The study does not establish that routine blood testing prevents dementia or improves clinical outcomes. (iStock)
The risk prediction model is not yet ready for routine screening of people without cognitive symptoms, according to the research team.

"There is no treatment that’s been approved for people who are [asymptomatic] but have the disease in the brain," Jack told Fox News Digital. "Therefore, there’s no reason to do the test. … The results of the test would not change your medical management at all since there’s no treatment available."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
That could change if preventive treatments are approved, he added.
The study does not establish that routine blood testing prevents dementia or improves clinical outcomes.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Many elderly people who have the pathology in the brain at lower levels will never develop symptoms in their lifetime," Jack added, noting that some people with Alzheimer’s-related pathology may also die of another cause before developing cognitive impairment.

title: New organ donation rules take effect after alarming reports of patients showing ‘signs of life’
summary: New HRSA organ donation rules take effect Nov. 18, adding a five-minute waiting period after circulatory death and a formal pause process for families.
story: Dr. Raymond Lynch, director of the Division of Transplantation at HRSA, discusses how updated federal organ donation guidelines seek to protect patients and improve communication with families facing difficult end-of-life decisions.
New organ donation guidelines have taken effect as of Nov. 18, updating procedures for some donors.

The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), a branch of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), previously announced the policy update in a press release after the changes were approved by the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network in August.

The new guidelines apply to donation after circulatory death (DCD), in which organs are recovered after the heart and lungs stop functioning. This differs from donation after brain death, when the donor is declared dead based on the irreversible loss of brain function.
BRIDE IS WALKED DOWN WEDDING AISLE BY MAN WHO RECEIVED HER LATE FATHER'S HEART
What the new rules require

The changes include a formal process to pause donation if patient safety concerns arise. Families, medical providers and other people involved in the process must be told they can request a pause and how to do so.
New guidelines for organ donation aim to better inform families and providers. (iStock)
Procedures will also be added for handling and reporting unplanned pauses, along with more detailed records of neurological assessments.
Additionally, a minimum five-minute waiting period will be put in place after circulation stops and before organ recovery begins.
Timing concerns

While the changes are intended to strengthen patient safeguards and improve communication with families, University of Rochester bioethicist Dr. Lainie Ross told NPR that allowing organ procurement teams to approach families before they decide whether to withdraw life-sustaining care could leave them feeling pressured or distrustful of doctors’ motives.
In public comments, the American Society of Transplantation said it supports honoring requests to pause the donation process at any point.
ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED 'SIGNS OF LIFE,' FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS

Previous cases in which organ recovery was reportedly begun before confirmation of death have raised questions about safeguards in the donation process. HRSA Division of Transplantation Director Dr. Raymond Lynch told Fox News Digital that "does not happen" under the process governed by the new guidelines.

"The point of these policies that were put into place is to make sure that we do preserve the sanctity of that decision and make sure that the technical parts of the operation ... pose no risk to the patient," Lynch told Fox News Digital.
New guidelines implement a minimum five-minute waiting period between circulatory death and the start of organ recovery. (iStock)
The HRSA director said these new guidelines improve the "safety, quality and consistency of care that's already being delivered across the United States."

Organ donation has changed just within the last decade, according to Lynch. Historically, most donors were declared as "brain-dead," meaning they were "legally deceased" at the time the decision was made.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Now, we're dealing with [DCD], which means that it's an individual who's not brain-dead, but they're very severely injured," he said. "The medical team and the family have come to the decision that they're going to change the goals of care and let that person have a natural, compassionate death."
"In that setting, shortly after they pass away, their organs are removed through a surgical procedure."
"The goal should always be to save lives through donation without ever compromising the care, dignity or safety of the donor."

The guidelines do not change the roles of the patient’s healthcare team or the organ procurement organization (OPO), the group that coordinates organ donation and recovery. Rather, they set clearer expectations for when donation-related discussions and procedures take place, according to Lynch.
"Historically, it was very, very late in the patient's medical course before there could be a discussion of them being an organ donor," he said. "And that really has two kinds of harm."
The HRSA aims to ensure that the quality and quantity of communication and medical care being delivered is "very high." (iStock)
One concern was that families may have felt "rushed or pressured" to decide whether to authorize organ donation before they had enough time to make an informed choice.
He said delays could deny patients "the chance to give the gift" of organ donation, as they intended when they signed up to be donors.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The other risk was an "insufficient delivery" of information and recording of decisions, according to Lynch.
He said the new guidelines bring more thorough conversations and clearer records of what information was shared with families, and when.
These conversations are "happening in truly tragic circumstances," Lynch noted, as families and loved ones are feeling fear and grief.

"We're making sure through these regulations that there is a level of professionalism and consistency, and that the care people's loved ones get is ... compassionate and respectful," said Dr. Raymond Lynch. (iStock)
The HRSA aims to ensure that the quality and quantity of communication and medical care is "very high."

"All of this is about elevating this to the level of a medical specialty," he said. "We're making sure through these regulations that there is a level of professionalism and consistency, and that the care people's loved ones are going to get is ... compassionate and respectful."
What families should know

Dr. Stephanie Widmer, New York City emergency medicine physician and Fox News medical contributor, said families should know that "there are now clearer safeguards," including the five-minute wait and the chance to pause the process.
She added that while organ donation saves lives, protection of the donor "must always come first."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"I think these changes are a positive step toward improving patient safety, transparency and public trust," Widmer, who was not involved in the guideline updates, told Fox News Digital. "My concern is whether these safeguards will be consistently enforced across hospitals and organ procurement organizations."
While organ donation saves lives, protection of the donor "must always come first," said Dr. Stephanie Widmer (not pictured). (iStock)
The doctor added that a policy is "only as effective as its implementation," and that additional procedural requirements don’t "unnecessarily interfere with a patient’s wishes to donate."
Widmer said she'd like to see stronger national standards for independent neurological assessments and "greater oversight" of organ procurement practices.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"The medical team caring for the patient should remain completely independent of the organ recovery process," she emphasized. "Families also deserve clear explanations of exactly what will happen, including any specialized procedures used to preserve organs."
"The goal should always be to save lives through donation without ever compromising the care, dignity or safety of the donor."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: RFK Jr faces fierce backlash after US loses measles-free status for first time in 26 years
summary: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faces criticism after the U.S. lost measles elimination status amid over 5,400 confirmed cases this year.
story: Dr. Marc Siegel warns that dropping measles vaccination rates could cost the U.S. its elimination status. The Fox News senior medical analyst joins hosts Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino to discuss the rise to over 5,000 cases in 2026. Siegel outlines what is driving the decline and explains how communities can protect public health.

Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is facing mounting criticism from Democrats after the United States lost its measles elimination status for the first time in more than 25 years.

The Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination designation amid a resurgence of the highly contagious virus, with more than 5,400 confirmed cases reported this year — the highest annual total in more than three decades.
The virus has spread largely among unvaccinated populations, prompting criticism from Democrats who have previously scrutinized Kennedy's stance on vaccines.
On Tuesday, Kennedy vowed to stop measles outbreaks and restore the country's measles elimination status, while continuing to recommend vaccination against the disease.
CNN'S DANA BASH SPARS WITH RFK JR OVER VACCINE EFFICACY, DEMANDS HE 'LOOK INTO THE CAMERA' AND PUSH VACCINES

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. defended the federal response to the measles outbreak as Democratic governors criticized his leadership following the United States' loss of its measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
"We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status," Kennedy said in a statement.
He added, "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
Several Democrats sharply criticized Kennedy following the announcement.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, whose state has reported its first measles-associated death in more than three decades, involving a child, accused Kennedy of contributing to declining vaccination rates through years of vaccine skepticism.
CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK
Kathy Hochul, governor of New York, speaks during a news conference at the WIN NYC family shelter in New York on Thursday, March 5, 2026. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"RFK Jr. promised to 'Make America Healthy Again.' Now America has lost its measles-free status for the first time in 26 years," Hochul said.
"A disgraceful display of incompetence from the nation's highest public health office," she added.
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro also blamed Kennedy, arguing that the loss of elimination status reflected the consequences of vaccine misinformation and skepticism.
"There is a clear line from the misinformation, vaccine skepticism, and incompetence of RFK Jr. to this devastating news and very real consequences," Shapiro said.
"Measles is preventable. We eliminated it in this country once, and we can do it again."
MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear speaks during an event titled "How Democrats Can Connect with America" at the Center for American Progress on Feb. 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Another Democratic governor called for Kennedy's removal from office.
"This dangerous setback was 100% avoidable and is the result of one person: RFK Jr.," Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear said. "Remove him now."

An HHS spokesperson pushed back on the Democratic governors' criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital, calling their attacks "baseless" and arguing that declining vaccination rates predated the Trump administration.

The spokesperson also said the administration remains focused on expanding vaccine access, closing immunization gaps and assisting state and local officials with outbreak investigations, while Kennedy continues to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles.

Responding specifically to Hochul, HHS said Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz had spoken directly with the governor and that federal epidemiologists were deployed to New York at the state's request. The department also said it provided $2.36 million to New York state and $2.07 million to New York City to support testing, vaccination efforts and community outreach.

The U.S., which had maintained the measles designation since 2000, is experiencing its worst measles outbreak since 1991 and has reported more than twice as many cases as in all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Measles elimination means there has been no continuous local transmission of the virus for at least 12 months. The U.S. reached the status in 2000 after years of coordinated immunization campaigns.
NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. makes his way to the inaugural Great American Farmers Market on the National Mall on Monday, August 4, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
Schwartz defended the agency's response to the ongoing outbreak, emphasizing that vaccination remains the most important tool for protecting Americans.
"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," Schwartz said.
She added that the CDC had invested approximately $100 million in state and local health departments to strengthen outbreak prevention and response.
The agency also noted that MMR vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% during the 2019–2020 school year to 92.7% in 2023–2024.

In his statement, Kennedy cited COVID-19-era disruptions as a factor in declining routine childhood vaccination coverage, noting that several other countries, including Canada, Mexico and the United Kingdom, had also lost their measles elimination status.

Fox News Digital has reached out to HHS for additional comment.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Pancreatic cancer mystery deepens as researchers make unexpected discovery
summary: University of Cincinnati study found Black patients' pancreatic tumors had more B cells and cells tied to drug resistance, pointing to tailored care.
story: Dr. Raymond Wadlow, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Inova Schar Cancer Institute in Virginia, said the surrounding immune cells and tissue may affect how a tumor behaves and responds to treatment.

A University of Cincinnati study found differences in pancreatic tumors that could help explain why that type of cancer affects some patients differently, potentially leading to more personalized treatments.

Researchers examined 22 pancreatic tumors from patients of different racial backgrounds across the U.S., looking for differences in cancer cells and how the immune system responds to them. The study included seven Black patients and 15 non-African American patients.
The findings were published in the journal Cancer Research.
FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE
Tumors from Black patients had fewer of the most common type of pancreatic cancer cells and more cells with a mix of different characteristics, the researchers found.
Some of those cell characteristics have been associated with drug resistance, but the study did not establish whether they affected patients’ treatment outcomes.
A University of Cincinnati study found differences in pancreatic tumors that could help explain why that type of cancer affects some patients differently. (iStock)

Additionally, tumors from Black patients contained more B cells, a type of immune cell, and larger clusters of immune cells. Researchers found signs that some B cells may suppress the body’s response to cancer, although the significance of these differences is unclear.
PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY

Dr. Raymond Wadlow, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Inova Schar Cancer Institute in Virginia, said that using immunotherapy to help the immune system attack the disease has been particularly challenging in pancreatic cancer.

"That's been very difficult to do in pancreatic cancer because the pancreatic tumor subverts the immune system so that it is fighting for it instead of for the host or the rest of the body," Wadlow, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.

Tumors from Black patients contained more B cells, a type of immune cell, and larger clusters of immune cells. Researchers found signs that some B cells may suppress the body’s response to cancer. (iStock)
The study found no significant differences between groups in the major genetic changes known to drive the disease.
Pancreatic cancer is approximately 20% more likely to develop in Black Americans than in non-African Americans, according to the researchers.
WHERE YOU LIVE COULD SHAPE YOUR RISK OF CANCER MORTALITY, STUDY SUGGESTS

The findings highlight the importance of including patients from different backgrounds in cancer research, according to lead study author Nina Steele, Ph.D., an assistant professor in UC’s College of Medicine.
"This study shows that ignoring diverse ancestry in medical research leaves blind spots in the search for a cure," she told Fox News Digital.
An oncologist (not pictured) encouraged newly diagnosed patients to ask about hereditary genetic testing, which can identify inherited mutations that may also affect relatives. (iStock)
Wadlow noted that pancreatic cancers can share major DNA mutations but can differ considerably in how their cells behave and interact with nearby immune cells and surrounding tissue.
"Those differences may also vary across patient populations, such as between Black and non-Black patients," he told Fox News Digital.
"While intriguing, these findings are still a long way from changing patient care."
"That is potentially important both for understanding disparities in pancreatic cancer and, ultimately, for developing more individualized treatments."
Pancreatic cancer can vary from one tumor to another, and even within the same tumor, Wadlow explained. "The cancer cell itself is only part of the story," he said.
Pancreatic cancer is approximately 20% more likely to develop in Black Americans than in non-African Americans, according to the researchers. (iStock)
The surrounding immune cells and tissue may affect how a tumor behaves and responds to treatment, helping to explain why a single treatment approach may not work for every patient.
The findings have several limitations.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Researchers have not established how the intermediate tumor cells affect survival or whether they respond differently to standard chemotherapy, Steele said.
The team also needs to study pancreatic tissue from people without cancer to better understand when these differences develop.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Wadlow cautioned that race and genetic ancestry do not fully account for the environmental, socioeconomic and biological factors that could explain the findings.
Larger studies involving patients from diverse backgrounds are needed to determine whether these differences affect treatment outcomes or survival, the oncologist said.
Immunotherapy to help the immune system attack cancer has been particularly challenging in pancreatic cancer, an oncologist said. (Aaron Chown/PA Images via Getty Images)
"While intriguing, these findings are still a long way from changing patient care," he added.
Wadlow encouraged newly diagnosed patients to ask about hereditary genetic testing, which can identify inherited mutations that may also affect relatives.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If we find an inherited mutation, then family members can be tested," he said.
Steele said the findings also underscore the need for clinical trials that represent the patients affected by pancreatic cancer.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It is also a reminder for the medical system to ensure that clinical trials reflect the entire population at risk, in order to find treatments that can help all patients, not just some patients," she told Fox News Digital.
The research was funded in part by the National Cancer Institute.

title: Widely used antidepressant outperformed by 3 other drugs in major study of 30,000 people
summary: A study of 20 antidepressants and over 30,000 patients found three medications may beat fluoxetine for long-term depression treatment results overall.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen, founder of Amen Clinics, identifies six behaviors people should avoid when experiencing depression, including drinking alcohol, withdrawing from others and consuming highly processed foods.
Three antidepressants may work better than fluoxetine, widely known by the brand name Prozac, at helping people with depression get better and stay well over time, a new study suggests.
The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, compared 20 antidepressants to determine how well they eased depression symptoms and helped prevent them from returning over time.
Researchers analyzed 115 previous clinical trials involving more than 30,000 people, according to a news release from Radboud University Medical Center in the Netherlands.
CERTAIN SLEEP HABITS COULD OFFER CLUES TO HIDDEN TYPE OF DEPRESSION, SCIENTISTS SAY

They found that escitalopram, sold under the brand name Lexapro; duloxetine, sold as Cymbalta; and agomelatine performed better over the long term than fluoxetine, which researchers used as the main comparison drug.

Eli Lilly told Fox News Digital that it discontinued manufacturing Prozac in 2024. The company noted that fluoxetine remains available in many FDA-approved generic medicines and that neither the study nor the university’s news release specifically referred to Prozac or any Lilly product.
A new study suggests three antidepressants may work better than fluoxetine at helping people recover from depression and stay well over time. (iStock)
The findings suggest that antidepressants can continue helping people after their symptoms improve, although some medications appeared to work better than others at keeping patients well.
Paul van Haaren, a researcher at Radboud University Medical Center who worked on the study, noted that the three medications have different benefits and drawbacks.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Escitalopram is already widely used," he said in the release. "Agomelatine works well, but one of its side effects is the risk of liver failure. Duloxetine is less well-known and is prescribed less frequently as a first-line treatment."

Escitalopram belongs to a common group of antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These medications are often recommended as a first option for treating depression, according to the release.
Researchers compared antidepressant treatments to better understand which medications may help patients maintain improvements and avoid a return of depression symptoms. (iStock)
Among the SSRIs included in the study, escitalopram appeared to work best at helping patients stay well over time.

Eric Ruhé, a professor of difficult-to-treat depression at Radboud University Medical Center, said the findings could eventually influence how doctors choose antidepressants. Still, the researchers stressed that this does not mean everyone with depression should take escitalopram.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"As a prescriber, you consider the balance between a medication's benefits and side effects," Ruhé said in the release. "That balance differs from person to person."
Dr. Carole Lieberman, a board-certified psychiatrist based in Beverly Hills, California, who was not involved in the study, urged caution when interpreting the findings.
Escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine appeared to outperform fluoxetine in maintaining improvements in depression symptoms over the long term. (iStock)
She noted that agomelatine is not approved in the U.S.
"The best way to treat someone with depression is not always with antidepressants, and certainly not with antidepressants alone," Lieberman told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Psychotherapy or talk therapy can also play an important role in treating depression, according to Lieberman, while some patients may benefit from using medication along with therapy.
There were some limitations to the study, the researchers acknowledged.
Researchers cautioned that the findings cannot predict which antidepressant will work best for a specific patient, emphasizing the need for individualized treatment decisions. (iStock)
Rather than enrolling a new group of patients and following them over time, the researchers combined results from 115 previous clinical trials to compare how the medications performed.

The findings also cannot predict which antidepressant will work best for a specific person. The researchers stressed that doctors and patients should consider both the potential benefits and side effects when choosing a medication.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
People with questions about their antidepressants should speak with their doctor before making any medication changes, according to the release.
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers and additional drug manufacturers for comment.

title: Woman’s kratom addiction spiraled from 4 capsules to 100 a day: ‘Zombie shell of myself’
summary: Hilary Tesluck shares how kratom capsules led to a spiraling addiction, with her daily intake climbing to 100 capsules before she sought help.
story: Hilary Tesluck, 30, executive director of End Kratom Addiction, shares her journey of dependence and recovery with Fox News Digital.
Kratom-related reports to U.S. poison centers rose about 1,200% from 2015 to 2025, reaching a record high of 3,434 last year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
For Hilary Tesluck, a 30-year-old woman in Michigan, the potential for addiction began well before those numbers emerged.
Tesluck, who now works to raise awareness of kratom addiction and support others in recovery, said she first tried kratom capsules in 2017 at age 21.
KRATOM INDUSTRY WARNS SYNTHETIC OPIOIDS SHOULD NOT BE CALLED 'KRATOM'

Her initial use involved leaf kratom rather than concentrated 7-OH products, she shared. The American Kratom Association argues that 7-OH should be distinguished from natural leaf kratom, while acknowledging that kratom itself can cause dependence.
Hilary Tesluck, who now works to raise awareness of kratom addiction and support others in recovery, said she first tried kratom capsules in 2017 at age 21. (Hilary Tesluck)

"It was introduced to me by a friend who knew that I was someone who suffered from anxiety and took prescription medication for it," Tesluck told Fox News Digital. "I wanted to be more holistic and natural in what I was consuming."
She noted that she doesn’t recall any dosing recommendations on the label. "I didn’t know how much to take, but my friend told me to take four capsules."
WHAT IS KRATOM? RISKS OF POPULAR SUBSTANCE REVEALED AFTER COLLEGE STUDENTS' DEATHS
At first, Tesluck – an undergraduate student at the time, who was also conducting research and tutoring – noticed the substance gave her a boost in energy, confidence and productivity.
Growing dependence
Tesluck's daily intake climbed gradually. "Very slowly, over time, I had to take just one more capsule or just one more dose, and then went all the way up to 100," she said.
Her day-to-day functioning began to suffer, she shared. "I was not doing very well at work. I was getting … written up for performance."
Physically, she had lost nearly 40 pounds and struggled to even stand in the shower "because my body was so wasted away."
Tesluck said a friend introduced her to kratom as a more "holistic and natural" alternative to her anxiety prescription medication. (Hilary Tesluck)
Tesluck’s belief that kratom was natural and legal made her growing dependence difficult to accept, she said.
"About a year and a half into my kratom addiction from just the leaf … I finally realized I needed to do something, and I needed help."
Seeking help
When she first sought treatment in 2020, Tesluck described feeling dismissed, saying that the facility’s urine test did not detect her use and that she had to explain what kratom was to the staff.
"They were confused why I was there," she said. "So I left after just a few days because I felt kind of humiliated, and I went right back to my use."
Tesluck found more help in 2021, when she attended an online recovery meeting.
"I had nothing to lose," she said. "It changed everything for me to hear other people telling my story for the first time."
After years of feeling alone in her addiction, she said, she finally felt surrounded by people who understood.
"It’s one problem at two strengths."

In 2023, Tesluck relapsed following her grandmother’s death. "I was just grief-stricken. She was really close to me," she said. "So I went to the smoke shop just to get a little bit of kratom, just one time."
She later experienced a separate relapse involving 7-OH, which she said followed the death of her cat and the end of a relationship on the same night.
MEN AND WOMEN WHO SMOKE MARIJUANA MAY EXPERIENCE DIFFERENT EFFECTS, STUDY SUGGESTS
7-OH, short for 7-hydroxymitragynine, occurs naturally in trace amounts in kratom. Concentrated 7-OH products contain much higher levels than the leaf itself.
The body converts some of kratom’s main active compound, mitragynine, into 7-OH, research shows. Both compounds act on opioid receptors and can contribute to dependence, according to the FDA.
"The 7-OH was very strong," Tesluck said. "I stayed on that for just a few months because of how intense it was."
At first, Tesluck — an undergraduate student at the time, who was also conducting research and tutoring — noticed that kratom gave her a boost in energy, confidence and productivity. (Hilary Tesluck)
She returned to her recovery group for support. "I had to take a leave of absence, and I got clean from 7-OH again with their help," she said.
Having struggled with both leaf kratom and 7-OH, Tesluck views them as closely connected. "It’s one problem at two strengths," she said.
‘SUPER-DRUG’ 10 TIMES STRONGER THAN FENTANYL LINKED TO DEATHS ACROSS MULTIPLE STATES

Mac Haddow, senior fellow on public policy for the American Kratom Association, disputed this characterization of leaf kratom and concentrated 7-OH. In comments to Fox News Digital, he argued that the body’s conversion of mitragynine into 7-OH does not produce equivalent exposure to concentrated products.
Haddow also raised the possibility that the capsules Tesluck initially consumed may have contained ingredients beyond natural leaf kratom.
Varying regulations
Kratom rules vary widely across the country, with states taking different approaches to age restrictions, product standards and bans.
"It’s really been a patchwork," Tesluck said. "It’s different from state to state. Some states ban it, some states regulate it."
Today, Tesluck describes herself as a "person in long-term recovery from both kratom and 7-OH addiction." (Hilary Tesluck)
Florida, for example, prohibits selling or providing kratom products to anyone under 21.
Washington’s health department says unscheduled kratom products remain largely unregulated there, without age restrictions, labeling standards or ingredient-testing requirements.
Texas law requires kratom product labels to include directions and a recommended serving size.
"We support stronger enforcement across the board."
Haddow also emphasized the need for consumer warnings, adding, "The American Kratom Association supports accurate labeling to warn consumers that kratom can cause dependence."
"We support stronger enforcement across the board, and excise taxes on kratom products to fund that enforcement."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
In an October interview with Fox News Digital, Haddow also backed age restrictions. "Twenty-one and up should be the only people who have access to these products," he said.
Tesluck also raised concerns about how the products are marketed, describing social media ads as looking "very harmless" or "very cool," potentially drawing consumers’ interest.
"It’s something that you might want to try just based on the marketing itself and the packaging," she warned.
Tesluck said her work regularly brings her into contact with parents grieving children whose deaths they attribute to kratom products, including in states with Kratom Consumer Protection Acts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The FDA says no kratom drugs are approved by the agency, and that kratom cannot legally be marketed as a dietary supplement or added to conventional foods.
In December 2025, federal authorities seized approximately 73,000 concentrated 7-OH products valued at roughly $1 million from three Missouri firms, according to the FDA.
Warning signs
People taking kratom should pay attention to whether their use is beginning to dictate their daily routines, including planning around obtaining it or worrying about running out, Tesluck urged.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Like making sure when the smoke shop closes that you have enough time to get there," she said.

Diminished appetite, weight loss and hair loss were among the effects Tesluck experienced. Other signs of problematic kratom use may include cravings, higher consumption than intended, unsuccessful attempts to stop and continued use despite problems at work or home, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.
Kratom rules vary widely across the country, with states taking different approaches to age restrictions, product standards and bans. (Getty Images)

Feeling unable to miss a dose was another concern for Tesluck. "If I took less than what I was taking, I would feel even worse and sicker," she recalled. "So I was kind of stuck at that baseline with kratom."
Haddow acknowledged that consumers can develop dependence or addiction.
"I was kind of like a zombie shell of myself overall."
"Kratom can cause physical dependence, and some consumers have reported they develop addiction to kratom," he told Fox News Digital.
Feelings of sedation, numbness or irritability may also occur, Tesluck said.
"I was kind of like a zombie shell of myself overall," she said. "I wasn’t really the same person, personality-wise. I was irritable. I was mean."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Today, Tesluck describes herself as a "person in long-term recovery from both kratom and 7-OH addiction." She serves as executive director of End Kratom Addiction, a Virginia-based nonprofit that aims to raise awareness of kratom-related risks and advocates for stronger regulation.
"My advocacy looks a lot like meeting one-on-one with families … and coordinating resources for those who are still in addiction," she said.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Common blood pressure drug helps more stroke survivors reach critical health target
summary: The REDUCE trial found spironolactone lowered blood pressure by nearly eight points in stroke survivors, but key questions about prevention remain.
story: Dr. Jason A. Gluck, vice chair of the Heart & Vascular Institute and system chief of cardiology at AtlantiCare in New Jersey, discusses a recent study that found stroke incidence has more than doubled among young adults.
A low-cost medication could help stroke survivors whose blood pressure remains elevated despite treatment, a new study suggests.

The research, known as the REDUCE trial, looked at whether adding spironolactone, a medication commonly known as a water pill, could help lower blood pressure after a stroke. The findings were presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions, Nov. 6-9, 2026, in Chicago.
Participants were split into two groups. One added spironolactone to their regular treatment, while the other continued with usual post-stroke care.
SIMPLE EXERCISE DONE JUST ONCE A WEEK COULD HELP LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE
Researchers tracked the participants' blood pressure at home over the following six months to determine whether adding the medication made a difference.

After three months, the top blood pressure number was nearly eight points lower on average among people taking spironolactone compared with those receiving usual care – about 126 versus 133, the study said.
Researchers found that adding spironolactone to regular post-stroke care helped lower blood pressure more than usual treatment alone. (iStock)
More patients taking spironolactone also reached the recommended blood pressure goal of less than 130/80. That included 52% of those taking the medication compared with 30% receiving usual care.

"Lowering blood pressure is the most important step in preventing another stroke, yet many survivors struggle to reach recommended blood pressure targets after a stroke," study co-lead author Dr. Jordana Cohen, an associate professor of medicine and epidemiology at the University of Pennsylvania, said in a news release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"When spironolactone was added to post-stroke care, we saw a meaningful drop in blood pressure that may lower the risk of future strokes and heart attacks," she added.

Dr. Alfred Joshua, a California-based board-certified emergency physician and former chief medical officer who was not involved in the research, said the findings are encouraging, but do not yet show that the medication prevents a subsequent stroke.
Researchers found that 52% of patients taking spironolactone reached the recommended blood pressure goal, compared with 30% receiving usual post-stroke care. (iStock)

"We already know that controlling blood pressure lowers the risk of another stroke," Joshua told Fox News Digital. "This study measured blood pressure, so whether adding spironolactone leads to fewer repeat strokes is still an open question."

Spironolactone works by helping the body get rid of extra salt and water, which can lower blood pressure, according to the U.S. National Library of Medicine. It also causes the body to hold onto potassium, so patients taking it need to have their levels checked, the drug’s prescribing information states.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Joshua warned that high potassium is one of the main safety concerns because it can develop without symptoms. The risk can be higher for people with kidney problems and those taking certain medications or potassium supplements.
The medication can also lower blood pressure enough to cause dizziness, he added.
Spironolactone helps the body eliminate excess salt and water, which can lower blood pressure in patients who need additional treatment. (iStock)
"If your blood pressure is still high after a stroke, bring your home readings to your clinician and ask whether this medication is a good fit," Joshua advised.
Study limitations
The trial ended early with 160 participants instead of the planned 200, and about 15% did not have blood pressure readings available at the three-month mark, the researchers noted.
People taking spironolactone were also taking slightly more blood pressure medications overall than those receiving usual care.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The study was not designed to determine whether spironolactone actually prevents another stroke or heart attack. Larger and longer studies are needed to answer that question, according to the researchers.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.
