title: Florida Christians rebel against Imam's prayer opening a city meeting with a message of their own
summary: Christian protesters reciting the Lord's Prayer interrupted Imam Sajid Bhuiya's invocation at a Bartow, Florida meeting before police stepped in.
story: A group of Floridians showed up to a city commission meeting in the town of Bartow to protest an Imam’s invocation, praying the Lord’s Prayer in response to the Imam’s invitation. (Credit: Citizens Defending Freedom)

An imam who was scheduled to deliver the invocation at a city commission meeting Monday evening in a southwest Florida town was interrupted by Christian protesters — who had a prayer of their own to share.

Footage from inside the meeting obtained by Fox News Digital shows dozens of Christian activists crowded into the back of a Bartow, Florida city commission meeting room. As Imam Sajid Bhuiya of the town's Masjid Al-Nur Mosque stepped up to the lectern to give the invocation, they began reciting the Lord's Prayer in unison. Some chants of "USA!" broke out, as well.

According to Robert Goodman, the southeast regional director of the conservative activist group Citizens Defending Freedom, news of Bhuiya's scheduled appearance began making the rounds on social media last weekend. He was among those who shared the news on social media. Goodman said about 100 people from different groups ended up attending the meeting.
IOWA CITY COUNCIL MEETING ERUPTS AFTER FORMER MEMBER OPENS WITH SATANIC PRAYER AND 'HAIL SATAN'
Christian protesters pack a city commission meeting in Bartow, Florida, as a local imam attempts to deliver the invocation. (Citizens Defending Freedom)

"Citizens Defending Freedom believes Christian voices deserve to be heard on matters affecting our communities, families, and freedoms, which is why we joined many other concerned citizens and organizations Monday night," Goodman told Fox News Digital.
He said the Quran teaches forced submission and permits men to strike their wives, while viewing the opinions of women as lesser than the opinions of men.

"We have every right to challenge teachings we believe conflict with human dignity, equality, religious liberty and America's founding principles, because we must be intolerant of intolerance while respecting every person's right to believe differently," he said.
Video from the city's official livestream of the event quickly went viral online.
PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH'
Some protesters made off-color comments, including telling Bhuiya to go back to his own country, which Goodman clarified that neither he nor his organization support.

"The disrespectful remarks made by two or three individuals Monday night do not represent me or Citizens Defending Freedom, because as Christians, we are called to speak truth with conviction and respect, not insults," Goodman said.
Goodman said Bhuiya was invited to deliver the invocation by a city official. Members of the commission mostly sat quietly, observing the commotion while police handled the crowd.
Police eventually escorted the Christian protesters out of the building, though no arrests were made.
Imam Sajid Bhuiya of Masjid Al-Nur Mosque delivering the invocation at a Bartow, Florida city commission meeting after being interrupted by Christian protesters. (Robert Goodman)

Bhuiya then spoke, quoting passages from the Quran that he said are meant to unify people. "This is a reminder that our differences in background, culture and faiths should not prevent us from treating one another with dignity," he said.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Masjid Al-Nur Mosque for comment on the disruption of Bhuiya's invocation.
SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT
The city of Bartow released a statement explaining the Imam's appearance at the meeting.
The statement said that residents, "joined by individuals from other cities, attempted to prevent the imam from speaking and the Mayor from proceeding to conduct the business at hand."
A holy Christian cross laying on an open Bible with an American flag in the background. (iStock)

"For years, it has been tradition to open Bartow City Commission meetings with a prayer offered by either a faith-based leader or one of the City's elected officials," it said. "While historically the opening invocation/prayer is one based on Christian traditions, the opportunity is open to all faiths. This is consistent with the United States Constitution."

In the statement, city officials called for residents, "including religious leaders of all faiths, to come together to ensure that Bartow continues to be a welcoming place for all who live, work and play in Polk County's capital city."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Long term coup’ ousted Christians, conservatives from major watchdog, insider claims
summary: A former SPLC director told FBI agents Christians and conservatives were pushed out first in what he called a "long-term coup" at the Southern Poverty Law Center.
story: Former Southern Poverty Law Center executive Heidi Beirich faces federal charges of wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy. The Department of Justice alleges Beirich hid over $4 million in payments from SPLC donors to fund White supremacy.

A former Southern Poverty Law Center official who led its hate-group tracking work told FBI agents he tried to make the watchdog’s controversial "Hate Map" more ideologically balanced, while saying Christians and conservatives were the first staffers pushed out in what he called a "long-term coup" at the organization after he left in 2013.

The former director said he pushed for a more evenhanded SPLC, arguing that its "Hate Map" — which lists conservative groups alongside Ku Klux Klan chapters — should also include left-wing extremists, including violent animal-rights and extremist environmental groups. However, the former director said the effort met resistance and that, as liberal leaders reshaped the organization, most of his 17-person team was replaced.

"There was some kind of coup, long-term coup going on there between some, what I would — what I heard were some pretty liberal people, extreme people that had other ideas about what we were doing," the unnamed former director told agents, as first reported by The Daily Signal's Tyler O'Neil, who has been covering the SPLC's legal troubles.
DOJ EXPANDS INDICTMENT AGAINST SPLC, ALLEGING $4M SECRETLY FUNNELED TO KKK AND EXTREMIST GROUPS
SPLC Intelligence Project Director Heidi Beirich speaks during an event on Jan. 12, 2018. (David Buchan/Variety/Penske Media via Getty Images)

The former director’s comments appeared in an FBI interview transcript filed as an exhibit to Dr. Heidi Beirich’s Nov. 2 court filing. Beirich, a former SPLC official charged alongside the organization in a federal case alleging a scheme to mislead donors and banks about donations used to pay informants associated with violent extremist groups, pointed to multiple FBI interviews with an unnamed former SPLC director, identified in the filing as "Individual-1."

In a January interview, Individual-1 told investigators he ran the SPLC’s field-source program, set up accounts used to pay sources and directed payments, according to Beirich’s filing. During a March 23 follow-up interview with Individual-1, FBI Special Agents David McDaniel and Parker Still framed the conversation around the program having "gone off the rails" under Beirich and told the former director they were not there to discuss the bank activity, noting he had "obviously nothing to do with all that," before questioning him about the SPLC’s alleged targeting of conservative organizations and Beirich’s role, according to the transcript.
EXCLUSIVE: SPLC'S 'FAR-LEFT,' 'ANTI-RACISM' CURRICULUM FOUND IN CLASSROOMS AS EARLY AS KINDERGARTEN: 'WATCHDOG'

Individual-1 responded that, as his "gut impression," he believed her actions were political and accused some liberals at the center of having "a good degree of hatred" for conservatism, according to the March 23 transcript.

Individual-1 also alleged a shift in power at the SPLC. After he left in 2013, he said, people were appointed to the SPLC’s board as "figureheads" and eventually gained enough voting power to take over the center. He said only one or two data-entry members of his roughly 17-person team remained, with the others replaced by staff he believed shared the new leadership’s politics.

"That's who they ran off first were the Christians and conservatives," the unnamed former director told agents when asked why Beirich took the actions she did after his departure. "Then they — then the rest they just replaced with people they liked, you know, that agreed with them politically."
HOW MUTINY AT SOUTHERN POVERTY LAW CENTER TRIGGERED LEADERSHIP COLLAPSE
The Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) building seen in March 2020 in Montgomery, Alabama. (Barry Lewis/InPictures via Getty Images)

In separate comments about the SPLC's controversial "Hate Map," Individual-1 said he persuaded SPLC staff, despite internal resistance, to list Black separatist groups, which he considered comparable to White racist groups, on the map. However, he said he unsuccessfully pushed the SPLC to include violent animal-rights and environmental extremist groups and described his team’s approach during his tenure as director as "very nonpartisan" and "middle of the road."
"We were very nonpartisan, or at least when I was running things, when I was director, we stayed right in the middle of the road," he said.

In a June follow-up, the unnamed former director also criticized the SPLC's "Hate Map" for listing local chapters separately, saying it made the map's totals of the extremist groups it chose to identify look larger.
WATCH: SPLC CHIEF DOUBLES DOWN ON PLACING CHARLIE KIRK'S TURNING POINT USA ON 'HATE MAP'

While the unnamed former director was not charged in the SPLC case, Beirich was. Her lawyers say the interviews with the unnamed director warrant discovery into whether she was singled out because of her perceived role in the SPLC’s political speech, arguing that investigators’ questions about the SPLC’s treatment of conservative groups — and her alleged role in that work — could show the prosecution was motivated by hostility to the center’s political speech.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Individual-1’s statements confirm my longstanding criticism of the Southern Poverty Law Center, that it exaggerates ‘hate’ by inflating the chapters on its ‘hate map’ and that it systematically demonizes conservatives and Christians while turning a blind eye to extremism on the Left," O’Neil, the author of "Making Hate Pay: The Corruption of the Southern Poverty Law Center," told Fox News Digital. "Now, we have the former director of the Intelligence Project saying the SPLC appears to have pushed out Christians and conservatives, while rejecting his suggestion to include environmentalist agitators on the map."

title: Hometown of accused US military plane saboteur is a known magnet for anti-Israel activism
summary: Cork, Ireland, hometown of Daithí O’Corráin, who faces U.S. charges of destroying a $60 million C-130, once banned Benjamin Netanyahu from its city limits.
story: Two people were arrested by Irish police after agitators gathered at Trinity College Dublin while former President Joe Biden made a surprise visit on Tuesday (Credit: Credit: PA Media via Reuters).
The European hometown of the man who single-handedly destroyed a U.S. military transport aircraft in an act of apparent protest has a rich history of pro-Palestinian support.

This includes the town council for Cork, Ireland, barring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from entering its city limits, citing his "illegal occupation of Palestine and bordering countries" and the continuous pro-Palestinian protests taking place every Saturday since October 2023, organized by the Cork Palestine Solidarity Campaign (CPSC).

Cork’s opposition to Israel adds context to the possible motives for why Daithí O’Corráin, an Irish national, allegedly destroyed a U.S. military C-130 Hercules aircraft in April. The incident also draws attention to several anti-Israel groups that have sprung up in Ireland in recent years.
IRELAND’S ELITES HAVE FOUND THEIR NEW RELIGION: HATING ISRAEL

Pro-Palestinian activists from the Ireland Palestine Solidarity Campaign, supported by members of left-wing parties including People Before Profit and the Socialist Party and students, participate in the National March for Palestine from the Garden of Remembrance to O'Connell Street and Leinster House, on May 18, 2024, in Dublin, Ireland. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Ireland’s anti-Israel foothold became international news in April when O’Corráin, a Cork native, barricaded himself inside a C-130, a U.S. military transport plane. Once inside, he tore out critical wiring, destroyed gauges, contaminated fuel tanks and even poured corrosive chemicals into the aircraft, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.
Although his motives remain unclear, several groups from Cork interpreted his actions as a form of resistance against Israel and U.S. military interventionism.

In one such case, a Cork business owner named Tracey Ryan launched an initiative to raise €20,000 for O’Corráin's legal defense, praising his efforts to resist "the unwanted presence of U.S. military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide."

"We, Daithí's friends and comrades, are raising funds to support him through his court case. We would really appreciate your support & will keep you updated here on ways to support Daithí," Ryan wrote in the description of the fundraising page.

According to her personal Facebook profile, Ryan joined a bus of pro-Palestinian activists who went to support O’Corráin at his court appearance. "Bus going to the high court to support Daithí on Thursday!!" Ryan wrote.
O’Corráin has also received support from CPSC, the Cork pro-Palestinian group.

As news of the incident spread, CPSC co-chair Anne McShane posted on her Palestinian advocacy Facebook page in support of O’Corráin, encouraging viewers to send him letters of encouragement after his incarceration.
"Daithi needs our support in order to keep up his morale. Letters are a lifeline for prisoners," an April 17 post read.

CPSC spearheads anti-Israel demonstrations in Cork. In addition to hosting several pro-Palestinian fundraising initiatives, the group facilitates weekly Saturday demonstrations and invites speakers. At one point, CPSC’s website featured a fundraising site for O’Corráin, but the page has since been removed.
INSIDE THE PROTEST PLAYBOOK TO VILIFY ISRAEL ON 'GLOBAL DAY OF ACTION'

Left: Smashed cockpit instruments inside a U.S. military C-130H Hercules aircraft allegedly destroyed at Shannon Airport in Ireland on April 11, 2026. Right: A separate U.S. Air Force C-130 Hercules aircraft at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, on March 18, 2026. (U.S. Department of Justice; Leon Neal/Getty Images)
In CPSC’s own words, the group is part of a larger pro-Palestinian movement.

"It’s not just the city. Towns across all of County Cork stand in solidarity with Palestinians, including Ballincollig, Bandon, Cobh, Charleville, Clonakilty, Fermoy, Kinsale, Macroom, Mallow, Mitchelstown, Skibbereen and more," the group states on its website.
"Cork Palestine Solidarity Campaign is a branch of the Irish Palestine Solidarity Campaign (IPSC)," it added.

As part of its sister groups’ efforts "to foster links between Palestine and Irish institutions and organizations," CPSC and IPSC have both applauded Cork’s city council efforts to promote pro-Palestinian policies.
"Well done to the Cork City Council which passed a motion … calling for the Central Bank to end the sale of Israeli bonds," one Facebook post reads.
The groups have also held Cork up as a template for Ireland’s national policy.

"We call on the Irish government to follow the example of both Dublin and Cork city councils by officially recognizing Israeli Apartheid – and acting to end any and all links to this regime," another statement reads.

For its own part, the Cork City Council has earned the support of IPSC and CPSC through a range of its official resolutions, making the town’s formal position to condemn any of Ireland’s ties to Israel.

In addition to banning Netanyahu from entering the city's limits in a 41-8 vote in 2024, Cork’s council has flown the Palestinian flag over city hall on U.N. International Day of Solidarity and called on Ireland to ban trade from Israeli settlements.
Cork has even passed a "twinning" mechanism with the Palestinian city of Nablus — a largely symbolic partnership.
IRISH PM REJECTS ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS IN IRELAND AMID DRAMATIC VOTE OVER BOYCOTTING ISRAEL GAME

Conoe Kelliher from Ballyvourney holds a Palestinian flag whilst attending a watch-along party in the town square of Ireland's Eurovision entrant Bambie Thug's hometown of Macroom in Co Cork, as the Eurovision final takes place at Malmo Arena on Saturday, May 11, 2024. (Noel Sweeney/PA Images via Getty Images)

Fergal Dennehy, the lord mayor of Cork from 2025 to 2026, hosted the mayor of Nablus in February, calling the partnership "just the beginning of what we hope will be a wonderful relationship between our two great cities."
Neither CPSC nor Cork City Council responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment on the city's pro-Palestinian positions or about connections to O’Corráin.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
O’Corráin is incarcerated in Ireland and faces criminal charges in the U.S. for "destruction of government property," valued at $60 million.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: AOC leaves door open to 2028 presidential run, signals willingness to work with Trump
summary: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez would not rule out a 2028 White House run, saying her focus is getting results for people after Democrats reclaimed the House majority.
story: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., told Fox News Digital she hopes to work with President Donald Trump on a stock trading ban and healthcare, while leaving the door open to a potential presidential run.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., is leaving the door open to a potential 2028 presidential bid as speculation grows over her political future.
"I think, right now, this election just happened. We got to work on getting results for people," Ocasio-Cortez told Fox News Digital when asked whether she was considering a presidential run in 2028.

The self-described democratic socialist also expressed a willingness to work with President Donald Trump on key legislative priorities as Democrats prepare to take control of the House following the 2026 midterm elections.
PROGRESSIVE ORG LAUNCHES CAMPAIGN URGING AOC TO RUN FOR PRESIDENT WHILE PROGRESSIVES EYE SOCIALIST CANDIDATE

Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Laurel Lee, R-Fla., and Kat Cammack, R-Fla., hold a news conference with media personality Paris Hilton urging Congress to pass the DEFIANCE Act (Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits Act) outside the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 17, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

Ocasio-Cortez, who has drawn support from the Democratic Socialists of America's (DSA) New York City chapter for a potential White House bid, emphasized her desire to advance legislation in the 120th Congress rather than focus on presidential politics.
Asked whether Democrats should work with Trump instead of prioritizing impeachment proceedings and congressional investigations, Ocasio-Cortez expressed optimism about finding common ground.
"I hope so," she told Fox News Digital.
"You know, I hope that President Trump can sign a congressional stock trading ban into law," Ocasio-Cortez continued.

The congresswoman also identified healthcare reform as a potential area for bipartisan cooperation, urging Trump to address changes to Medicaid that she warned could threaten coverage for millions of Americans.
DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID
President Donald Trump speaks in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)

"I hope President Trump will be willing to work with us in really adjusting this Medicaid and confronting this Medicaid cliff that stands to kick off millions of working Americans off of their healthcare," she said.
"And so, you know, there are going to be areas where we're going to have real disagreement and real confrontation or worse," she continued.
Despite those disagreements, Ocasio-Cortez argued that lawmakers should prioritize legislation addressing Americans' immediate concerns.
"My hope is that we can prioritize the things that can actually change people's lives for the better as quickly as possible," she said.
Her remarks came hours after House Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., for speaker of the 120th Congress.

At least five of the 11 Democrats who opposed Jeffries’ nomination are incoming Congress members and self-described democratic socialists who argued that the party's leadership does not adequately represent their political priorities.
JEFFRIES SURVIVES DEM VOTE TO SECURE SPEAKER POSITION AS PROGRESSIVE RESISTANCE CLOUDS HIS CHANCES
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks during a press conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images)
Ocasio-Cortez, a DSA member, acknowledged that ideological disagreements between Jeffries and the party's socialist wing could continue throughout the next Congress.
"Of course, there are going to be areas where leader Jeffries and DSA are going to be in strong opposition," Ocasio-Cortez told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
However, she expressed confidence that Democrats could unite around shared priorities, including expanding access to publicly funded healthcare.

Her comments highlight the competing pressures facing House Democrats as they prepare to govern with a new majority while balancing progressive policy demands, internal ideological divisions and potential opportunities to work with the Trump administration.
Jeffries did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Hackers use Microsoft Outlook security flaw to steal your login data
summary: Microsoft Outlook flaw CVE-2026-124194 lets a malicious .msg file expose NTLMv2 authentication data, and Microsoft confirms hackers already exploited it.
story: Cybersecurity researchers warn a fake Microsoft update site uses a look-alike URL and a familiar download button to deliver data-stealing malware. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

You probably know better than to enter your password on a suspicious website. But what if hackers could steal information tied to your Windows login without ever asking for your password? That's the concern behind a Microsoft Outlook security flaw that hackers are already exploiting. Attackers can trick someone into opening a malicious Outlook file that quietly exposes Windows authentication information. That information could help a criminal impersonate you and potentially gain access to systems you use.

Microsoft released a fix on Nov. 10. However, the company confirms hackers were exploiting the vulnerability before the update became available. If you use Outlook for work, this is one security update you should check right away.

FAKE AI EVENT INVITES TARGET MICROSOFT AND GOOGLE LOGINS
Microsoft Outlook users could unknowingly expose Windows authentication information by opening a malicious message file, potentially allowing hackers to impersonate them. (Microsoft)
How hackers exploit the Microsoft Outlook security flaw

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, involves how Outlook handles specially crafted message files. An attacker can create a malicious Outlook message file, such as one using the .msg format. The hacker then needs to convince someone to open that file in an affected version of Outlook. Once opened, the malicious file can cause Outlook to connect to a server controlled by the attacker. That connection happens without the usual warning about accessing external content. During the connection, Windows can reveal NTLMv2 authentication information. This data helps Windows verify your identity when connecting to certain network services.

The information differs from your actual password. However, hackers may be able to use it in a follow-up attack to impersonate you. For someone using Outlook at work, that could potentially expose company resources their account can access. The outcome depends on the network's security protections and whether the attacker can successfully misuse the authentication information. Here's what makes this especially concerning. The attack doesn't require you to type your password into a fake login page. Opening the malicious file can be enough if your computer can connect to the attacker's network location. Microsoft says simply viewing the message through Outlook's Preview Pane does not trigger this particular vulnerability. Someone must open the malicious file for the attack to work.
Microsoft confirms hackers are already exploiting the flaw

Microsoft included the Outlook fix in its November Patch Tuesday security updates. The company's core release addressed 1,093 vulnerabilities, including 63 rated critical. Interestingly, Microsoft classified this particular Outlook vulnerability as moderate, giving it a CVSS severity score of 6.5 out of 10. However, that rating tells only part of the story. Microsoft confirms attackers have already exploited the flaw. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) also added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 10. In other words, hackers are already taking advantage of this security weakness. Microsoft has not publicly identified who carried out the attacks or disclosed how many people were affected. The company also hasn't provided detailed information about the incidents. With hackers already exploiting the flaw, it's important to install the security update as soon as possible.
FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
Microsoft released a security fix for the Outlook vulnerability, which users can install by selecting Update Now under Office's Update Options menu. (Microsoft)
Who is affected by the Outlook security vulnerability?
According to Microsoft's security advisory, the affected products include:

Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise: Affected versions of Outlook included with enterprise subscriptions.Microsoft Office LTSC 2021: Affected installations of Microsoft's long-term servicing edition.Microsoft Office LTSC 2024: Affected installations of the newer long-term servicing edition.
Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise: Affected versions of Outlook included with enterprise subscriptions.
Microsoft Office LTSC 2021: Affected installations of Microsoft's long-term servicing edition.
Microsoft Office LTSC 2024: Affected installations of the newer long-term servicing edition.

The vulnerability concerns affected desktop Office installations on Windows computers. Microsoft's advisory does not list Outlook.com in a web browser or the Outlook mobile apps as affected products. If your employer manages your Microsoft 365 software, your IT department may handle these updates. However, it's worth confirming that the security fix has been installed. For people who manage their own computers, here's how to check.
How to protect yourself from the Outlook security flaw
The most important thing you can do is update Microsoft Office. However, a few additional precautions can help reduce your exposure to suspicious files and account attacks.
Microsoft has released security updates addressing the vulnerability. You can manually check for updates in supported Windows versions of Office.

Open Microsoft Word or another installed Office application and create or open a document.Click File and select Account. In classic Outlook, the option may appear as Office Account.Under Product Information, select Update Options.Click Update Now and allow Microsoft to check for available updates.If prompted, save your work and allow Office to close any open applications, so the updates can finish installing.Wait for the "You're up to date!" or "Updates were installed" confirmation.
Open Microsoft Word or another installed Office application and create or open a document.
Click File and select Account. In classic Outlook, the option may appear as Office Account.
Under Product Information, select Update Options.
Click Update Now and allow Microsoft to check for available updates.
If prompted, save your work and allow Office to close any open applications, so the updates can finish installing.
Wait for the "You're up to date!" or "Updates were installed" confirmation.

If you don't see Update Now, you may need to select Enable Updates first. If the entire Update Options menu is missing, your employer may manage updates centrally. Contact your IT department rather than assuming the software has already been patched. You can also review Microsoft's official Office update instructions.
After installing the update, you can check which version of Office is running on your computer.

Open Microsoft Word or another installed Office application.Click File and select Account.Look under Product Information for the version and build information.Select About Word if you need to see the complete build number.
Open Microsoft Word or another installed Office application.
Click File and select Account.
Look under Product Information for the version and build information.
Select About Word if you need to see the complete build number.
For affected volume-licensed installations, Microsoft's November 10 security release includes these updated builds:
Office LTSC 2021: Build 14334.21048Office LTSC 2024: Build 17932.21140
Office LTSC 2021: Build 14334.21048
Office LTSC 2024: Build 17932.21140

These build numbers apply to the specified LTSC editions. They shouldn't be used to check other Office versions. If you're using Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, the correct build depends on your organization's update channel. You can check Microsoft's Office security release notes or contact your IT department to confirm the fix.
Although this vulnerability requires an Office fix, keeping Windows updated remains important.
On Windows 11:
Open Settings.Click Windows Update.Select Check for updates.Install available security updates.Restart your computer if prompted.
Open Settings.
Click Windows Update.
Select Check for updates.
Install available security updates.
Restart your computer if prompted.
Next, check whether Windows can receive updates for other Microsoft products.
From Windows Update, click Advanced options.Find Receive updates for other Microsoft products.Turn the setting On if available.
From Windows Update, click Advanced options.
Find Receive updates for other Microsoft products.
Turn the setting On if available.

This can help Windows deliver updates for supported Microsoft products. However, some Office installations receive updates through separate services or employer-managed systems. Remember that checking Windows Update alone may not confirm you've installed the specific Outlook fix. Check Office separately. It's also smart to back up important files before installing major operating system updates.
Outlook's built-in Report Phishing feature lets users flag suspicious emails without opening potentially dangerous attachments. (Microsoft)

A message file from an unfamiliar sender deserves extra caution, especially if you weren't expecting it. Watch for attachments ending in .msg, a common file format for saved Outlook messages. The format itself is legitimate. However, attackers can abuse it to deliver this exploit. If an email claims you need to open an attached message to review an invoice or urgent workplace request, verify it through another trusted channel. Even attachments appearing to come from coworkers deserve a second look when the request seems unusual.
If something looks suspicious, avoid opening the attachment. Instead, report the message using Outlook's built-in reporting tools when available.
In supported versions of Outlook:

Select the suspicious email in your inbox without opening its attachment.Look for Report or Report phishing in the toolbar.Choose Report phishing if that option appears.Follow the prompts to submit the report.
Select the suspicious email in your inbox without opening its attachment.
Look for Report or Report phishing in the toolbar.
Choose Report phishing if that option appears.
Follow the prompts to submit the report.

The exact menu location depends on your Outlook version and your employer's settings. If you're using a work account and don't see a reporting option, contact your IT department. Avoid forwarding the suspicious attachment to other coworkers.

Strong antivirus software can help identify suspicious attachments and malicious activity before they cause further damage. Look for protection that includes real-time scanning and behavior-based detection. These features may help catch threats that traditional virus signatures miss. However, antivirus software cannot replace Microsoft's security patch. Installing the Outlook update remains essential for closing this particular vulnerability. Multifactor authentication (MFA) adds another layer of account protection by requiring additional verification when you sign in. Enable it on your Microsoft account and other important services whenever available. Keep in mind that MFA may not stop attacks involving stolen Windows authentication information. That's another reason updating Outlook takes priority.
Know what to do if you opened a suspicious file
If you recently opened an unexpected Outlook message attachment, don't assume everything is fine because nothing unusual appeared on your screen. Here's what to do next.

Close the suspicious file: Stop interacting with the attachment. Don't reopen it or forward it to anyone else.Notify your IT department if it's a work computer: Report what happened right away. Your security team can investigate suspicious authentication activity and determine whether additional action is needed.Update Microsoft Office: Install the latest security updates to protect against further attempts to exploit the Outlook vulnerability.Run a security scan: Use your antivirus software to check for other suspicious activity or malware. Keep in mind that a clean scan cannot rule out stolen authentication information.Check your account activity: Review your Microsoft account for unfamiliar sign-ins or unexpected security changes. However, normal sign-in activity doesn't guarantee your authentication information wasn't exposed.Secure your personal accounts: If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device. Make sure multifactor authentication is enabled wherever available.
Close the suspicious file: Stop interacting with the attachment. Don't reopen it or forward it to anyone else.

Notify your IT department if it's a work computer: Report what happened right away. Your security team can investigate suspicious authentication activity and determine whether additional action is needed.
Update Microsoft Office: Install the latest security updates to protect against further attempts to exploit the Outlook vulnerability.
Run a security scan: Use your antivirus software to check for other suspicious activity or malware. Keep in mind that a clean scan cannot rule out stolen authentication information.

Check your account activity: Review your Microsoft account for unfamiliar sign-ins or unexpected security changes. However, normal sign-in activity doesn't guarantee your authentication information wasn't exposed.
Secure your personal accounts: If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device. Make sure multifactor authentication is enabled wherever available.

One important reminder: Changing your password alone may not address every potential exposure from this vulnerability. If you opened the attachment on a work computer, let your IT team determine whether additional security measures are necessary.
Why Microsoft's latest security update deserves attention

Microsoft's November security release covers far more than Outlook. It also fixes weaknesses that could allow attackers to gain additional privileges or remotely execute malicious code. For those of you using a Windows PC every day, the sheer number of vulnerabilities may sound overwhelming. However, not every flaw carries the same immediate risk. In this case, the Outlook weakness deserves your attention because Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation.

The larger concern is how easily a malicious file can take advantage of trusted software. Outlook is part of everyday communication for countless businesses, and opening saved email messages may seem harmless. This vulnerability shows why keeping Office updated deserves the same attention as updating Windows.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me about this Outlook flaw is how little someone has to do to put their information at risk. You could receive what looks like a routine work attachment, open it and unknowingly expose information that helps a hacker impersonate you. There's no obvious warning telling you something went wrong. And by the time you realize it, the damage may already be done. I also find it troubling that Microsoft rated this vulnerability moderate even though attackers were already exploiting it. Most people aren't going to spend their day reviewing security ratings, and they shouldn't have to. They need software that protects them and updates that are easy to install. My advice is simple. If you use Outlook on a Windows computer, check for Office updates today. Don't assume your computer has already taken care of it.

title: Former Secret Service investigator sounds alarm over AI scams as Americans grow increasingly anxious
summary: Former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warns AI voice cloning scams could trick families into losing thousands of dollars this holiday season.
story: Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator, warns that AI-powered voice cloning and impersonation scams are making it increasingly difficult for Americans to distinguish real communications from fake ones.

A former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator warned that Americans are increasingly on edge following a wave of major technology disruptions, while artificial intelligence is making scams targeting families and consumers more sophisticated.

Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator and iCounter's director of customer advisory and counter fraud lead, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that Americans have reason to be increasingly cautious about technology.
"Everybody's on edge," Brown said.

"There's been a lot of stuff that has happened in the past week in particular that people are concerned about," he continued, citing recent technology outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and several financial institutions.
TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS
The more details a scam includes, the more likely it is built from your publicly available data. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Brown acknowledged that some incidents involved infrastructure problems while others remained under investigation.

With the holiday season approaching, Brown warned that AI has made it easier for criminals to create convincing fraudulent messages, eliminating many of the warning signs consumers previously relied on.
"AI has just made the criminal a lot more efficient and a little bit more effective," Brown said.

Spelling mistakes, poor grammar and awkward phrasing — once common indicators of fraudulent messages — are becoming less reliable as criminals use AI to generate more convincing communications, he explained.
AI VOICE SCAM TRAPS MOM IN 5-HOUR KIDNAPPING NIGHTMARE

Former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warned that artificial intelligence is making scams more sophisticated and increasingly difficult for Americans to recognize. (Fox News Digital)
AI also allows criminals to impersonate familiar voices, potentially tricking victims into believing they are speaking with a family member in distress.
Brown described a scenario in which a scammer uses a short voice recording to impersonate someone's relative and demand thousands of dollars in gift cards.
"AI just makes them a lot more efficient and a lot less prone to errors," he said, warning that Americans must become more skeptical of suspicious messages.
"Unfortunately, we're at a point where everybody needs to have that level of distrust," he said.
As holiday shopping ramps up, Brown said scammers are likely to impersonate major delivery companies, including UPS, FedEx and the U.S. Postal Service.
FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

Scammers may impersonate major delivery companies during the holiday shopping season, sending fraudulent messages claiming packages cannot be delivered without additional payment. (Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)
He warned that fraudulent messages may claim packages cannot be delivered until additional postage is paid, with scammers demanding payment through cryptocurrency or gift cards.
"If it comes from crypto, especially if it comes from gift cards, that's a red flag for sure," Brown said.

Beyond the emotional toll, Brown warned that increasingly sophisticated scams can result in significant financial losses. He cited FBI reporting that he said identified more than 22,000 AI-related fraud cases in 2025, with losses exceeding $890 million.
Brown noted that businesses are also vulnerable to schemes in which criminals impersonate trusted vendors and redirect legitimate payments into fraudulent accounts.
AGING MEANS LEARNING HOW TO PREVENT COSTLY SCAMS TARGETING OLDER AMERICANS

Former Secret Service investigator Jason Brown warned holiday shoppers to be cautious of suspicious delivery notifications appearing to come from UPS, FedEx or the U.S. Postal Service. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The holiday season can create additional vulnerabilities as executives travel, employees take time off and temporary workers join company operations, he said.

Brown urged Americans to independently verify suspicious messages and take additional precautions when communicating with family members, including establishing a "safe word" to help confirm someone's identity during an unexpected call.

"Another thing that we always talk about with family members, set up a safe word ahead of time. Have that conversation now," he said, adding that even if a caller provides the correct word, people should still end the call and contact the person independently using a trusted number.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The biggest safety valve for anybody in a scam when it comes over the internet via your cell phone, over the computer is stop, think and then independently verify," he added.

title: Data broker opt-out steps retirees need before the holidays
summary: A single data broker opt-out may not be enough. Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can still expose your address and family details to scammers.
story: Artificial intelligence is rapidly accelerating elder fraud schemes across the U.S., targeting older Americans who hold a significant share of household wealth. ScamSkeptic founder Matt Sanner joins 'America's Newsroom' to highlight how fraudsters utilize AI to mimic voices and create deepfakes. Sanner provides key strategies for families to identify these scams and protect their vulnerable loved ones.

Many retirees think they're protecting their privacy by staying off social media, removing their information from one people-search site or paying for credit monitoring. But a single data broker opt-out request may leave your home address, phone number and family details exposed elsewhere. With the holidays approaching, now is a good time to find out what's available about you online and take steps to remove it.

People-search sites like Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can make personal details available to strangers. Some information is free to view, while more detailed reports may require payment. And here's where it gets concerning. A scammer who knows your grandson's name or where your daughter lives could use those details to make a fake emergency call sound convincing. Here's where that information comes from, how to remove it and what you can do to help protect your family before the holidays.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Submitting opt-out requests and checking for new listings regularly can help reduce your personal information online. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Where your personal information comes from

You don't need a social media account to have your information collected. Data brokers gather information from public records, including property deeds, voter registration records where accessible and court filings. They may also obtain details from commercial databases, online activity and companies that collect personal information. Over time, those details can become part of a profile showing where you live, previous addresses, phone numbers and possible family connections.

According to the Federal Trade Commission, opting out of one people-search site doesn't remove your information from others. Your details may also reappear when public records change or websites collect updated information. For older adults, the financial risks can be especially serious. An FTC report released in October 2026 found that adults ages 60 and older reported approximately $3 billion in fraud losses during 2025. Although older adults reported losing money to fraud less frequently than younger adults overall, their reported individual losses tended to be higher.

You can use a free exposure scanner at CyberGuy.com to check whether your personal information appears on publicly searchable websites. Keep in mind that a free scan cannot uncover every private data broker database. The results might surprise you.
The data broker opt-out steps to take now
You can start removing your personal information yourself without paying for a service.

Search for your information. Look up your name on major people-search sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified, Intelius and TruthFinder. Try searching your phone number and home address, too.Find each site's opt-out page. Look for links labeled "Opt Out," "Remove My Information" or "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information." You can usually find these in the website's footer or privacy policy.Submit removal requests. Follow each site's instructions. Some may require email confirmation or other verification. Share only the personal information necessary to complete the request, and make sure you're using the legitimate website.Keep a record of your requests. Save the website addresses and dates when you submitted them. This makes it easier to follow up if your information remains visible.Check again regularly. Return after about a month to see whether your information has been removed. Then check every few months because new listings may appear.Freeze your credit. Contact Experian, Equifax and TransUnion to request a free credit freeze. This can help prevent identity thieves from opening new credit accounts in your name.
Search for your information. Look up your name on major people-search sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified, Intelius and TruthFinder. Try searching your phone number and home address, too.

Find each site's opt-out page. Look for links labeled "Opt Out," "Remove My Information" or "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information." You can usually find these in the website's footer or privacy policy.

Submit removal requests. Follow each site's instructions. Some may require email confirmation or other verification. Share only the personal information necessary to complete the request, and make sure you're using the legitimate website.
Keep a record of your requests. Save the website addresses and dates when you submitted them. This makes it easier to follow up if your information remains visible.
Check again regularly. Return after about a month to see whether your information has been removed. Then check every few months because new listings may appear.
Freeze your credit. Contact Experian, Equifax and TransUnion to request a free credit freeze. This can help prevent identity thieves from opening new credit accounts in your name.

A credit freeze won't remove your information from data brokers, and credit monitoring generally alerts you to possible problems rather than preventing your details from appearing online. These tools serve different purposes.

One thing to remember: Removing your information from people-search sites doesn't erase public records. Your details may still appear in property records, court documents or even listings connected to family members. That's why it's important to check more than your own name. Doing this yourself can take hours, especially when you're dealing with multiple websites. And because data brokers continue collecting information, the work may need to be repeated.
DATA BROKER OPT-OUT: HOW RETIREES CAN PROTECT THEIR DATA
Searching for your personal information online is the first step toward identifying data broker listings you may want removed. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Free tools that can help remove your information
Before paying for a data removal service, there are two other options worth knowing about.

Google offers a free tool called Results about you that can help you find personal information appearing in Google Search. Depending on eligibility, you may be able to request the removal of results containing your home address, phone number or email address.
Here's how to get started:

Open the Google app and tap your profile picture, then select Results about you. You can also access the tool through Google's website.Select Get started or Settings.Enter your name and the personal contact information you want Google to check.Review any matching results and request removal of eligible listings.Check the tool for updates on your requests.
Open the Google app and tap your profile picture, then select Results about you. You can also access the tool through Google's website.
Select Get started or Settings.
Enter your name and the personal contact information you want Google to check.
Review any matching results and request removal of eligible listings.
Check the tool for updates on your requests.
Keep in mind that removing a Google search result doesn't delete the information from the original website. You may still need to contact the site directly.

If you live in California, you have another option. The state's free Delete Request and Opt-out Platform, called DROP, launched in January 2026. It allows eligible California residents to submit a single deletion request covering more than 600 registered data brokers.

Beginning Aug. 1, 2026, covered data brokers were required to start processing requests through the system. Removal can take time, and some information may be exempt under the law. You can submit a request and check its status at California's official DROP website at privacy.ca.gov/drop/. Other states also have privacy laws that may give residents additional rights to request deletion of their information.
WHY REMOVING YOUR DATA ONLINE MAY STILL LEAVE YOUR FAMILY EXPOSED
Retirees can unknowingly have their home addresses, phone numbers and family details listed on people-search websites. (iStock)
How a personal data removal service can help
If you don't want to spend hours contacting websites and tracking removal requests, a personal data removal service can help.
These services contact data brokers on your behalf and submit requests to remove your personal information. Depending on the provider and plan, features may include:

Automated removal requests sent to participating data brokers and people-search websites.Recurring removal requests to help address personal information that reappears online.Progress tracking so you can monitor the status of removal requests.Family protection options that allow you to include additional family members.Custom removal requests for websites that may not be covered by standard automated services.
Automated removal requests sent to participating data brokers and people-search websites.
Recurring removal requests to help address personal information that reappears online.
Progress tracking so you can monitor the status of removal requests.
Family protection options that allow you to include additional family members.
Custom removal requests for websites that may not be covered by standard automated services.

Some services offer ongoing monitoring and follow-up requests, which can save time compared with handling each website yourself. It's important to understand that no service can guarantee every piece of personal information will disappear from the internet. Public records may remain accessible, and some websites may fall outside the service's coverage. Still, reducing the number of places where your information appears can make your personal details harder to find.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Bring this conversation to the Thanksgiving table

Thanksgiving brings families together, making it a great opportunity to talk about protecting everyone's personal information. You don't need to make it a lengthy discussion. A few simple checks can help everyone understand what scammers may already know about them.

After dinner, sit down with a family member and search your names on a few people-search sites. Look for home addresses, phone numbers and family connections. If you find something you don't want publicly available, discuss how to request its removal. Check your parents' information, too, with their permission. Even if you've removed your own details, your name or address may still appear in a relative's profile.

Choose a private phrase that family members can use if someone calls claiming there's an emergency. Avoid birthdays, pet names or other details someone could easily discover online. Agree on the phrase privately rather than sharing it in a group chat. A code word adds another layer of protection, but it shouldn't be your only way to verify someone's identity.

If someone claims to be a grandchild or another relative who urgently needs money, don't send anything until you've checked the story. Hang up and call your loved one directly using a phone number you already know. If you can't reach them, contact another trusted family member. Scammers can now use AI voice cloning to sound like someone you love. That means even a familiar voice may not be enough to prove who's calling. Learn more about how AI voice scams can clone your family's voice and what you can do to protect yourself. And be especially suspicious if someone demands payment through gift cards, cryptocurrency or wire transfers.

Agree that nobody will send emergency money based solely on an unexpected phone call or text. If something sounds suspicious, contact another family member before taking action. Scammers often pressure people to respond immediately or keep the situation secret. The more your family talks about these tactics ahead of time, the easier it becomes to recognize a suspicious request. Scammers may already know more about your family than you realize. A private code word adds protection, but always confirm an unexpected emergency by contacting your loved one directly before sending money.
Kurt's key takeaways

Here's what concerns me. You can be careful about what you share online and still have your home address, phone number and family details available on people-search sites. Removing that information once is a good start, but it can show up again. That's why I recommend checking these sites regularly or using a trusted data removal service to help handle the work. And with Thanksgiving bringing families together, this is a great time to talk about scams and make sure everyone knows what to do if a suspicious call comes in. A few simple steps now could help keep your family's personal information out of the wrong hands.

title: Apple Photos AI watermark can tag your real pictures
summary: Apple Photos now embeds an invisible SynthID watermark in images edited with Apple Intelligence tools like Clean Up, Extend and Reframe in iOS 27.2.
story: Apple's Clean Up, Extend and Reframe tools let you change photos using AI, with certain edits now receiving an invisible SynthID watermark. (Apple)

You take a great family photo, but there's one problem. Someone you don't know walked into the background. So you open Apple Photos, use Clean Up to remove the person and save your picture. Problem solved, right? Well, there's something new happening behind the scenes.

With iOS 27.2, Apple Photos can now add an invisible AI watermark to pictures you edit using certain Apple Intelligence tools. You won't see it on your screen. And if you share the photo, the person receiving it probably won't notice anything different either. But the watermark could still be there.

Apple introduced the feature in its Oct. 26 update. It uses Google's SynthID technology to identify images created or modified with artificial intelligence. Even a photo you took yourself can receive this hidden marker after certain AI edits. So how does it work, and what does it mean for the photos you share?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
STOP LOSING PHOTO QUALITY WHEN YOU SHARE PICTURES
Why Apple Photos is adding invisible AI watermarks

AI photo editing has come a long way. What once required complicated software can now take a few taps on your phone. That's convenient when you want to improve a picture. However, it also makes it harder to tell what's real. Someone can remove an important detail from a photo without leaving an obvious trace. AI can even generate parts of a scene that the camera never captured.

Apple's new watermarking feature gives people a way to tell when AI has been used to create or change an image. According to Apple's official support documentation, certain Apple Intelligence tools now add a hidden SynthID watermark when you create or edit images.

SynthID is technology developed by Google. It embeds a digital signal into an image that compatible detection tools can recognize. The watermark doesn't visibly change your photo. There's no stamp across the bottom or warning in the corner. Instead, the marker remains hidden unless someone checks the image with a SynthID detector.
Which Apple Photos tools add an AI watermark?
Apple says the feature applies to certain Apple Intelligence tools starting with iOS 27.2. Here's where you might encounter it.

Clean Up lets you erase distractions from your pictures. Maybe someone wandered into your vacation photo. Or perhaps there's an object in the background you wish you could remove. You can use Clean Up to erase that distraction while AI fills in the missing area. With iOS 27.2, some photos edited this way can receive a SynthID watermark. However, Apple doesn't say that every small edit will trigger one. The watermark can depend on the changes made to the image.

Have you ever taken a picture and realized you were standing too close? Apple's Extend tool can help by generating additional scenery beyond the original edges of your photo. For example, you might have cropped out part of a building. Extend can generate additional background to make the composition look better. The result may look like you captured a wider shot in the first place. However, because AI creates part of the finished image, the photo can receive a hidden SynthID watermark. We've previously explained how Extend works in our article on fixing badly framed photos after you take them.

Apple also includes Spatial Reframing, called Reframe in Photos, among the tools covered by SynthID. Reframe lets you change the apparent perspective of a picture after you've taken it. You can adjust the angle or shift the composition while Apple Intelligence generates the necessary visual information. That can make a photo look quite different from what your camera originally captured. And because AI helps create that result, the edited image may carry a watermark.

Apple's watermarking feature also covers images generated using Image Playground and Image Wand. Image Playground lets you create images with AI using descriptions or other visual inputs. Image Wand can turn a rough sketch into a more developed image. Since these tools generate visual content, their inclusion makes sense. But Apple's decision to mark certain edits to genuine photos raises a more interesting question. Should a real photo receive an AI marker because you removed one distracting object?
NEW YORK MAKES HISTORY WITH FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND LAW REGULATING AI-POWERED COMMERCIALS
Apple Photos uses Google’s SynthID technology to mark certain AI-edited images, but detecting a watermark does not necessarily mean a picture is fake. (iStock)
How to check whether a photo has Apple's AI watermark

You might be wondering whether there's an easy way to see if a photo contains one of these hidden markers. There is, although you'll need to use an online detector. Apple recommends Google's SynthID Detector, which can analyze an uploaded image for the watermark.

Open a web browser on your iPhone, iPad, Mac or computer.Visit synthid.com.Upload the picture you want to check.Follow the on-screen instructions.Review the result to see whether the detector identifies a SynthID watermark.
Open a web browser on your iPhone, iPad, Mac or computer.
Visit synthid.com.
Upload the picture you want to check.
Follow the on-screen instructions.
Review the result to see whether the detector identifies a SynthID watermark.

One thing to understand: finding a watermark doesn't automatically mean a photo is fake. It simply indicates that AI was involved in creating or modifying the image. And the reverse is also true. If no watermark appears, that doesn't prove the picture is genuine. Other AI image generators may not use SynthID. Detection can also have limitations. I would also be careful about uploading private family pictures or sensitive images to any online service. Review how the service handles uploaded files before submitting them.
Will Apple add watermarks to your older photos?

Apple says photos created or edited before the 27.2 update won't automatically receive a new SynthID watermark from Apple. So you don't have to worry about the update going through your entire photo library and adding markers to everything.

However, that changes if you open an older picture and edit it using one of the supported AI tools. For example, you could take a photo from five years ago and use Extend to improve the framing today. The newly edited version may then receive the invisible watermark.

Apple has also expanded this feature beyond iPhones. According to the company, SynthID support begins with these software versions: iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 and visionOS 27.2. Keep in mind that the software update and Apple Intelligence have different device requirements.
OPENAI CHILD SAFETY TOOLS TARGET AI-GENERATED ABUSE

Apple’s Photos app can add invisible AI watermarks to real pictures edited with certain Apple Intelligence tools, including Clean Up, Extend and Reframe. (Photo by Katharina Kausche/Picture Alliance via Getty Images)
Which iPhones support Apple's AI photo tools?

You'll need an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone to use the editing features that trigger these watermarks. Apple Intelligence works on the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max, along with iPhone 16 models and newer compatible iPhones. The standard iPhone 15 can install iOS 27.2, but it doesn't support these Apple Intelligence editing features. Availability may also depend on your region and language.
To check for the latest software update:
Open Settings on your iPhone.Tap General.Select Software Update.Install an available update if your device supports it.
Open Settings on your iPhone.
Tap General.
Select Software Update.
Install an available update if your device supports it.
Can invisible watermarks help you spot fake photos?

I like the idea of giving people another way to question what they're seeing online. But there's an important limitation. Let's say you use Clean Up to remove someone standing behind your family in a vacation photo. Now compare that with an AI-generated picture showing an event that never happened. Both images could carry SynthID watermarks, even though the circumstances are very different.

The detector may identify AI involvement. However, it won't necessarily explain what was changed or how significant those changes were. That's a pretty big limitation when you're trying to decide whether to trust an image.

There's also the issue of AI-generated pictures that have no detectable watermark. So, while SynthID can provide a useful clue, it shouldn't be your only way of evaluating a suspicious photo. If a picture online seems questionable, look for the original source. You can also use a reverse image search to see where a photo originally appeared and whether earlier versions exist.
Kurt's key takeaways

I can see why Apple is doing this. AI has gotten so good at changing photos that it's becoming harder to know what you're actually looking at. And I think that's a real concern. At the same time, I like having tools that can fix a great picture when someone walks into the background. Why should that photo get the same kind of watermark as a picture created entirely by AI? That's where I think Apple could do better. I'd love to see a way to check a photo and find out exactly what AI changed. Was it something minor, or did someone completely alter what happened? That's what I'd want to know before deciding whether to trust what I'm seeing.

Should Apple put a hidden AI watermark on your personal photos simply because you removed something from the background? Or should these markers be reserved for images that AI creates entirely? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fake vacation rental sites use live chat to steal your data
summary: Fortra researchers say fake vacation rental sites use live customer support chats to trick travelers into handing over credit card details this holiday.
story: Travel expert and advisor Bobby Laurie explains when Europe's ETIAS travel authorization system is expected to launch, how the application process will work and what travelers should know about potential scams taking place right now.

You're booking a vacation rental for the holidays when a message appears saying there's a problem with your reservation. Before you can figure out what's wrong, a customer support chat opens and offers to help. You're told your credit card won't be charged, but you'll need to enter the number to complete a security check. Sounds helpful, right? That's exactly what scammers want you to think.

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered fake vacation rental sites that look remarkably similar to legitimate booking platforms. Some even include live customer support chats designed to convince travelers to hand over their credit card information. With Thanksgiving travel approaching, it's worth knowing how these scams work before you book your next trip.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
