title: Freeze, fraud alert or monitoring? What to do after a breach
summary: A credit freeze, fraud alert and identity monitoring each protect different parts of your financial life after a data breach. Here's how to choose.
story: A credit freeze, fraud alert and identity monitoring service offer different protections against identity theft. Knowing how each works can help you respond to a data breach. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

A data breach notice can leave you with plenty of questions. Should you freeze your credit? Is a fraud alert enough? Do you need an identity monitoring service? The right response depends on what information was exposed and whether someone has already tried to use it. Here's the important distinction. A company saying your information was involved in a breach does not automatically mean someone has opened an account in your name.

An unfamiliar credit inquiry deserves attention, but it does not always prove fraud occurred. However, once you confirm someone has used your information fraudulently, the situation becomes more urgent. So, which protection should you choose? Let's look at what each one actually does.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
YOU HAVE A CREDIT FREEZE; IT STILL ISN’T ENOUGH
What a credit freeze does

A credit freeze restricts access to your credit file. It makes it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name because most lenders need to review your credit information before approving an application. Credit freezes are completely free. You must place one separately with each of the three major credit bureaus:
EquifaxExperianTransUnion
Equifax
Experian
TransUnion

A freeze stays in place until you remove it, and it does not affect your credit score. If you apply for a mortgage, car loan or credit card, you may need to temporarily lift the freeze so the lender can review your report. You can do that for free.

Employment and tenant-screening checks follow different rules and generally are not blocked by a credit freeze. A freeze is a strong option if your Social Security number was exposed or you simply want to reduce the risk of someone opening new credit in your name. However, it cannot protect an existing bank account, stop a scam payment or remove a fraudulent account that was already opened.
What a fraud alert does

A fraud alert tells lenders to take additional steps to verify your identity before approving new credit. Unlike a freeze, a fraud alert does not restrict access to your credit report. Instead, it warns lenders that someone may be trying to use your information.
There are two main types:

Initial fraud alert: Free, lasts one year and can be renewed. You only need to contact one major credit bureau, which must notify the other two.Extended fraud alert: Free, lasts seven years and is available to identity theft victims who provide an FTC identity theft report or police report.
Initial fraud alert: Free, lasts one year and can be renewed. You only need to contact one major credit bureau, which must notify the other two.
Extended fraud alert: Free, lasts seven years and is available to identity theft victims who provide an FTC identity theft report or police report.

A fraud alert can be convenient if you're actively applying for a mortgage, loan or credit card and don't want to manage multiple credit freezes. Still, it offers less control than a freeze because lenders can continue accessing your credit file after completing the required identity checks. If someone has already opened an account fraudulently, placing an alert can help reduce additional risk. However, you'll still need to contact the creditor and dispute the fraudulent account.
What identity monitoring does
Identity monitoring watches for certain changes involving your personal or financial information and notifies you when suspicious activity appears.
Depending on the service, those alerts may include:

New credit accounts or hard inquiriesCollections activity or changes to credit reportsSuspicious financial account activityPersonal information found in known data breachesCertain phone account changes or identity-related activity
New credit accounts or hard inquiries
Collections activity or changes to credit reports
Suspicious financial account activity
Personal information found in known data breaches
Certain phone account changes or identity-related activity

Monitoring is useful because it can give you an earlier warning that someone may be misusing your information. But there's an important limitation. Monitoring generally alerts you after suspicious activity is detected. It does not necessarily prevent that activity from happening. And no service can monitor everything. For example, basic credit monitoring may not detect an email account takeover, medical identity theft or a payment you authorized after being tricked by a scammer.
Which tool fits your situation?
The right protection depends on what happened to your information and whether someone has already tried to use it. Here's what to do in each situation.

Start by reviewing the breach notice to understand exactly what information was involved. If passwords were exposed, change them immediately. Use unique passwords for each account and enable multifactor authentication, especially on your primary email account. If your Social Security number was compromised, consider freezing your credit with all three major bureaus right away. You can also take advantage of free credit monitoring offered by the affected company, if available. Just verify the offer through the company's official website.

An unfamiliar credit inquiry deserves a closer look, but it doesn't always mean someone has stolen your identity. Contact the company listed on the inquiry using its official website or customer service number. Ask whether an application was submitted using your information. You should also review your credit reports from all three bureaus. You can get free weekly credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. If you suspect someone is trying to open credit in your name, consider placing a free credit freeze immediately while you investigate. You can also add a fraud alert.
If you confirm that someone opened an account fraudulently, act immediately.

Contact the creditor's fraud department. Explain that the account was opened without your permission and ask for written confirmation of your fraud report.Dispute the fraudulent account with the credit bureaus. Check all three reports because the account may not appear on each one.Report the identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov to file a report with the Federal Trade Commission and create a personalized recovery plan.Consider placing a credit freeze and fraud alert. An extended seven-year fraud alert may be available once you have the required identity theft documentation.
Contact the creditor's fraud department. Explain that the account was opened without your permission and ask for written confirmation of your fraud report.
Dispute the fraudulent account with the credit bureaus. Check all three reports because the account may not appear on each one.
Report the identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov to file a report with the Federal Trade Commission and create a personalized recovery plan.
Consider placing a credit freeze and fraud alert. An extended seven-year fraud alert may be available once you have the required identity theft documentation.
Keep copies of your reports, correspondence and case numbers while the investigation continues.

A credit freeze alone won't help if someone already has access to one of your existing accounts. Contact the financial institution or service provider immediately. If your bank account is involved, report unauthorized transactions and ask what protections can be placed on the account. If your email was compromised, change the password from a trusted device, review recovery information and sign out of unfamiliar sessions. And if your phone suddenly loses service for no obvious reason, contact your wireless carrier immediately. An unexpected loss of service can be a warning sign of a SIM-swap attack.
WAS YOUR IDENTITY STOLEN? WHAT TO DO IN THE FIRST 24 HOURS
A free credit freeze can make it harder for criminals to open new accounts in your name, but it won't stop every type of identity theft. (Danylo Antoniuk/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
What to do during the first week after a breach
You don't need to spend the entire week worrying about what might happen. However, you should address the most serious risks right away.

On the first day, verify the breach notice through an official source. Secure any compromised accounts and change exposed or reused passwords. If your Social Security number was involved, consider freezing your credit immediately.Next, review your credit reports and look for accounts or inquiries you don't recognize.During the rest of the week, check your bank transactions, payment accounts and mobile phone account for unusual activity. Enable available security alerts and continue monitoring for suspicious changes.

On the first day, verify the breach notice through an official source. Secure any compromised accounts and change exposed or reused passwords. If your Social Security number was involved, consider freezing your credit immediately.
Next, review your credit reports and look for accounts or inquiries you don't recognize.

During the rest of the week, check your bank transactions, payment accounts and mobile phone account for unusual activity. Enable available security alerts and continue monitoring for suspicious changes.

Also, watch out for follow-up scams. Criminals sometimes use major data breaches as an excuse to contact people with fake monitoring offers or recovery services. They may ask for your Social Security number, passwords or payment information. Don't trust a caller simply because they know details about the breach. Instead, verify offers by going directly to the affected company's official website.
A simple decision guide
Here's the easiest way to think about these protections.

Choose a credit freeze when your priority is making it harder for someone to open new credit in your name. You can temporarily lift it when needed.Choose a fraud alert when you want lenders to verify your identity more carefully but prefer to keep your credit file accessible.Choose identity monitoring when you want notifications about certain suspicious changes and additional visibility into potential misuse of your information.
Choose a credit freeze when your priority is making it harder for someone to open new credit in your name. You can temporarily lift it when needed.
Choose a fraud alert when you want lenders to verify your identity more carefully but prefer to keep your credit file accessible.
Choose identity monitoring when you want notifications about certain suspicious changes and additional visibility into potential misuse of your information.

You can use more than one tool. In fact, a credit freeze and monitoring service can complement each other. Just remember that none of these options replaces contacting your bank, creditor or service provider when fraud has already occurred.
When identity monitoring can complement a credit freeze

A credit freeze makes it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts in your name, but it won't alert you to every suspicious change involving your personal information. An identity monitoring service can complement that protection by watching for certain warning signs.

Depending on the plan, you may also have access to identity restoration specialists who can help you navigate disputes, documentation and recovery after identity theft. Neither tool guarantees complete protection, but together they can help you prevent certain problems and respond more quickly when suspicious activity appears.
Not all monitoring services offer the same protections. Before choosing one, consider these features:

Credit monitoring: Alerts you to certain changes in your credit reports, including new accounts and suspicious inquiries.Financial account monitoring: Watches for certain unusual activity involving eligible linked bank or financial accounts.Dark web monitoring: Looks for exposed personal information in certain known data breaches and dark web sources.Identity restoration assistance: Provides professional guidance to help you recover if someone steals your identity.Identity theft expense coverage: Some plans provide reimbursement for eligible recovery expenses or stolen funds, subject to plan terms, coverage limits and exclusions. Coverage varies and may not apply to every type of loss.
Credit monitoring: Alerts you to certain changes in your credit reports, including new accounts and suspicious inquiries.
Financial account monitoring: Watches for certain unusual activity involving eligible linked bank or financial accounts.
Dark web monitoring: Looks for exposed personal information in certain known data breaches and dark web sources.
Identity restoration assistance: Provides professional guidance to help you recover if someone steals your identity.

Identity theft expense coverage: Some plans provide reimbursement for eligible recovery expenses or stolen funds, subject to plan terms, coverage limits and exclusions. Coverage varies and may not apply to every type of loss.

Keep in mind that identity monitoring cannot prevent every form of fraud or guarantee that suspicious activity will always be detected. You'll still need to contact your bank, credit card company or other affected institution directly if you discover unauthorized activity.

The bottom line: A credit freeze can help prevent someone from opening new credit accounts, while identity monitoring can help you spot certain warning signs sooner. Using both can give you broader protection and make it easier to respond when something goes wrong.

Ask one question first: am I trying to block new credit, receive an early warning or recover from confirmed fraud? A freeze focuses on blocking access, a fraud alert adds verification and monitoring provides visibility. You may use more than one, but you do not need to activate every tool simply because a breach occurred.
9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE
Fraud alerts require lenders to take additional steps to verify your identity, while credit freezes restrict access to your credit report. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

One thing I've noticed about data breaches is that most people don't realize how vulnerable their personal information can be until something goes wrong. And by then, the damage may already be done. That's why I think it's smart to be proactive. A free credit freeze is a great place to start, but it only protects one part of your financial life.

What I like about an identity protection service is that it adds another layer of protection by monitoring for suspicious activity that you might otherwise miss. And if someone does steal your identity, having access to restoration specialists can make a stressful situation easier to manage. No service can stop every scam, but having someone watching for warning signs and helping you respond can make a real difference. For me, it's about getting ahead of the problem rather than finding out about it after the damage is done.

title: OpenAI child safety tools target AI-generated abuse
summary: OpenAI's new classifier flags 48% fewer images for review while detecting similar levels of CSAM, and ChatGPT now suspends users for 24 hours.
story: OpenAI's new ChatGPT warnings explain why child sexual abuse material is prohibited and show a 24-hour account suspension for flagged activity. (OpenAI)

A teenager posts a perfectly innocent photo online. Before long, someone uses artificial intelligence to turn it into a sexually explicit fake and shares it with classmates. It's disturbing to think that something as simple as sharing a photo could lead to this kind of abuse. And for the child involved, the damage can last long after the fake picture gets taken down.

Now OpenAI is stepping up its efforts to tackle the problem. The company is introducing a new AI tool designed to detect suspected child sexual abuse material, including content created with artificial intelligence. It's also cracking down on attempts to find abusive material through ChatGPT, with new warnings and 24-hour suspensions. Here's a closer look at what's changing and what parents need to know.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. No technical experience is needed.

ROBLOX SHARES AI CHILD-SAFETY TOOLS PARENTS SHOULD KNOW
How OpenAI's new child safety tool works

Finding child sexual abuse material online has become more complicated as AI-generated content spreads. Many existing detection systems use digital fingerprints, called hashes, to recognize previously identified abusive files. However, newly created material may have no matching fingerprint. OpenAI's new classifier examines visual signs of potential child sexual abuse material, also known as CSAM. That allows it to flag suspected abuse even when the content has never been identified before.

The system assigns scores to potentially abusive pictures so human reviewers can decide which cases need attention first. OpenAI says it developed and evaluated the technology with help from the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) at missingkids.org/. The company is offering the classifier at no cost to vetted organizations through its API. That could give smaller child protection teams access to detection technology they otherwise couldn't afford.
Early testing shows fewer false alarms

OpenAI says its early testing produced encouraging results. In an evaluation involving pictures uploaded to its systems, the company compared the new classifier with its existing protections. The findings suggest the new tool could flag 48% fewer pictures for review while detecting roughly the same amount of abusive material. Pictures flagged by the new classifier were also about twice as likely to contain abuse.

Outside organizations reported additional results. AI platform Fal said its reviewers confirmed 72% of high-confidence flags as previously unidentified CSAM. Meanwhile, SafetyKit reported that the classifier detected 90% of cases involving drawings or animations that sexualize children in its evaluation. These results come from OpenAI and participating organizations. Independent testing will help determine how reliably the technology performs across different platforms.
INSTAGRAM'S AI MAY CATCH TEENS LYING ABOUT THEIR AGE
ChatGPT adds warnings and 24-hour suspensions

OpenAI is also changing how ChatGPT responds when someone attempts to find child sexual abuse material. New warnings will interrupt those attempts and explain the harm caused by sexualizing children. The warnings specifically address AI-generated material, which can cause serious harm even when a picture has been digitally fabricated. Along with displaying a warning, OpenAI says it will remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours. The warning will also direct the person toward specialist support designed to help prevent harmful behavior.

Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions or permanent account closure. OpenAI says they could also result in reports to authorities. The new warnings focus on attempts to find abusive material. Under its existing policies, OpenAI says it bans accounts and reports attempts to generate or upload CSAM to NCMEC. The company developed the warnings with input from child protection organizations and researchers who study ways to interrupt harmful online behavior. However, whether these interventions prevent future abuse will require continued evaluation.
OpenAI is introducing stronger ChatGPT safeguards to interrupt attempts to find child sexual abuse material and discourage further violations. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
OpenAI gives investigators new tools to fight child exploitation

OpenAI is expanding its work with organizations investigating online child exploitation. The company says it has begun participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program, which allows organizations to share information about suspected exploitation across platforms. It's also introducing specialized AI tools and training for child safety law enforcement units. The first investigative tool will help authorized teams review lengthy chat logs and records obtained through legal processes. Investigators can use it to identify potential connections and organize timelines, with findings linked to source material. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. OpenAI is also publishing guidance to help developers detect suspected abuse and establish procedures for reviewing potentially harmful content.
IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT?
How to help protect your child from AI-generated abuse
You can't control every way someone might misuse a child's photo. However, a few steps can help families reduce exposure and respond if something happens.

Talk about AI-generated fakes. Explain that someone can manipulate an innocent photo into something inappropriate. Encourage your child to tell you immediately if they discover a fake picture involving themselves or a classmate.Review social media privacy settings. Make your child's accounts private when possible and check who can see their photos. Remind family members to ask before posting pictures of children publicly.Report suspected abusive material. Contact the platform and NCMEC's CyberTipline at missingkids.org/gethelpnow/cybertipline. Avoid downloading, screenshotting or forwarding suspected abusive content, even when your intention is to report it.Know about Take It Down. NCMEC offers a free service called Take It Down at takeitdown.ncmec.org that can help limit the spread of eligible nude or sexually explicit pictures and videos involving someone under 18. The service also supports AI-generated content. It creates a digital fingerprint from a file already on your device without uploading the original. It works with participating platforms, so removal everywhere cannot be guaranteed. Never download abusive content to use the service.

Talk about AI-generated fakes. Explain that someone can manipulate an innocent photo into something inappropriate. Encourage your child to tell you immediately if they discover a fake picture involving themselves or a classmate.
Review social media privacy settings. Make your child's accounts private when possible and check who can see their photos. Remind family members to ask before posting pictures of children publicly.

Report suspected abusive material. Contact the platform and NCMEC's CyberTipline at missingkids.org/gethelpnow/cybertipline. Avoid downloading, screenshotting or forwarding suspected abusive content, even when your intention is to report it.

NCMEC offers a free service called Take It Down at takeitdown.ncmec.org that can help limit the spread of eligible nude or sexually explicit pictures and videos involving someone under 18. The service also supports AI-generated content. It creates a digital fingerprint from a file already on your device without uploading the original. It works with participating platforms, so removal everywhere cannot be guaranteed. Never download abusive content to use the service.
Most importantly, make sure children know they can come to you without automatically losing access to their devices. That conversation may help them speak up before harmful content spreads further.
HAWLEY CHAMPIONS GUARD ACT AS HEARTBROKEN FAMILIES SAY AI CHATBOTS ALLEGEDLY PUSHED TEENS TO SELF-HARM
OpenAI is expanding its efforts to combat AI-generated child sexual abuse material and protect children online. (Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
What this means to you

If you're a parent or grandparent, these developments could help improve protection against AI-generated child sexual abuse material. However, the new classifier works behind the scenes. Its impact will depend on how widely organizations adopt it and how effectively their safety teams respond to warnings.

The scale of the problem is alarming. According to NCMEC, its CyberTipline received more than 400,000 reports involving generative AI in 2025. These reports cover several categories of AI-related child exploitation, although not all involved the creation or sharing of AI-generated abuse material.
Kurt's key takeaways

I'm glad to see OpenAI making this detection technology available to vetted organizations for free. The early results are encouraging, especially if investigators can spend less time reviewing false alarms and more time identifying children who need help. I also support putting consequences behind ChatGPT's warnings. A 24-hour suspension sends a stronger message than simply telling someone their request violates the rules. We've already seen how AI-generated content can be used to harm children, and technology companies need to stay ahead of those who misuse their tools. OpenAI is taking steps in the right direction, and I hope other AI companies follow its lead.

title: AI mosquito trap targets deadly dengue outbreak
summary: USF researchers built an AI mosquito trap with over 98% accuracy as Florida battles its largest dengue outbreak in decades with 524 local cases.
story: Florida is combatting its largest dengue fever outbreak in decades, with over 290 locally acquired cases reported. Former CDC Director Dr. Robert Redfield breaks down the risks of transmission and essential prevention measures. Meanwhile, Hillsborough County mosquito management teams deploy aerial spraying to target the mosquitoes carrying the virus.

You probably aren't thinking much about mosquitoes in November. In much of the country, cooler weather has sent those annoying little bloodsuckers into hiding. But in Florida, mosquitoes are still causing serious trouble. The state is dealing with its largest dengue outbreak in decades, and hundreds of people have caught the virus without leaving the state.

Now, researchers at the University of South Florida have developed an AI mosquito trap that could help health officials find dangerous mosquito species much faster. It can identify mosquito species with more than 98% accuracy in laboratory testing. And with dengue still spreading in Florida, the timing couldn't be more important.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE
The Digitomy AI mosquito trap uses built-in cameras and artificial intelligence to identify mosquito species that can spread diseases like dengue. (University of South Florida)
Why Florida's dengue outbreak is making headlines now

If you thought mosquito season ended when summer did, Florida has a different story to tell. According to the Florida Department of Health's latest available weekly surveillance report, Hillsborough County has recorded 407 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, the county's largest outbreak on record. Across Florida, health officials have reported 524 locally acquired cases through October 31. That means people contracted the virus from mosquitoes in the area rather than while traveling overseas.

The Tampa area has been hit especially hard. In October, the Florida Department of Health confirmed that Hillsborough County was still responding to an ongoing dengue outbreak. Dengue can cause high fever, severe headaches and intense muscle pain. In serious cases, it can lead to life-threatening complications. Health officials continue to encourage residents to take precautions against mosquito bites.

On November 13, Hillsborough County announced that it had extended its state of local emergency through November 19 as mosquito control crews increased aerial and ground treatments to help contain the outbreak. County officials say mosquito surveillance continues to detect dengue virus activity in neighborhoods across the area.

And here's why we're talking about this in November. While mosquitoes have largely disappeared from colder parts of the country, they can remain active in warmer states. Florida's outbreak shows that the threat doesn't disappear simply because summer is over. Meanwhile, a new generation of technology could give communities a better way to respond before mosquito populations get out of control.
How the new AI mosquito trap works

The technology comes from Digitomy, a startup founded by researchers at the University of South Florida. Associate Professor Ryan Carney and Professor Sriram Chellappan have been developing the system through research dating back to 2018. Their goal is to help mosquito control teams identify the insects they're catching without spending days examining them under a microscope.

The trap itself looks fairly straightforward. Workers can hang it from a low tree branch or place it on the ground. A light or bait attracts mosquitoes, and a small fan pulls them inside. Once the insects land on a sticky pad, two built-in cameras photograph them. Artificial intelligence then compares those images against a large database to determine which mosquito species have been captured.

But the technology goes further. It can also identify whether a mosquito is male or female and whether it has recently fed on blood. That's useful information because female mosquitoes bite people and can transmit diseases. The researchers say their system achieved more than 98% accuracy in identifying mosquito species during laboratory testing.
GOOGLE WANTS TO RELEASE MILLIONS OF MOSQUITOES
A researcher displays mosquitoes collected by the smart trap, which uses AI to identify potentially dangerous species much faster than traditional methods. (University of South Florida)
Why identifying mosquitoes faster could save lives

Traditional mosquito surveillance can take two to three days because specialists often need to examine captured insects under a microscope. That's valuable work, but when health officials are trying to track a disease outbreak, waiting several days can slow their response. Digitomy wants to shorten that process dramatically. Its system uses AI and cloud computing with the goal of identifying captured mosquito species the same day. That could help mosquito control teams see where potentially dangerous species are appearing and decide where to concentrate their efforts.

This is especially important with Aedes aegypti, the mosquito species primarily responsible for spreading dengue in Florida. There are roughly 3,500 mosquito species worldwide, but only certain species spread particular diseases. Knowing which ones are present can help officials make better decisions. There's one important point to understand. The trap identifies mosquito species capable of carrying disease. It does not automatically prove that a captured mosquito is infected with dengue. Health officials would still need laboratory testing to confirm the presence of the virus.
AI mosquito traps could create an early warning system

What I find particularly interesting is what happens after the trap identifies a mosquito. Digitomy can send that information to a mapping dashboard, allowing mosquito control teams to see where certain species are appearing. The goal is to give mosquito control teams access to that information the same day, helping them identify where potentially dangerous species are appearing. Think about how useful that could be during an outbreak. If several traps begin detecting more Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in one neighborhood, officials could investigate that area and consider targeted mosquito control measures. Instead of waiting for more people to become sick, they could use surveillance data to guide their response.

The researchers have already integrated trap information into a private layer of their Global Mosquito Observations Dashboard at mosquitodashboard.org/. That system also incorporates more than half a million citizen science reports. The idea is to combine information from automated traps with observations from people who help track mosquitoes. Digitomy's technology could also complement an existing early warning system developed by Carney for dengue and West Nile virus. Together, these tools could give public health departments a clearer view of mosquito activity across communities. Of course, detecting mosquitoes early doesn't guarantee that an outbreak can be prevented. But faster information could help officials respond sooner, particularly in areas where mosquito control resources are limited.
When could communities start using these smart traps?

Digitomy has already tested its technology at the University of South Florida and worked with the Anastasia Mosquito Control District in St. Johns County, which includes St. Augustine. The researchers are also preparing for field validation with Hillsborough County, where Florida's dengue outbreak has been especially severe. The startup is working with USF's Technology Transfer office to license the AI identification system to established mosquito trap manufacturers. That could allow companies to add the technology to equipment they already produce.

Digitomy is working toward commercial availability by licensing its AI technology to established mosquito trap manufacturers. For now, the university has not announced a consumer launch date or retail price. The company also received a $25,000 grant from the USF Research Foundation's Bull Ring Accelerator during summer 2026. The funding is intended to help accelerate the licensing and commercialization of university-developed technology. The team is also developing an online education platform that would allow mosquito control professionals and the public to practice identifying mosquito species using images and AI-generated feedback.
THIRD PERSON DIES AFTER MOSQUITO IS REPORTEDLY TRAPPED ON PLANE TO GERMANY IN 'AIRPORT MALARIA' PHENOMENON

Researchers test the AI-powered mosquito trap in a controlled environment as they work to improve mosquito surveillance and help communities respond faster to disease threats. (University of South Florida)
What this AI mosquito trap means for you

You probably won't be hanging a Digitomy trap in your backyard anytime soon. But that doesn't mean this technology couldn't eventually affect your community. If mosquito control departments adopt smarter surveillance systems, they may be able to identify dangerous mosquito populations sooner and make better decisions about where to intervene. And even though we're heading into November, people living in warmer areas still need to pay attention to mosquito activity. If you're traveling to Florida or another place where mosquitoes remain active, taking precautions is important.

For now, the best protection is still fairly simple. Empty standing water from flowerpots and other outdoor containers because mosquitoes can breed in surprisingly small amounts of water. Use an EPA-registered insect repellent when spending time outdoors. Wearing long sleeves and pants can also help reduce exposed skin. We've covered some useful products that can help keep mosquitoes away, including repellents and outdoor gadgets.
You can find them in our guide to mosquito and tick repellents at CyberGuy.com
Kurt's key takeaways

I think this is one of those uses of AI that could make a real difference in people's lives. Most of us see mosquitoes as an annoying part of summer. But Florida's dengue outbreak is a reminder that these tiny insects can cause serious health problems, even late in the year. What interests me about Digitomy is the possibility of giving mosquito control teams information while they still have time to act. The technology looks promising, especially with its reported accuracy in laboratory testing. But I want to see how it performs in real-world conditions before calling it a breakthrough. If it works as researchers hope, communities could have a valuable new tool to help protect people from mosquito-borne diseases. And that's a use of AI I can get behind.

title: Fake AI event invites target Microsoft and Google logins
summary: Fake OpenAI event pages promise free ChatGPT Pro subscriptions, then trick employees into handing over Microsoft and Google account credentials.
story: Google General Counsel Halimah Delaine Prado joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail how Google is fighting AI-powered phishing scams.

An invitation to an exclusive OpenAI event lands in your inbox. It promises a look at the latest AI tools and even offers three months of ChatGPT Pro for free. All you have to do is register using your work account. Sounds like a pretty good deal, right? Well, before you click that registration button, there's something you should know. Cybercriminals are using fake AI event invitations to trick employees into giving them access to their Microsoft and Google accounts. And some of these attacks can get past the extra security checks many of us rely on.

According to a new report from Push Security, attackers have created convincing event registration pages impersonating OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic. Push Security says it detected and blocked visits to the malicious event registration pages on its customers' browsers in late October 2026. The concerning part is how easily an invitation that appears legitimate can lead to someone handing over access to their work account. Here's what researchers discovered and how to protect yourself.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN

Cybercriminals are impersonating OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic with fake AI event invitations designed to steal employees’ Microsoft and Google login credentials. (Tristan Spinski for The Washington Post via Getty Images)
Fake AI event invites promise free access to premium tools

The attackers are taking advantage of the growing interest in artificial intelligence. After all, plenty of employees want to learn how AI can make their jobs easier. A free premium subscription could be enough to get someone's attention. The phishing pages discovered by Push Security promote events that appear to come from recognizable technology companies. One fake OpenAI event advertised a November 4 livestream called "ChatGPT for Social & Digital Marketing Teams." The registration page promised three months of ChatGPT Pro to participants. Another page promoted an invitation-only SpaceX briefing scheduled for November 12. Visitors could supposedly choose between three months of Grok Heavy or a "SpaceX share."

Researchers also identified a phishing page impersonating an Anthropic event at AWS re 2026. That page was no longer active when they investigated it. These pages impersonated legitimate technology companies, and the advertised rewards were part of the phishing scheme. Push Security did not suggest that OpenAI, SpaceX or Anthropic operated these fraudulent events. And here's where things get especially concerning. The fake websites tell visitors they must sign in using their corporate Microsoft or Google accounts to complete registration and claim the promised rewards. That request opens the door to the phishing attack.
How fake AI event invitations trick employees

The criminals have put considerable effort into making these invitations appear credible. Rather than sending people directly to an obvious phishing website, they use familiar online services to help disguise where the links lead. Push Security found that the campaign routed visitors through shortened links associated with Google and Zapier. Earlier related attacks also used legitimate Zoom event pages and GoTo Webinar's email infrastructure. As a result, someone checking an invitation might see a familiar service before reaching the malicious registration page. Researchers have not confirmed the initial delivery method for every invitation in the newer campaign.

Once someone reaches the suspicious site, another familiar feature appears. A Cloudflare security challenge asks visitors to confirm they are human. You have probably encountered similar checks while shopping or visiting legitimate websites. However, criminals can use them too. In this campaign, the challenge also made it harder for automated security scanners to examine the malicious pages. After completing the check, visitors arrive at what looks like a professional event registration website. They're presented with two familiar buttons: "Continue with Microsoft" and "Continue with Google." Depending on which button someone selects, the attackers launch a different method designed to capture access to that account.
How hackers target Microsoft accounts without a password

This is where the attack gets clever. If someone selects "Continue with Microsoft," the phishing website connects to a service called Kali365. It's a phishing-as-a-service platform that criminals can use to carry out account attacks. Kali365 generates a Microsoft device authentication code. The fake registration page then instructs the visitor to copy that code and enter it on Microsoft's legitimate sign-in website.

Now, here's why that can fool someone. Microsoft's device authentication process is real. You may have used something similar when connecting a streaming device to an account. However, the attacker started this authentication request. When the victim enters the supplied code and approves the sign-in, Microsoft can issue authentication tokens to the attacker's session.

Those tokens may provide access to Microsoft 365 resources without the attacker needing the account password. And the attack may continue from there. Push Security found that the campaign redirects Microsoft users to another phishing service called VoidProxy after the device code step. That second stage attempts to capture their password and authenticated session cookie. A successful compromise could expose company email or documents stored in Microsoft 365. Other connected workplace applications may also be at risk, depending on the permissions and access associated with the compromised account.
How the Google phishing attack steals login sessions

The Google option takes another approach. When visitors click "Continue with Google," the phishing page opens a pop-up that appears to contain Google's familiar sign-in screen. However, that login process runs through VoidProxy, which acts as an intermediary between the person signing in and Google's actual authentication service.

As someone enters their credentials, the phishing service can capture the information. It can also intercept certain multifactor authentication responses and steal session cookies. So, what exactly is a session cookie? Think of it as a digital pass that helps a website remember you've already signed in. Once your identity has been verified, that cookie can allow you to continue using your account without entering your password on every page.

If a criminal obtains a usable session cookie, they may be able to reuse that authenticated session and gain access without completing the usual login process again. That's why these attacks are particularly dangerous for people who believe that enabling multifactor authentication automatically protects them from every account takeover attempt. It's important to note that Push Security documented the malicious infrastructure and blocked visits to the phishing pages. Its report did not establish how many accounts, if any, were successfully compromised through this campaign.
HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS
A convincing Google sign-in window appears over a fraudulent SpaceX event page, allowing attackers to capture login credentials and authentication sessions. (Push Security)
Why these fake AI event scams are difficult to spot

The attackers are combining two phishing services behind the same registration pages. Kali365 targets Microsoft's device authentication process, while VoidProxy targets authenticated login sessions. Meanwhile, the fake event websites borrow the appearance of familiar brands. The criminals can also change their websites and event themes as older pages get discovered. Researchers also discovered that the fraudulent registration pages could automatically display content in a visitor's language. That allowed the attackers to adapt the same phishing campaign for people in different regions without creating entirely new websites. Push Security identified two phishing kits used to create the fake event pages. The researchers call them ZoomMock and MSDRoot. They found evidence suggesting the same operators were responsible for both kits, although the connection was not conclusively established.

Researchers also found no evidence linking the developers of Kali365 and VoidProxy. Instead, they believe the attackers behind the event campaign are customers of both phishing services. The result is an attack that can appear credible at several points. A shortened link may use a recognized service. A security challenge can look legitimate. Even the Microsoft authentication page can be genuine. For employees who regularly attend virtual meetings or participate in industry webinars, that familiarity could make the scam harder to recognize.

In response to our request for comment, a Microsoft spokesperson said, "We take reports of malicious online activity seriously and continuously work to help protect our customers from evolving threats. Microsoft Defender includes detections to block the threats identified in the report."
We also reached out to Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX for comment but did not receive responses before our deadline.
How to protect yourself from fake AI event phishing scams
A few careful habits can significantly reduce your chances of falling for these attacks. Here's how to protect yourself.

If you receive an unexpected invitation from OpenAI, SpaceX or another technology company, take a moment to check whether the event actually exists. Open a new browser tab and visit the organization's official website yourself. Look for the event through its verified channels. If necessary, contact the organizer using information obtained independently of the invitation. Be especially careful when an unfamiliar event requests your corporate account credentials.

An invitation promising premium AI access may sound appealing, especially when the offer appears to come from a respected technology company. However, the promise of something valuable can encourage people to act before checking the details. If registration requires you to sign in with a work account to receive a reward, verify the offer independently before proceeding.

This is one of the most important lessons from the campaign. If a website asks you to copy a device authentication code and enter it on a Microsoft page, consider whether you initiated a legitimate device sign-in. If you were simply registering for a webinar, that unexpected device code request should raise concerns. Even a legitimate Microsoft authentication webpage can become part of a phishing attack when criminals trick you into approving their request. Pay attention to any Microsoft sign-in prompt asking you to approve access. Even if the website address is legitimate, you could be authorizing a session started by a criminal.
THE BEST DEFENSE AGAINST HIGH-TECH AI SCAMS IS LOW-TECH SKEPTICISM, EXPERT WARNS

Hackers are using fraudulent AI event registration pages promising free ChatGPT Pro subscriptions and exclusive access to trick employees into compromising their work accounts. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)

Before entering account credentials, examine the website address and consider how you arrived there. A page displaying familiar branding may still belong to a criminal. Shortened links can also conceal the final destination. Whenever possible, open Microsoft or Google directly through a trusted bookmark or the official website. Remember that a padlock icon and HTTPS connection do not guarantee that a website is trustworthy.

Continue using multifactor authentication, even though some phishing attacks can defeat certain forms of it. For stronger protection, consider phishing-resistant authentication, such as FIDO2 security keys or supported passkeys. These methods can help prevent attackers from stealing credentials through fraudulent login websites. While these methods offer stronger protection against phishing, they cannot guarantee protection if an attacker obtains a valid authenticated session through another method. However, no single security measure stops every possible attack. Organizations should also consider additional controls to protect authenticated sessions and reduce the risk of stolen tokens being reused. Microsoft recommends restricting device code authentication wherever it isn't necessary. IT administrators can apply those restrictions through Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies after reviewing legitimate business needs.

Strong antivirus software and browser protections can help identify suspicious links and dangerous websites before you interact with them. Look for protection that helps detect phishing pages and malicious downloads. Keep your browser and security tools updated so they can benefit from the latest available protections. However, remember that attackers frequently create new websites to evade detection. Security software can reduce your exposure, but it cannot guarantee that every fraudulent invitation will be blocked. What to do if you already clicked a fake AI event invitation
If you've already clicked on a suspicious event invitation, don't panic. What you do next depends on how far you got in the sign-in process. Here are the steps to take to protect your accounts.

Close the suspicious page. If you clicked the invitation but did not enter account details or approve a sign-in, close the website. Report the invitation through your organization's security reporting process.Contact your IT or security team immediately. If you entered your work credentials or approved a Microsoft device code, let your company's security team know right away.Explain exactly what happened. Tell your security team whether you entered a device code, submitted your password or completed a Google sign-in. These details can help them identify the attack.Secure your accounts. Your IT team may need to reset your password, revoke active sessions and authentication tokens, and investigate suspicious access to connected applications.Don't assume changing your password fixes everything. Attackers may already have a valid authentication token or session cookie. Even after sessions are revoked, some access tokens may remain valid until they expire.

Close the suspicious page. If you clicked the invitation but did not enter account details or approve a sign-in, close the website. Report the invitation through your organization's security reporting process.
Contact your IT or security team immediately. If you entered your work credentials or approved a Microsoft device code, let your company's security team know right away.
Explain exactly what happened. Tell your security team whether you entered a device code, submitted your password or completed a Google sign-in. These details can help them identify the attack.
Secure your accounts. Your IT team may need to reset your password, revoke active sessions and authentication tokens, and investigate suspicious access to connected applications.

Don't assume changing your password fixes everything. Attackers may already have a valid authentication token or session cookie. Even after sessions are revoked, some access tokens may remain valid until they expire.
The sooner you report suspicious activity, the better the chances of stopping unauthorized access before more damage occurs.
Kurt's key takeaways

Criminals know people are eager to keep up with AI, and they're using that interest to make their scams more convincing. An invitation offering free ChatGPT Pro or access to an exclusive event sounds pretty tempting. But what really concerns me is that you can land on Microsoft's actual sign-in page and still give a hacker access to your account. Think about that. Even checking the website address may not be enough to protect you. So before you sign up for that next AI event, take a minute to make sure it's legitimate. I'd rather miss out on a free offer than hand a criminal access to my work account.

title: Ford privacy promise raises questions about your car data
summary: Ford's new privacy promise pledges not to sell driving data to insurers or brokers, but disabling connected car data sharing could cost you key features.
story: Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on Norway's confirmation that Chinese-owned rental cars recorded military data on 'Fox Report.'

Your car probably knows more about you than you realize. It can track where you drive, how fast you go and whether something under the hood needs attention. Depending on the vehicle, that information may also travel back to the manufacturer. And, chances are, you haven't spent much time thinking about who gets to see it.

Now, Ford wants to put those privacy concerns in the spotlight. On Nov. 2, the automaker announced a new Ford privacy promise designed to give drivers more transparency and control over their personal information. The company also says it won't sell data about how customers drive to insurance companies or data brokers.

That sounds encouraging. But there's a catch worth understanding. Turning off certain data-sharing settings could also mean losing some of the connected features you've come to rely on. So, how much privacy can you get without giving up the technology you paid for?
LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover five ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Ford's new privacy promise gives drivers more information about how their vehicles collect and share personal data, but disabling certain settings could limit connected features. (Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
What is Ford's new privacy promise?

Ford says its new privacy initiative will make it easier for drivers to understand what information their vehicles collect and how the company uses it. The automaker has also launched a dedicated data and privacy website where owners can learn about their options. The announcement centers on several commitments.

Ford says it designs its products with privacy in mind and wants customers to have clearer information about their choices. It also promises to respect the privacy settings drivers select. Perhaps the biggest commitment involves what happens to driving information. Ford specifically says it does not sell data about how customers drive to insurance companies or data brokers.

However, that promise does not mean Ford stops collecting connected vehicle data altogether. The company still uses information from equipped vehicles to operate services and improve its technology. Ford's chief privacy officer, Kristin Jones, explained to TechCrunch that the company wants to build greater trust by helping customers understand its data practices.

The effort comes as Ford prepares to introduce more connected vehicles, including models built on its upcoming universal electric vehicle platform. Importantly, many of Ford's privacy controls already existed. The new initiative focuses on making those controls easier to understand and find.
What information can your Ford collect?
Modern Ford vehicles can generate a surprising amount of information. Exactly what gets collected depends on your model, its connected features and the privacy settings you select.
For example, Ford says equipped connected vehicles may share information about:

Vehicle location: Precise location information that can support navigation and roadside assistance.Driving behavior: Information about speed, braking and how the vehicle is operated.Vehicle health: Diagnostic information, including tire pressure, fuel levels and possible mechanical problems.Vehicle identification: Details such as your vehicle identification number (VIN) and software information.
Vehicle location: Precise location information that can support navigation and roadside assistance.
Driving behavior: Information about speed, braking and how the vehicle is operated.
Vehicle health: Diagnostic information, including tire pressure, fuel levels and possible mechanical problems.
Vehicle identification: Details such as your vehicle identification number (VIN) and software information.

There are practical benefits to some of this sharing. Vehicle diagnostics can help identify maintenance problems earlier. Location information can support roadside assistance or help you find your parked car. Ford also says it may use connected vehicle data to improve future technologies.

With your consent, certain information can support personalization and relevant offers. Still, your driving habits can reveal personal details about your daily routine. That's why understanding which settings are enabled deserves your attention.
Why Ford's privacy promise comes at a critical time

Ford's announcement follows increased scrutiny of how automakers handle customer information. On Oct. 29, a coalition of 36 attorneys general announced a $220 million settlement with General Motors over allegations involving drivers' personal information. The states alleged that GM collected and sold driving behavior and location data to third parties, including data brokers that supplied information to insurance companies.

According to the state attorneys general, some insurers used that information when calculating insurance rates. The settlement requires GM to obtain affirmative, express consent before collecting or disclosing covered driving and location data.

GM previously discontinued its Smart Driver program. The case shows why vehicle privacy has become such a sensitive issue. Drivers may agree to connected features without fully understanding how much information those systems collect.

We've explored similar concerns in our CyberGuy article, "Is it worth saving money to let a car insurance company track your every move?" Insurance monitoring programs can offer savings, but drivers should understand what information they are agreeing to share. Against that backdrop, Ford's public commitment could help set expectations for how automakers handle sensitive driving information.
The privacy tradeoff that could affect your Ford's features

Ford says customers can turn off connected vehicle data sharing. However, doing so may affect some of the features that make newer vehicles convenient. Depending on your Ford model, equipment and which settings you disable, you could lose access to:

Remote start: Starting your vehicle through the Ford app.Connected navigation: Receiving real-time traffic information and other online navigation services.Vehicle location: Checking where your car is parked through the app.BlueCruise: Using Ford's available hands-free highway driving assistance system.Software updates: Receiving certain vehicle updates over the air.Connected roadside assistance: Accessing services that depend on a vehicle data connection or location sharing.
Remote start: Starting your vehicle through the Ford app.
Connected navigation: Receiving real-time traffic information and other online navigation services.
Vehicle location: Checking where your car is parked through the app.
BlueCruise: Using Ford's available hands-free highway driving assistance system.
Software updates: Receiving certain vehicle updates over the air.
Connected roadside assistance: Accessing services that depend on a vehicle data connection or location sharing.

The exact impact depends on which settings you disable and the technology installed in your vehicle. Turning off all vehicle connectivity can affect more features than changing individual data-sharing preferences. Some features can continue working even when connected vehicle data sharing is disabled. Ford says features such as Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility can continue working without sharing connected vehicle data with Ford. Local Bluetooth connections and regular radio playback can also remain available.

Of course, availability depends on your vehicle's equipment and software. Before turning anything off, check which services your particular Ford needs. Disabling one optional sharing preference does not automatically disable every connected feature. And remember, Apple CarPlay and Android Auto use smartphone technology. Your phone and its apps may have their own data collection settings that you'll want to review separately.
How to change your Ford's privacy settings

Ford gives owners several ways to review their data-sharing preferences. You can manage vehicle connectivity through the car's touchscreen. The Ford app and your online Ford account provide additional controls for certain uses of your information.
Start with the vehicle parked safely. Ford recommends that owners of vehicles built in 2018 or later review their connected vehicle settings.

On your vehicle's center touchscreen, open Settings.Look for Vehicle Connectivity or the available Privacy and Data Sharing settings.Review the available options for Vehicle Data, Driving Data and Vehicle Location.Turn off any optional sharing you do not want enabled.Read any warning that appears before confirming a change.
On your vehicle's center touchscreen, open Settings.
Look for Vehicle Connectivity or the available Privacy and Data Sharing settings.
Review the available options for Vehicle Data, Driving Data and Vehicle Location.
Turn off any optional sharing you do not want enabled.
Read any warning that appears before confirming a change.

Menu names and available controls vary by Ford model and infotainment system. If you want to stop sharing connected vehicle data with Ford, the company says to find Vehicle Connectivity in your vehicle's settings and turn it off. However, this broader change can limit connected services and other features. Ford provides additional guidance through its official privacy settings page.
GM WANTS DRIVERS TO TAKE THEIR EYES OFF THE ROAD BY 2028
Ford says it does not sell customers' driving behavior data to insurance companies or data brokers as it introduces a new vehicle privacy initiative. (John Keeble/Getty Images)
You can also adjust certain information-sharing preferences through the Ford app on your smartphone.

Open the Ford app.Tap the account icon on the home screen.Scroll to Settings and select Legal and privacy.Tap Privacy and data sharing.Select Set Preferences under Manage Data with Ford or Manage Data with Third Parties.Under Manage Data with Ford, review the available Personalization and Marketing settings for vehicle and driving data.Adjust the preferences you want to change.
Open the Ford app.
Tap the account icon on the home screen.
Scroll to Settings and select Legal and privacy.
Tap Privacy and data sharing.
Select Set Preferences under Manage Data with Ford or Manage Data with Third Parties.
Under Manage Data with Ford, review the available Personalization and Marketing settings for vehicle and driving data.
Adjust the preferences you want to change.

Ford also provides controls related to Google Maps in the app and certain preferred dealer notifications. Keep in mind that the app's personalization and marketing controls are separate from the vehicle's main connectivity controls. Changing one does not necessarily change the other. If you own more than one Ford, review each vehicle's settings separately.

You may also want to find out what personal information Ford already holds. The company provides options to request access to personal data and seek corrections or deletion, subject to applicable privacy laws and exceptions. You can find those options through Ford's privacy notice.

If you're selling or trading in your Ford, perform a factory reset to remove stored personal information from the vehicle. Ford says this can erase saved addresses, connected accounts and programmed garage door opener codes. You should also make sure the vehicle is disconnected from your Ford account. Depending on its connectivity equipment, you may need to remove the vehicle's VIN from your account as well. Simply deleting the Ford app will not stop vehicle data sharing. However, that reset will not erase data the company already received. Any request to delete that information must be handled separately.
Does Ford's promise mean your data stays completely private?

There's an important point worth keeping in mind. Ford's commitment about selling driving behavior data to brokers and insurers is specific. It does not prohibit every form of data collection or disclosure. Ford's privacy notice describes circumstances in which information may be shared with service providers or other parties. It also addresses disclosures made in response to valid legal requests.

Meanwhile, Ford offers personalization and marketing settings that deserve a separate review. And even though Ford says it doesn't sell driving behavior data to insurance companies, that doesn't mean an insurer can't collect information about how you drive through a separate smartphone app or a voluntary insurance monitoring program.

There are also exceptions to Ford's privacy controls. The company says it may collect vehicle location data in certain circumstances even when location sharing is turned off. These can include legal requirements, emergencies and protection of property. Vehicles equipped with the Ford Security Package may also share location information when a Theft Alert is triggered.

So even with Ford's new promise, I would still encourage drivers to examine their individual settings. A company can make a meaningful privacy commitment while continuing to collect information needed for its services. And if you're shopping for a new vehicle, consider privacy before making the purchase.
What this means to you

If you own a newer Ford, this announcement gives you a good reason to check your privacy settings. You may discover that your vehicle shares more information than you expected. You might also find settings you can disable without affecting the features you enjoy. However, you should understand the tradeoff before switching off all connectivity. Losing remote access or other useful services could be inconvenient, especially if you rely on them regularly.

The same advice applies if you drive another brand. Take a few minutes to find your manufacturer's privacy settings and learn what information your vehicle shares. You can explore the broader privacy concerns in our article, What your car knows about you and could be telling the world. Ultimately, knowing what your car collects gives you a better chance of controlling your personal information.
DATA BROKERS DON'T JUST COLLECT FACTS. THEY GUESS ABOUT YOU

Ford owners can adjust vehicle data-sharing settings to protect their privacy, though turning off connectivity may affect remote start, navigation and other features. (Matthias Balk/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I like seeing Ford make a public commitment about protecting driving data. Especially after what we've learned about how vehicle information can end up in the hands of insurance companies. But here's what I keep coming back to. When you spend tens of thousands of dollars on a vehicle, how much of your personal information should you have to share to enjoy the features you already paid for? I understand why Ford needs certain data to make connected technology work. Real-time traffic updates can be useful.

So can getting an alert before a mechanical problem leaves you stranded. But I also think automakers need to make privacy choices much easier to understand. Drivers shouldn't have to dig through complicated menus to figure out what's happening with their information. Ford's promise is encouraging, and I hope other manufacturers pay attention. The real test will be how well these commitments hold up as vehicles become even more connected.

Would you sacrifice features like remote start or live navigation to keep your driving data private, or should automakers be required to offer those conveniences without collecting so much personal information? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

Forty years after their toddler vanished, a Southern California family is living a bizarre nightmare: a woman allegedly staking out their home claims to be their missing daughter, but refuses a basic ancestry DNA test unless it's a court-admissible lab procedure.

According to a recent report by the Los Angeles Times, the woman, legally named Cindy Rae Enders, won’t leave 83-year-old Mike Bradbury and his surviving daughter, Emily, alone. title: NYC Mayor Mamdani announces delayed plan to close city's largest jail
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani says his administration is closing Rikers Island for good, with four new jails by 2029 near public transit.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards hold a news conference outlining a five-year delay and revised strategy to shut down the notorious jail complex.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on X Friday, before holding a news conference on the issue, that he will be closing the city's largest jail at Rikers Island — but not until five years after the existing deadline.

"Our administration is closing Rikers Island, once and for all, and building a city where we ask ourseelves what a person needs, not just what they're accused of," Mamdani said in a video where he appears alongside Department of Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards, who said he had also once been an inmate there.

"We know that detaining more New Yorkers does not make us safer," Mamdani told reporters in a news briefing later Friday morning. He cited a dramatic decline in Big Apple murders between the 1990s and present day as evidence — from thousands to under 300 a year.

title: FBI arrests Georgia man accused of sending cryptocurrency to ISIS-linked individuals and groups
summary: Georgia man Younes Moustafa Younes faces federal charges for allegedly sending more than $26,000 to ISIS affiliates, the Department of Justice announced.
story: Georgia man faces federal charges after allegedly sending more than $26,000 to ISIS-linked individuals and groups, with FBI agents discovering damaged cellphones and shredded documents submerged in liquid during a search of his apartment.
A Georgia man is facing federal charges after allegedly sending more than $26,000 to individuals and groups affiliated with ISIS, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced.
Younes Moustafa Younes, 34, of Lavonia, Georgia, was charged with one count of international money laundering and one count of destruction of evidence, according to the DOJ.
Younes was arrested Nov. 18 and made his initial appearance Thursday in federal court.

Federal prosecutors allege Younes altered and destroyed evidence leading up to his arrest. During a search of his apartment, FBI agents discovered three cellphones submerged in an unknown solution, including one that had been smashed and another with its identification number removed, according to the criminal complaint.
FBI ARRESTS 3 MEN WHO ALLEGEDLY PLEDGED ALLEGIANCE TO ISIS, FUNDED DRONE ATTACKS TARGETING US TROOPS OVERSEAS

Investigators also found shredded documents submerged in an unknown solution inside a bathtub.

According to the complaint, Younes sent approximately $16,807 through cryptocurrency transactions between December 2025 and June 2026, using multiple phone numbers and accounts allegedly intended to conceal his identity.
Investigators say at least some of the funds were intended to support ISIS operations in Syria.
Prosecutors also allege that Younes sent approximately $9,206 through 11 cryptocurrency transactions between December 2021 and April 2022, using an alias to conceal his involvement.
NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS

The FBI first identified Younes in 2020 after he allegedly accessed ISIS propaganda online, according to the complaint.
During an interview with law enforcement, Younes acknowledged viewing the material but denied supporting extremist ideologies.
Prosecutors allege he later became increasingly radicalized, expressing support for ISIS and other terrorist figures through encrypted communications.
If convicted, Younes faces up to 20 years in federal prison on each charge, according to the Justice Department.
The international money laundering charge also carries a potential fine of up to $500,000, while the destruction of evidence charge carries a potential fine of up to $250,000.

story: Texas inmate Reinaldo Dennes repeatedly complained of severe pain during a lengthy lethal injection as prison staff struggled to establish IV access, while officials maintained that all execution procedures were followed.

A Texas inmate's execution lasted more than an hour Thursday as prison staff struggled to find suitable veins for a lethal injection, with the condemned man repeatedly complaining of severe pain before being pronounced dead.

Reinaldo Dennes, who was convicted of capital murder in the 1996 killing of Houston diamond dealer Janos Szucs, repeatedly cried out during the procedure at the state penitentiary in Huntsville, according to The Associated Press.
Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m., one minute after the procedure was completed.

The procedure lasted 63 minutes from the time Dennes was strapped to the gurney until its completion, as prison staff struggled to find suitable veins for the intravenous needles used to administer pentobarbital.
CHRISTA PIKE'S EXECUTION DOCTOR SAYS MISPLACED IV SENT LETHAL DRUGS INTO HER ARMS INSTEAD OF VEINS
Texas death row inmate Reinaldo Dennes was executed Thursday after a lengthy lethal injection procedure during which he repeatedly complained of pain. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP)

The execution comes amid renewed scrutiny of lethal injection procedures following a failed execution attempt in Tennessee in September involving death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her attorneys said did not properly enter her bloodstream, causing serious injuries.
Dennes repeatedly complained of pain after Thursday's procedure began, groaning and calling out to God, according to witnesses cited by the AP.
"The pain! Go! Go!" Dennes exclaimed.
"My right leg is killing me!" he later shouted, describing the sensation as a cramp.
"I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon," he added.
CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS
The state of Texas execution chamber in Huntsville, Texas, is seen on May 27, 2008. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP; AP Photo/Pat Sullivan)

Texas Department of Criminal Justice spokesperson Amanda Hernandez said all procedures were followed appropriately but acknowledged that staff made multiple unsuccessful attempts to establish IV access before placing needles in Dennes' left foot and the left side of his neck.
Hernandez said she did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but maintained that the locations ultimately used complied with the state's execution procedures.
She also suggested that Dennes may have exaggerated his discomfort, noting that he complained of pain before the drugs began flowing and in areas where no IV had been placed.
According to the AP, when asked whether Dennes was faking his pain, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."
INDIANA, FLORIDA AND ALABAMA CARRY OUT RARE US TRIPLE EXECUTION DAY

Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials defended the execution of Reinaldo Dennes, saying all procedures were followed appropriately despite his repeated complaints of pain. (Texas Department of Corrections/AFP via Getty Images)
"This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.

Dennes was the second person executed in the United States on Thursday, following Florida's execution of Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, who was convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion.
Overton's execution marked Florida's 20th of the year, a state record, according to the AP.
